topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Data-driven NLP and label dependence
topic_metadata.description: Modern NLP systems are primarily built on data-driven machine learning models whose performance critically depends on both the quality and quantity of labeled training data. Achieving high performance generally requires substantial supervised data, which is not always easy or cheap to obtain. This dependence motivates methods that can make more efficient use of scarce labels.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, sentences 1–4 ('The majority of modern natural language processing (NLP) systems...' to '...the available target training data.')

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Survey Literature Collection Methodology
topic_metadata.description: The authors explain their process for constructing the survey corpus of AL papers for NLP, beginning with a keyword search for 'active' in ACL Anthology titles. This initial set is refined through manual filtering, followed by iterative inclusion of relevant works missed by the keyword search and from other venues discovered via reference chasing. This process underpins the bibliometric counts and the coverage of the survey.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'In order to provide an NLP-specific AL survey,1 we start by searching the ACL Anthology...' through the sentence mentioning Appendix B

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Typical Active Learning Procedure Loop
topic_metadata.description: Algorithm 1 lays out a standard AL loop: initialize a seed labeled set from the unlabeled pool, train a model, repeatedly select informative instances, obtain annotations, update labeled and unlabeled sets, and retrain until a stopping criterion is met. The main components are the seeding strategy, model training routine, query function, annotation step, and stopping rule. This procedural decomposition structures the rest of the survey.
topic_metadata.text_span: Block labeled 'Algorithm 1 A typical active learning procedure' and its surrounding explanatory paragraph

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Informativeness-Based Query Strategies
topic_metadata.description: One core category of AL query strategies is based on informativeness, where instances are selected because the current model is uncertain about them or expects them to yield the largest performance gain. Metrics such as prediction entropy, margin, or expected error reduction typically operationalize informativeness. The survey devotes a subsection to categorizing and comparing such approaches in NLP.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point: 'In §2, we discuss the core aspect of AL: Query strategies, with a fine-grained categorization over informativeness (§2.1)...'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: AL for Structured Prediction in NLP
topic_metadata.description: The authors point out that applying AL to NLP must handle structured outputs such as sequences and trees, as found in tasks like parsing, sequence labeling, and machine translation. AL methods must therefore reason about informativeness at the level of structured instances or substructures, which complicates query design and uncertainty estimation. A dedicated subsection surveys these structured prediction–specific techniques.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point: 'In §3, we cover the two additional important topics... AL for structured prediction tasks (§3.1)...'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Active Learning with Advanced Learning Techniques
topic_metadata.description: The survey discusses integrating AL with advanced learning paradigms, particularly modern deep learning approaches. This includes using neural architectures, transfer learning, or semi-supervised techniques within the AL loop to better exploit both labeled and unlabeled data. A subsection surveys how these advanced methods interact with query strategies and model training dynamics.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point for §4, focusing on 'AL with advanced learning techniques (§4.2)' and earlier mention of 'deep active learning'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Initialization Strategies for Starting AL
topic_metadata.description: Starting active learning requires choosing an initial seed set from the unlabeled pool, which can affect convergence speed and stability. The survey identifies this as a distinct design choice, covering methods such as random seeding, diversity-based initialization, or heuristic selection to ensure a reasonable starting model. A subsection systematically reviews these initialization strategies.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point: 'In §5, we examine methods for starting (§5.1)...'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Output uncertainty and uncertainty sampling
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty sampling selects unlabeled instances for which a single model is most uncertain about its prediction. For probabilistic models, common measures include entropy, least-confidence, and margin sampling; for non-probabilistic models like SVMs, proximity to the decision boundary plays a similar role. These methods have been revisited for modern Transformer-based NLP systems as well.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.1.1, first half (discussion of entropy-based, least-confidence, margin, and SVM boundary-based methods)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Local region divergence for uncertainty
topic_metadata.description: Beyond raw output scores, uncertainty can be measured by how much a model’s predictions vary in an instance’s local neighborhood. If the instance is near a decision boundary, small changes (e.g., nearest-neighbor replacements, adversarial perturbations, or data augmentation) can cause divergent predictions, indicating high uncertainty. Recent work operationalizes this idea using nearest-neighbor search, adversarial attacks, and augmented variants of each instance.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.1.1, second half ('Another way to measure output uncertainty is to check the divergence of a model’s predictions...')

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Gradient-based expected gradient length querying
topic_metadata.description: Gradient-based strategies select instances expected to most strongly affect the model’s parameters, typically measured by the norm of the loss gradient. Since unlabeled instances lack gold labels, the loss and gradients are computed as expectations over possible labels, leading to the Expected Gradient Length (EGL) criterion. EGL has been applied to sequence labeling and speech recognition, with variants that focus specifically on embedding gradients in neural NLP models.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.1.3 (description of gradient information, EGL, and neural embedding-gradient variant)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Error and ambiguity-based performance predictors
topic_metadata.description: A simpler performance-oriented idea is to directly target instances that are currently erroneous or ambiguous for the task model. This can involve training an auxiliary model to predict instance-wise loss, judge correctness of predictions, or determine when expert querying is needed in structured prediction. Inspired by data maps, some methods look for instances with intermediate average correctness over training, and in machine translation, error-prone examples are identified via backward translation (round-trip consistency) or quality estimation models.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.1.4, later paragraphs (Yoo and Kweon; Wang et al.; Brantley et al.; Zhang and Plank; MT-specific techniques)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Density-based representativeness measures
topic_metadata.description: Density-based methods prioritize instances that lie in dense regions of the unlabeled data, so that labeled examples are representative rather than outliers. Simple proxies include n-gram or word-count statistics, while more general approaches compute each instance’s average similarity to all others. To reduce computational cost, k-nearest neighbor similarity is often used instead of full pairwise similarity over the pool.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.2.1 (density-based strategies, n-gram/word counts, average similarity, k-nearest neighbors)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Discriminative representativeness versus labeled data
topic_metadata.description: Discriminative strategies select unlabeled instances that differ most from the already labeled set, emphasizing coverage of novel features and domains. This can be operationalized with feature-based metrics such as unseen n-grams or out-of-vocabulary words, or via similarity scores that prefer instances dissimilar to labeled examples. More sophisticated methods explicitly train a classifier or adversarial model to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data, and in domain adaptation settings, domain separators serve a similar filtering role.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.2.2 (feature-based metrics, similarity to labeled set, discriminator and adversarial training, domain separators)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Greedy and clustering-based batch diversity
topic_metadata.description: Two main families of methods ensure batch diversity: greedy iterative selection and clustering-based selection. Iterative methods build batches step by step, each time choosing instances that are both useful and dissimilar from those already chosen, and can approximate advanced criteria like coresets or determinantal point processes. Clustering-based approaches partition the unlabeled pool into clusters and select representatives from different clusters, using similarities based on input features, learned representations, model-based similarity, gradients, or masked LM surprisal embeddings.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.2.3, middle and final paragraphs (iterative selection, clustering-based methods, coreset/DPP, similarity computation variants)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Static hybrid combinations of query criteria
topic_metadata.description: Hybrid strategies combine informativeness and representativeness into a single scoring function for each instance. Simple static combinations include weighted sums or multiplicative formulas that merge multiple criteria, such as uncertainty and density. These methods do not adapt during training but provide a straightforward way to balance competing objectives in query selection.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.3, first paragraph ('There is no surprise that informativeness and representativeness can be combined...')

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Integrated hybrids: clustering, gradients, and DPPs
topic_metadata.description: Some methods integrate multiple criteria more organically into a single selection mechanism. Examples include uncertainty-weighted clustering, where cluster selection is biased by instance uncertainty; diverse gradient selection, where gradient vectors encode both uncertainty and diversity; and DPP-based methods that factorize quality (e.g., informativeness) and diversity in a probabilistic selection model. These approaches jointly model what is informative and how to diversify the selected set.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.3, second paragraph (uncertainty-weighted clustering, diverse gradient selection, DPP with quality-diversity decomposition)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Multi-step and dynamic hybrid querying
topic_metadata.description: Multi-step querying applies different criteria in sequence, such as first filtering highly uncertain instances and then clustering them, or selecting the most uncertain instance within each cluster. Dynamic hybrids go further by changing the mixture of strategies over time, recognizing that representativeness may matter more in early AL stages while uncertainty becomes more reliable later. Methods like DUAL and GraDUAL formalize this by switching or interpolating between density-based and uncertainty-based selectors, and other work uses predefined monotonic functions to control combination weights throughout the AL process.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 2.3, remaining paragraphs (multi-step querying examples and dynamic combination: DUAL, GraDUAL, Wu et al.)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Active learning for structured prediction
topic_metadata.description: Many NLP tasks require predicting structured outputs (e.g., label sequences, parse trees) composed of interdependent variables, which complicates querying and annotation compared to flat classification. A central design decision is whether to query labels for entire structures or only for selected sub-structures. This choice affects how utilities, uncertainties, and annotation workflows are defined and computed.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening of §3.1 and transition to §§3.1.1–3.1.2 ('AL has been widely studied for classification tasks, while in NLP, many tasks involve structured prediction... One main decision is whether to annotate full structures... or allow the annotation of only partial structures').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Full-structure active learning utilities
topic_metadata.description: When querying full output structures, uncertainty-based strategies such as entropy must evaluate probabilities over an exponentially large output space. This is approximated using dynamic-programming algorithms for tree- and sequence-entropy, or via top-k approximations that treat k-best predicted structures as a proxy for the full space. These techniques adapt standard active learning criteria to settings where explicit enumeration of all structures is infeasible.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.1.1, first half ('Some uncertainty sampling strategies, such as entropy... algorithms for tree-entropy and sequence-entropy... Instead of considering the full output space, top-k approximation is a simpler alternative...').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Disagreement, length bias, and aggregation in full-structure AL
topic_metadata.description: For disagreement-based strategies in structured prediction, exact full-structure agreement is often too strict, so partial-disagreement measures and fine-grained scores (e.g., F1 for sequence labeling) are used. Because longer instances tend to appear more uncertain, length normalization is employed to mitigate length bias, though there is debate about whether long sequences should be discouraged. Utilities for a whole structure can also be built by aggregating token- or factor-level scores, using operations such as sums, averages, frequency-weighted sums, or selecting only the least-probable sub-structure.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.1.1, middle and end ('For disagreement-based strategies... F1 score for sequence labeling... length normalization... aggregation is also often utilized by gathering utilities of its sub-structures... summing or averaging the uncertainties of all the tokens... weighted sum by word frequency... using only the most uncertain one').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Coarser sub-structures and grouped queries
topic_metadata.description: Instead of querying the smallest possible units, many approaches select larger sub-structures (e.g., sub-sequences, head edges, neighborhood pools, phrases) to better align with how annotators read and to reduce context switching. Coarser granularity can alleviate the missed-class effect, where rare or difficult classes are overlooked when sampling too locally. Grouping strategies—such as first selecting uncertain sentences and then uncertain tokens within them, or choosing nearby instances sequentially—further streamline annotation and reduce cognitive load.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.1.2, middle ('At many times, choosing larger sub-structures is preferable... Typical examples of larger sub-structures include sub-sequences... head edges... neighborhood pools... mention-wise anaphoric links... phrases for MT... grouping queries can also help... two-stage selection of choosing uncertain tokens from uncertain sentences... selecting nearby instances in a row').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Computer-assisted and interactive annotation
topic_metadata.description: Direct cost reduction can be achieved by tighter model–annotator interaction, such as pre-annotation where models supply best or top-k predictions that annotators correct instead of labeling from scratch. This paradigm underlies post-editing in machine translation and has been shown effective when combined with AL. More interactive systems continuously propagate user corrections back into the model during annotation sessions—e.g., interactive machine translation where the system updates its prediction after each corrected character—thereby reducing human effort further; AL can be integrated into such systems to prioritize which segments to present. Crowdsourcing is highlighted as another complementary cost-reduction mechanism.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.2.3 ('In addition to better query strategies, there are other ways of directly reducing annotation cost, such as computer-assisted annotation... Pre-annotation... model’s best or top-k predictions... Post-editing for MT is also a typical example... interactive AL system where the user’s corrections can propagate to the model... Interactive machine translation (IMT)... AL has also been combined with IMT... Crowdsourcing is another way to reduce annotation costs').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Reducing wait time in active learning loops
topic_metadata.description: Active learning involves iterative cycles of training and querying that impose wait time on annotators, motivating methods to accelerate these stages. Query-time speedups include sub-sampling large unlabeled pools, caching invariant computations, and approximating densities or nearest neighbors with k-NN methods. For training, incremental warm-starting may seem natural but can harm neural performance, so full retraining is often preferred, sometimes paired with using a lightweight model for querying and a stronger model for final training. Additional reductions come from accepting stale model information via batch-mode AL and parallel AL architectures that decouple and continuously run annotation, training, and scoring processes.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.2.4 ('In AL iterations, the annotators may need to wait... To speed up querying, sub-sampling... pre-calculating and caching... approximation with k-nearest neighbours... To reduce training time... incremental training across AL iterations... warm-start may lead to sub-optimal performance... use an efficient model for querying and a more powerful model for final training... Another idea... querying with stale information... batch-mode AL... parallel AL, which maintains separate loops of annotating, training, and scoring').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Distilled and proxy models for querying
topic_metadata.description: To improve efficiency without sacrificing too much active learning performance, smaller distilled or proxy models can be used for query selection. Distillation compresses a large pre-trained model into a smaller one that approximates its behavior, enabling faster querying and shorter annotator wait time. Works cited show that these proxy models can be periodically synchronized with the main model via distillation, sometimes combined with pseudo-labeling and sub-sampling to further reduce computational cost.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 4.1, second paragraph (from 'For efficiency purposes, distillation...' through the discussion of Shelmanov et al., Tsvigun et al., and Nguyen et al.)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Pretraining and continual transfer in AL
topic_metadata.description: Transfer learning is integrated with active learning by initializing models from large pre-trained language models and further adapting them through continual training. Pretrained representations reduce the amount of task-specific annotation needed, while continual training allows incremental adaptation to new domains or tasks during the AL process. Meta-learning is also used to initialize models so they can learn effectively from small actively acquired datasets, and similar transfer ideas are applied to the model-based query policy itself.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 4.2, 'Transfer learning.' portion discussing pre-trained models, continual training, and meta-learning (from 'AL can be easily combined with transfer learning...' through 'Initializing the model via meta-learning has also been found helpful' and the sentence on query policy transfer)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Transductive, domain, and cross-lingual transfer
topic_metadata.description: Transductive learning within active learning transfers information from specific target unlabeled sets, such as other domains or languages, to reduce annotation needs. Methods leverage labeled or unlabeled data from related domains to guide selection and learning in the target domain, and similarly exploit cross-lingual signals when data in one language is scarce. This creates a multi-source scenario where active learning decisions and model updates are informed by heterogeneous but related data distributions.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 4.2, 'Transfer learning.' sentences on transductive learning and domain/language transfer (from 'Moreover, transductive learning is commonly combined with AL...' through the enumeration of domain and language transfer works)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Weak supervision integrated with active learning
topic_metadata.description: Weak supervision is combined with active learning by using imperfect or indirect supervision sources such as execution results, structure-based heuristics, gazetteers, and interactively discovered labeling rules. In this setting, actively selected instances may be labeled not only by humans but also by weak labeling functions or auxiliary resources, thereby reducing manual annotation effort. The section illustrates this with examples from semantic parsing, entity representation, sequence labeling, and rule-learning workflows.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 4.2, 'Weak supervision.' paragraph (from 'AL can also be combined with weakly supervised learning.' to the end of that paragraph)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Data augmentation and query synthesis in AL
topic_metadata.description: Data augmentation techniques are applied within active learning to expand training data and improve generalization, using methods such as iterative back-translation, mixup for sequence labeling, and phrase-to-sentence transformations for machine translation. Augmentation can also be tied directly to instance querying, where transformations inform which examples to select. An advanced variant, query synthesis, generates new synthetic instances for annotation instead of sampling from an existing pool, and has shown promise for simpler text classification scenarios despite the challenges of realistic text generation.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 4.2, 'Data augmentation.' paragraph (from 'Augmentation is also applicable in AL...' to the end of the section discussing query synthesis)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Random and representativeness-based seeding strategies
topic_metadata.description: Random sampling is widely used to initialize AL because it preserves the original data distribution and is simple to apply. More sophisticated representativeness-based strategies select instances near clustering centroids to obtain seed sets that are both representative and diverse. These seeding methods aim to provide a strong starting point before more complex query strategies are applied.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 5.1, part describing random sampling and representativeness-based querying (sentences beginning 'Random sampling is probably the most commonly utilized strategy...' through 'selecting points near the clustering centroids...').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Advanced models for AL initialization
topic_metadata.description: Advanced learning techniques can assist in selecting informative seed instances before standard AL cycles begin. These include transfer learning and unsupervised methods to capture structure in unlabeled data, as well as language-model-based approaches. Examples include selecting low-probability words for word sense disambiguation or choosing cluster centers using surprisal embeddings from pre-trained contextualized LMs.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 5.1, later part mentioning transfer learning, unsupervised methods, and language models (sentences starting 'Moreover, some advanced learning techniques...' through 'choose cluster centers with surprisal embeddings...').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Dataset choices for computing stopping metrics
topic_metadata.description: The dataset used to compute stopping metrics can significantly affect the stability and reliability of stopping decisions. Improperly chosen sets may lead to unstable measurements, motivating the use of a separate unlabeled dataset for monitoring. Since many stopping metrics do not require gold labels, this auxiliary dataset can be large to reduce variance, though increased size can also introduce practical concerns such as longer evaluation wait times.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 5.2, paragraph on the 'dataset' aspect (sentences starting 'The dataset to calculate the stopping metric requires careful choosing...' through 'though wait time would be another factor to consider in this case').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Curriculum learning integrated with AL
topic_metadata.description: Curriculum learning arranges training instances in a meaningful or progressively harder order, and can be combined with AL to guide which examples to query and when. This integration considers both informativeness (from AL) and pedagogical ordering (from curriculum learning) to improve training efficiency and model performance.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 7.1, sentences mentioning curriculum learning and its integration with AL

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Model efficiency and wait time in AL
topic_metadata.description: Model efficiency is emphasized as crucial in AL to reduce the annotator’s wait time between query selection and labeling. Because AL involves repeated retraining or updating models as new labels arrive, computational efficiency and system latency directly affect the practicality and user experience of AL systems.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 7.1, sentences on model efficiency and reducing wait time (§3.2.4)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Applying AL to complex NLP tasks
topic_metadata.description: The survey notes that AL has been used mainly for simple classification, while more complex tasks like text generation, NLI, and QA remain underexplored. These tasks involve richer outputs and more complex inputs, making unlabeled data collection and annotation harder, yet early work suggests AL can still aid data collection and model training for them.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 7.2, 'Complex tasks.' paragraph

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: AL beyond direct target labeling
topic_metadata.description: AL can query not only task labels but also auxiliary supervision such as features, rationales, explanations, evaluations, or symbolic rules. By selecting informative instances for these richer annotation types, AL can support tasks like feature labeling, rationale collection, explanation annotation, and rule discovery to enhance downstream models.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 7.2, 'Beyond direct target labeling.' paragraph

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Practical deployment challenges of AL
topic_metadata.description: Most AL research simulates annotation using existing labeled datasets, overlooking real-world issues like true annotation cost, efficiency and wait time, data reuse, and when to start or stop AL. In practice, AL processes are often non-repeatable, making the choice of query strategies and hyperparameters critical yet difficult, and addressing these challenges is key for wider industrial adoption.
topic_metadata.text_span: subsection 7.2, 'AL in practice.' paragraph

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Cross-domain transfer of AL methods
topic_metadata.description: The limitations section highlights that many AL techniques, particularly querying strategies developed in computer vision, may be transferable to NLP tasks. It advocates looking beyond NLP-specific work and leveraging insights and algorithms from other domains to improve AL for language applications.
topic_metadata.text_span: Limitations section, sentences on AL works in other fields and CV strategies for NLP

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Need for comparative AL experiments
topic_metadata.description: The survey acknowledges the lack of empirical comparisons across AL strategies within the work itself, pointing to a broader need for systematic experimental studies. Comparative benchmarks evaluating multiple AL methods under shared conditions could yield more actionable guidance for practitioners selecting strategies for specific NLP tasks.
topic_metadata.text_span: Limitations section, final sentences on absence of experiments and call for comparative studies

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Supervised models in remote sensing
topic_metadata.description: The section highlights the widespread use of statistical learning models—especially Support Vector Machines and neural networks—for supervised classification of land use from modern satellite imagery. It notes their effectiveness on very high spatial and spectral resolution data, framing them as state-of-the-art techniques in remote sensing image classification.
topic_metadata.text_span: First paragraph up to 'have proven their efficiency for handling remote sensing data.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Training set representativeness and cost
topic_metadata.description: Performance of supervised classifiers is described as heavily dependent on how representative the training data are of the underlying classes. Constructing such appropriate training sets is portrayed as difficult and expensive, since it often requires extensive manual analysis via visual inspection or field surveys followed by sample labeling.
topic_metadata.text_span: First paragraph from 'However, the performances of supervised algorithms...' through the end of the paragraph.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Requirements for compact, informative training sets
topic_metadata.description: The section concludes that desirable training sets should be small yet constructed 'in a smart way,' focusing on discriminative pixels that accurately capture class boundaries. This requirement is especially critical for very high spatial or spectral resolution classification, where feature spaces are large and complex but training information is limited.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final paragraph starting 'Summing up, besides being small...' to section end.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Pool-based active learning notation
topic_metadata.description: The section formally defines the labeled training set X = {x_i, y_i} with class labels y_i in {1, …, N} and feature vectors x_i in a d-dimensional input space ℝ^d. It also defines the unlabeled set U = {x_i}, a large pool of candidate pixels (u ≫ l) from which the algorithm selects samples to be labeled. This establishes the pool-based setting common in active learning for remote sensing.
topic_metadata.text_span: Part beginning 'Let X = {xi, yi}^l_{i=1} be a training set…' through the definition of U as the set of unlabeled pixels.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Iterative sampling and model adaptation
topic_metadata.description: Active learning algorithms are described as iterative sampling schemes in which the classification model is regularly updated by incorporating newly labeled pixels. The new samples are chosen to be those most beneficial for improving model performance, typically based on some informativeness criterion. This captures the core process of alternating between sample selection, labeling, and model refinement.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final sentence starting 'Active learning algorithms are iterative sampling schemes…' describing model adaptation with new labeled pixels.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Heuristic-based candidate evaluation and ranking
topic_metadata.description: Each unlabeled candidate in the pool is scored with a user-defined heuristic that quantifies its interest for labeling. The candidates are then ranked according to this heuristic score, guiding which samples are most informative to query. This mechanism allows the algorithm to prioritize samples expected to most improve the model.
topic_metadata.text_span: Algorithm 1, lines 'for each candidate in Uϵ do', 'Evaluate a user-defined heuristic', and 'Rank the candidates in Uϵ according to the score of the heuristic'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty reduction as selection objective
topic_metadata.description: The selection strategy aims to target areas where the model exhibits low confidence. By adding such uncertain samples to the training set, the algorithm forces the classifier to resolve these regions of uncertainty, simultaneously seeking to maximize performance gain. This articulates the underlying objective guiding the heuristic used in candidate selection.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'areas of uncertainty of the model and their inclusion in the training set forces the model to solve the regions of low confidence...'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Bagging-based committee construction
topic_metadata.description: A committee of classifiers is built using bagging, where k training sets are generated by drawing with replacement from the original labeled data. Each bootstrapped set is used to train a separate classifier, and the committee collectively predicts labels for unlabeled candidate pixels. This results in k labelings for each candidate pixel, forming the basis for estimating uncertainty. The approach leverages only a part of the available labeled pixels in each bag to induce diversity among committee members.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting with 'In the implementations of [25], bagging [29] is proposed to build the committee' through 'At the end of the procedure, k labelings are provided for each candidate pixel xi ∈U.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Multi-view committees via feature partitioning
topic_metadata.description: High-dimensional remote sensing data are handled by splitting the original feature space into multiple disjoint subsets or views, and building a committee of classifiers, each operating on a different view. For hyperspectral images, these views can be derived from the block-diagonal structure of the covariance matrix, so that each block defines a feature subset. Each view produces an independent classification of the same pixel, enabling disagreement-based or entropy-based query heuristics similar to nEQB. This multi-view construction underpins the later definition of the AMD selection rule.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'When confronted to high dimensional data, it may be relevant to construct the committee by splitting the feature space...' through '...can be used similarly to nEQB.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: SVM decision function and confidence
topic_metadata.description: This topic details the SVM decision function used in active learning, including the kernel-based representation, dual coefficients, and support vectors. It highlights how the absolute value of f(xi), the distance from a sample to the hyperplane, serves as a confidence indicator, with larger margins implying more certain classifications. The entities involved include kernels K(xj, xi), support vectors xj with non-zero αj, and binary labels yj.

The MS (Margin Sampling) and MCLU heuristics are compared by showing that areas of maximal uncertainty correspond to regions minimizing their respective objective functions (Eq. (7) and Eq. (9)). topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Alternative names for margin sampling
topic_metadata.description: The text notes that the margin sampling heuristic appears in the literature under several different names. These include “most ambiguous,” “binary level uncertainty,” and “SVMSIMPLE,” reflecting slight terminological variations across studies. Despite the naming differences, these methods all implement the same core idea of querying samples near the SVM decision boundary.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Significance space construction using SV coefficients
topic_metadata.description: Significance space construction (SSC) replaces distance to the SVM hyperplane as the uncertainty measure with a detection problem based on support vector coefficients. Training samples with α_j > 0 (support vectors) are treated as one class and samples with α_j = 0 as the other, defining a second classifier f(x)^SSC for support vector detection. Applied to the unlabeled pool, this classifier predicts which pixels are likely to become future support vectors, and the selection rule x̂_SSC = arg_{x_i∈U} f(x_i)^SSC > 0 focuses on these significant candidates. After identifying this subset, a random selection among the predicted support-vector-like samples is performed for labeling.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 'C. Significance space construction (SSC)', including equation (10) and the subsequent description of candidate selection

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: MCLU-ABD uncertainty-diversity trade-off
topic_metadata.description: The MCLU-ABD (multi-class level uncertainty – angle-based diversity) heuristic combines multiclass uncertainty with a kernel-based diversity term. Candidate samples are first restricted to those maximizing the MCLU uncertainty measure, then a query function balances uncertainty f(xi)_MC and normalized kernel similarity to already selected samples using a trade-off parameter λ. This generalizes MAO to arbitrary kernels by normalizing in feature space and explicitly integrating uncertainty and diversity in a single objective.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph beginning 'In [39], the MAO criterion is combined with the MCLU uncertainty estimation...' including equations (12)–(13) and the mention of normalization in feature space.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Support-vector-based margin diversification
topic_metadata.description: Diversity is enforced by constraining margin sampling to points associated with different closest support vectors, leading to the cSV-based selection rule. This divides the margin in feature space according to the geometric distribution of support vectors, ensuring that queried samples are diverse with respect to the current SVM decision structure. However, it may still select mutually close samples if they are linked to different support vectors, so inter-sample diversity is not guaranteed.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'In [21], the diversity of the chosen candidates is enforced...' and the subsequent definition of x̂_cSV and equation (14).

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Boosting and computational limits of KL method
topic_metadata.description: An extension of the KL-divergence approach uses boosting to down-weight previously selected pixels that have become less relevant to the current classifier. This heuristic is practical only with classifiers of low computational cost, because each active learning iteration requires training u+1 models (one per candidate plus the base model). Consequently, it is considered unsuitable for computationally demanding methods such as SVMs and does not naturally support selecting batches of pixels. The topic highlights a trade-off between informativeness of the criterion and computational feasibility in large-scale remote sensing settings.
topic_metadata.text_span: First paragraph, from 'Recently, the authors of [49] extended this approach...' through 'Moreover, a selection of batches of pixels is not possible.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Platt scaling for SVM probability estimates
topic_metadata.description: To apply BT with SVMs, decision function outputs are converted into approximate posterior probabilities using Platt’s method. This involves fitting a sigmoid of the form p(y*i = ω|xi) = 1 / (1 + e^(A f(xi, ω) + B)), where A and B are estimated parameters. Although these quantities are not Bayesian posteriors in a strict sense, they serve as practical per-class probability estimates usable by active learning heuristics. This calibration step enables SVMs to participate in probability-based selection criteria like BT.
topic_metadata.text_span: Second paragraph, from 'A possibility to obtain posterior probabilities from SVM outputs...' through the sigmoid formula (19) and the note about these not being true Bayesian probabilities.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Link between BT and MCLU for SVMs
topic_metadata.description: A close relationship is highlighted between the Breaking Ties heuristic and the Margin-based Confidence-based Learning Utility (MCLU) heuristic when using SVM classifiers. By comparing the BT formulation in equation (20) with equation (8), the text notes that both methods effectively target samples with minimal margin between top class hypotheses. This establishes BT as conceptually aligned with margin-based active learning strategies in SVM-based remote sensing classification.

topic_metadata.title: Nonlinear manifolds and classifier choice
topic_metadata.description: Spectral mean profiles and manifold visualizations reveal high nonlinearity and strong class overlap in the hyperspectral dataset. These characteristics imply that linear decision boundaries are inadequate, leading to poor performance by linear classifiers. Consequently, linear models are explicitly excluded from the subsequent experiments on this dataset.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Morphological contextual feature extraction
topic_metadata.description: To address spectral similarity between certain land-use classes, 16 contextual bands are derived using morphological opening and closing operators applied to the image. These features are concatenated with the original 4 spectral bands, producing a 20-dimensional representation that captures spatial structure in addition to spectral information. The opening features enhance discrimination of vegetation-related classes, while closing features improve separability of asphalt-related classes such as roads and parking lots.

topic_metadata.title: Experimental protocol for active learning
topic_metadata.description: The section describes how labeled pixels are iteratively added to the training set (N+5 and N+20 pixels per iteration) and how many iterations are run for three different images until convergence. It specifies different iteration counts for SVM and LDA experiments and configures nEQB with varying committee sizes and proportions of available training data. This protocol defines the process by which the active learning algorithms are evaluated over time.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Heuristic families and comparison goals
topic_metadata.description: The numerical results compare several active learning heuristics—nEQB, MS, MCLU, MCLU-ABD, and BT—on three datasets, alongside Random Sampling and the base learner (Standard SVM/LDA). Rather than identifying a universally best heuristic, the study aims to characterize the strengths and weaknesses of different method families relative to data characteristics. This framework is intended to guide users in selecting suitable active learning strategies for specific remote sensing problems.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Margin-based heuristics with SVM classifiers
topic_metadata.description: When using SVM classifiers, the results (Figure 4) show that Margin Sampling (MS) outperforms nEQB and BT, as MS directly ranks candidates using the SVM decision function without extra probability estimation. nEQB suffers from too-small bags of training pixels, and BT has difficulty estimating posterior probabilities via Platt scaling when the initial training set is small, leading to early performance similar to Random Sampling. The analysis concludes that, under SVMs, large-margin heuristics are generally the most reasonable choice among the active learning families considered.
topic_metadata.text_span: Last paragraph, from 'Figure 4 compares a heuristic for each family presented...' to 'the most logical choice among the families seems to be a large margin heuristic.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: MS and MCLU uncertainty criteria
topic_metadata.description: The MS and MCLU heuristics are compared as uncertainty-based criteria for selecting informative samples. Both are found to characterize the uncertainty of candidate instances in a similar way, leading to comparable effectiveness in active learning. This suggests that either measure can be reliably used for uncertainty-driven sample selection with SVMs.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of section text: 'Figures 5 compares the MS and MCLU criteria and shows that both describe the uncertainty of the candidates in a similar way. Therefore, both can be used for efﬁcient active learning.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Spectral diversity via MCLU-ABD
topic_metadata.description: Adding a diversity criterion, particularly a spectral diversity measure such as MCLU-ABD, slightly improves classification performance in most cases. The improvement comes with little additional computational cost, and no degradation is observed compared to using uncertainty alone. An exception is noted for the AVIRIS image, where strong spectral mixing reduces the benefit of the diversity criterion.
topic_metadata.text_span: Later part of section text: 'The use of a diversity criterion seems to slightly improve the quality of the results (Fig. 6): except for the AVIRIS image – well known for the high degree of mixture of its spectral signatures – a spectral diversity criterion such as MCLU-ABD efﬁciently increases performances with little added computational cost. None of the solutions obtained with the inclusion of the diversity criterion degrade the ones relying on the uncertainty assumption only.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Active sampling for LDA subspace estimation
topic_metadata.description: This topic describes how active sampling improves the estimation of the discriminant subspace in LDA by focusing on informative samples. Random sampling can incorporate noise and outliers, biasing the Fisher’s ratio and leading to a suboptimal linear combination of features in the decision function. By strategically querying pixels, the active learner refines the subspace that better separates classes in the feature space.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences: 'In this case, both heuristics perform similarly and show a very interesting behavior: active sampling helps the LDA to estimate the subspace that better separates data. In fact, when sampling randomly, noise and outliers can make the estimation of the Fisher’s ratio biased, resulting in a suboptimal linear combination of variables in the decision function.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Refining class statistics via heuristic sampling
topic_metadata.description: This topic focuses on how heuristic-guided sampling and correct labeling improve estimates of per-class statistics in LDA, specifically class means (positions) and covariances (extents). Better estimates of these parameters lead to more accurate discriminant functions and improved classification performance. The text notes that beyond approximately 330 labeled pixels, the active learning–based training sets outperform standard LDA, yielding more harmonious classification maps.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences: 'Sampling and assigning correct labels to the pixels returned by these heuristics help estimating the correct per-class extent (covariance) and position (mean). From 330 pixels up, the standard LDA result is improved by the active learning training sets, providing more harmonious solutions...'

topic_metadata.description: Active learning heuristics consistently outperform random selection of pixels once convergence is reached. By selectively querying informative pixels, these heuristics achieve higher classification accuracy than random sampling for the same labeling effort. topic_metadata.title: Multi-view strategies for hyperspectral images
topic_metadata.description: For high-dimensional hyperspectral images, strategies that leverage the intrinsic data structure are recommended, particularly multi-view heuristics such as AMD and ECBD-ABD. AMD exploits cross-information directly in the spectral band space, while ECBD-ABD selects candidates using spectral angles between pixels to capture spectral similarity. These methods are presented as especially well-suited to the characteristics of hyperspectral data.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty estimation and class statistics
topic_metadata.description: The section highlights that estimating classification confidence (e.g., probabilities or margins) can be unreliable when it depends heavily on estimated class statistics, as in Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). Poorly estimated class means and covariances can propagate into misleading uncertainty measures, negatively affecting active learning sample selection. A similar issue arises for committee-based methods using bagging when each bag contains only a small portion of the original samples, making committee disagreement unstable.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences starting with 'be avoided, since such estimation strongly depends...' down to '...especially if the bags contain a small share of the original samples.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Handling complex manifolds via feature-space modeling
topic_metadata.description: For data lying on complex manifolds, redundancy among samples can severely degrade the quality of the active learning sampling and the resulting training set. The text advocates modeling relationships among samples in feature space to better capture manifold structure and select representative pixels. Methods such as kernel k-means within MCLU-ECBD and hMCS, as well as distance to support vectors in the cSV heuristic, are cited as concrete strategies to exploit this relational structure.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Sequential sampling with moving sensors
topic_metadata.description: In scenarios where moving sensors acquire samples sequentially via an automatic device, batch-based querying is unnecessary and potentially inefficient. The priority shifts to models and heuristics with very low computational cost that can be updated rapidly and suggest the next sampling location almost in real time. Within this context, BT (e.g., breaking ties) and KL-max heuristics are identified as particularly suitable due to their favorable computational properties.

topic_metadata.title: Active selection in semi-supervised classification
topic_metadata.description: This topic concerns actively selecting unlabeled pixels to improve semi-supervised classification in remote sensing imagery. Active learning strategies query the most informative unlabeled pixels so that limited labeling effort yields maximal gain in classifier performance. It focuses on the interaction between labeled and unlabeled data under a semi-supervised learning regime.

topic_metadata.title: Spatially adaptive active learning heuristics
topic_metadata.description: Spatially adaptive heuristics adjust active learning query strategies based on spatial properties of the image, such as neighborhood structure or spatial context. Instead of treating each pixel independently, these methods exploit spatial patterns to guide which samples to label. This leads to more efficient learning in spatially correlated remote sensing data.

topic_metadata.title: Active learning for cross-domain model adaptation
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses using active learning to adapt models across different domains or scenes, such as transferring a classifier from one geographic area or sensor condition to another. By selectively querying labels in the target domain, the model can be efficiently adapted while minimizing annotation cost. It focuses on domain shift and transfer learning in remote sensing classification.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Contextual information in query heuristics
topic_metadata.description: Here, the focus is on extending active learning heuristics beyond purely spectral criteria to explicitly incorporate contextual information such as positional data and texture. While current methods largely rely on spectral features or embed context only as additional attributes in the data vector, the text highlights the lack of heuristics that directly reason over spatial position and texture. This involves designing query strategies that model spatial relationships and local image structure.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences beginning 'Further steps for active learning methods are the inclusion of contextual information in the heuristics...' to '...but few heuristics directly consider positional information and/or textures.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Robustness of uncertainty-based heuristics to noise
topic_metadata.description: This topic concerns the vulnerability of uncertainty-driven active learning heuristics to high levels of image noise, particularly in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data. Since these methods rely on model uncertainty at the pixel level, heavy noise can render uncertainty estimates unreliable and the heuristics ineffective. The text notes that designing noise-robust active learning strategies for such conditions remains an open and largely unexplored research area.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences 'Another crucial issue is the robustness to noise: since they are based on the uncertainty of the pixels, current heuristics are useless for images related to high levels of noise such as SAR. This field remains, at present, totally unexplored.'

topic_metadata.title: Limitations of crowdsourcing for medical images
topic_metadata.description: While crowdsourcing significantly reduces annotation costs for general computer vision tasks, it is poorly suited for medical image analysis. High-quality medical labels require domain-specific medical knowledge and clinical expertise, and even for simpler tasks, crowd workers tend to produce lower-quality annotations than trained professionals. Privacy concerns further restrict the use of open crowdsourcing platforms for sensitive medical data.

topic_metadata.title: Expert annotation burden and variability
topic_metadata.description: Replacing crowd workers with clinical experts shifts the bottleneck to the high cost and time demands of expert annotation. For example, a radiologist may need about 60 minutes to manually segment brain tumors per patient, with high hourly compensation, making large-scale labeling very expensive. To reduce bias, multiple annotation rounds or multiple annotators per case are often used, introducing intra- and inter-annotator variability that further increases annotation cost and complexity.

topic_metadata.title: Existing surveys on active learning
topic_metadata.description: Previous surveys have examined active learning from several angles, including the role of humans in developing and deploying deep learning in medical imaging, AL for segmentation with imperfect annotations, and AL as a label-efficient learning method focusing on model and data uncertainty. Other general AL surveys in machine learning and computer vision have provided foundational introductions and reviewed deep AL developments in CV and NLP, as well as taxonomies of model-driven and data-driven sample selectors and fair re-implementations of high-impact methods. These works form the background against which the current medical imaging-focused survey is positioned.

topic_metadata.title: Identified gaps in current AL surveys
topic_metadata.description: The section highlights several limitations of existing AL surveys: rapid methodological progress has outpaced current reviews, leaving new ideas and techniques under-covered. There is insufficient synthesis on combining AL with other label-efficient methods, despite this being a recognized future direction. Moreover, few surveys systematically evaluate AL methods on medical imaging datasets, and current reviews insufficiently address AL’s elevated importance under high medical annotation costs.

topic_metadata.title: Scope and paper selection of this survey
topic_metadata.description: The survey aims to comprehensively cover AL for medical image analysis, including core methods, integration with label-efficient techniques, and domain-specific adaptations. Papers are primarily sourced from medical image analysis using keyword-based searches on Google Scholar and arXiv, then expanded via citation tracing. Seminal AL works from general computer vision are also included to maintain a coherent taxonomy, and the surveyed works are largely drawn from top-tier journals and conferences, totaling 164 AL works with 234 references.

topic_metadata.section_heading: Problem Settings and Formulations of Active Learning
topic_metadata.title: Canonical active learning problem settings
topic_metadata.description: Active learning is framed around three primary problem settings: membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based active learning. Each setting defines different assumptions about how unlabeled samples are obtained and how queries to the oracle are made. This classification underpins the formulation and comparison of active learning strategies across applications, including medical image analysis.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.section_heading: Problem Settings and Formulations of Active Learning
topic_metadata.title: Stream-based selective sampling under memory constraints
topic_metadata.description: Stream-based selective sampling assumes that unlabeled samples arrive sequentially in a stream, and the learner must immediately decide whether to query their labels. This setting is well-suited for environments with limited memory, such as edge computing devices, because it does not require storing a large pool of data. However, it typically ignores correlations between samples in the stream, which may limit selection efficiency.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences introducing stream-based selective sampling and its properties ('Stream-based selective sampling assumes that samples arrive one by one... but it neglects sample correlations.')

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.section_heading: Problem Settings and Formulations of Active Learning
topic_metadata.title: Batch-mode selection in deep active learning
topic_metadata.description: When multiple samples are selected for labeling at once, the process is termed batch-mode active learning. Deep active learning typically assumes batch-mode pool-based settings because retraining deep models after each individual annotation is computationally impractical, and a single labeled example rarely yields a significant performance gain. Consequently, the survey treats batch-mode pool-based active learning as the default setup for deep active learning methods it reviews.

topic_metadata.title: Sample selection via informativeness functions
topic_metadata.description: In each round, an informativeness function I evaluates every sample in the unlabeled pool Du_t to quantify its utility for model improvement. Based on these scores, a sampling strategy S selects a batch of the most informative samples to form the queried set Dq_t. This mechanism focuses annotation effort on samples expected to maximally benefit the deep model f_{θ_{t−1}}.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences starting 'Sample Selection: In the t-th round of annotation...' through the formula defining Dq_t and description of I, S, and f_{θ_{t−1}}.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.section_heading: Assuming a total of T annotation rounds, active learning
topic_metadata.title: Queried and unlabeled datasets with budget
topic_metadata.description: The queried dataset Dq_t in round t is a subset of the unlabeled pool Du_t, defined by applying the sampling strategy S to informativeness evaluations I(x, f_{θ_{t−1}}). The annotation budget b governs how many samples are selected per round, enforcing b = |Dq_t| ≪ |Du_t| to ensure only a small fraction of data is labeled. topic_metadata.title: Prediction-probability uncertainty metrics
topic_metadata.description: This topic covers classical uncertainty measures computed directly from a model’s prediction probabilities p = Softmax(fθ(x)) over C classes. Metrics include Least Confidence (1 − max_i p_i or equivalently using max_i p_i with ↓ direction), Entropy (−∑_i p_i log p_i with ↑ direction), Margin (difference between top-1 and top-2 class probabilities with ↓ direction), and Mean Variance of class probabilities (↑ direction). These metrics quantify how spread or peaky the predicted distribution is, and serve as basic uncertainty scores in active learning query strategies.

topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty for medical image active learning
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty estimation is positioned as crucial for deploying deep learning in clinical practice, where medical images exhibit high variability and training data are limited. Predictive uncertainty allows models to flag ambiguities, artifacts, and unseen patterns, making it a natural informativeness metric in active learning. Samples with higher uncertainty are treated as harder and more error-prone, so querying and annotating them helps the model learn novel patterns and improve overall performance.

topic_metadata.title: Aleatoric, epistemic, and predictive uncertainty
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty is decomposed into aleatoric uncertainty (AU) and epistemic uncertainty (EU). AU represents data-driven noise such as motion or metal artifacts in MRI/CT and cannot be reduced by collecting more data, while EU reflects model uncertainty due to unlearned knowledge and can be reduced with additional labeled data. In practice, most active learning work does not explicitly separate AU and EU, so 'uncertainty' typically refers to predictive uncertainty, the combined effect of both, because disentangling the two is difficult and often offers limited practical benefit.

topic_metadata.title: Taxonomy of uncertainty-based active learning
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty-based active learning methods are organized into five main categories: multiple inference, gradient-based uncertainty, performance estimation, uncertainty-aware models, and adversarial-based uncertainty. Multiple inference methods include MC Dropout, data disagreement, model disagreement, and model ensembles; gradient-based approaches use gradients, Fisher Information, or influence functions; performance estimation employs surrogate metrics or learnable performance predictors; uncertainty-aware models encompass evidential deep learning and mixture density networks; adversarial-based methods leverage adversarial samples and adversarial training. This taxonomy structures the design space of uncertainty exploitation beyond simple probability-based measures.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Model ensembles and snapshot ensembles for AL
topic_metadata.description: Model ensemble approaches train multiple independent deep models whose predictions are combined to estimate uncertainty, often outperforming MC dropout but at higher computational cost. Snapshot ensembles reduce this overhead by capturing multiple model checkpoints along a single training trajectory using cyclic learning rate schedules, though naïve variants may underperform full ensembles. An improved snapshot ensemble maintains optimization trajectories across active learning rounds with parameter regularization and can surpass standard ensembles. Additionally, stein variational gradient descent is used to train diverse ensembles for organ and tumor segmentation in CT and MRI, improving performance over competing methods.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Query-by-Committee model disagreement in segmentation
topic_metadata.description: Model disagreement, formalized as Query-by-Committee (QBC), selects samples where multiple models’ outputs diverge most, indicating high epistemic uncertainty. Suggestive Annotation (SA) trains several segmentation networks via bootstrapping and uses prediction variance as a disagreement metric, achieving strong performance in gland and lymph node segmentation. Other works train multiple distinct segmentation models and measure disagreement (e.g., prediction variance or KL divergence between teacher and student models) to prioritize cases for annotation in tasks like abdominal multi-organ and carotid intima-media segmentation.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: CAM-based disagreement and geometric uncertainty metrics
topic_metadata.description: Some approaches leverage class activation maps (CAMs) and geometric similarity measures to refine disagreement-based active learning. In polyp segmentation, multiple decoders are trained on CAMs from a classification network, and both model disagreement (entropy and Dice between decoder outputs) and CAM disagreement (Dice between CAMs and decoder outputs) are used to select informative samples; low model but high CAM disagreement cases are turned into pseudo-labels for semi-supervised learning. Other methods quantify disagreement between CAMs using Hausdorff distance or between MC dropout predictions via vote entropy, capturing spatial or categorical uncertainty for tasks such as rib fracture detection.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Data disagreement via input perturbations and viewpoints
topic_metadata.description: Data disagreement methods avoid training many models by instead perturbing inputs (e.g., augmentations or viewpoint changes) and measuring predictive inconsistency across these variants. KL divergence is a central metric, used to compare predictions for different augmented CT scans in COVID diagnosis and different viewpoints in 3D scenes, with higher KL indicating more informative samples. Extensions include an input-end committee that randomly augments inputs and quantifies classification and localization disagreement using cross-entropy and variance, respectively, providing a flexible framework for image-level and region-level uncertainty estimation.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Feature-space interpolation disagreement with prototypes
topic_metadata.description: Feature-space interpolation strategies assess whether unlabeled data introduce novel information by interpolating between unlabeled feature vectors and labeled class prototypes. If the interpolated point’s prediction disagrees with the prototype’s label, this is interpreted as evidence that the unlabeled sample lies in a region not well represented by existing labels and should be annotated. This prototype-based disagreement mechanism has shown improvements across multiple datasets and settings, offering a representation-level perspective on uncertainty beyond raw prediction variance.

(2017) adopt the classic expected gradient length criterion to drive annotation decisions, leveraging the connection between gradient magnitude and sample value. This illustrates how traditional gradient-based active learning ideas are applied in medical imaging.

topic_metadata.title: Manifold-projected gradients for MRI segmentation
topic_metadata.description: Dai et al. propose an active learning method that projects segmentation loss gradients onto a learned data manifold to guide sample selection. A variational autoencoder (VAE) is first trained to capture the manifold of MRI brain images, and then a segmentation model is trained whose Dice-loss gradients are computed on labeled data. Query samples are chosen based on the components of these gradients that lie along the manifold, aiming to focus on realistic and informative variations. Their extended work demonstrates superior performance in both MRI brain tumor and whole-brain segmentation tasks.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Layer-wise and last-layer Fisher approximations
topic_metadata.description: To make FI-based active learning feasible in deep models, approximations are introduced that reduce computational cost. Sourati et al. compute FI using average gradients per network layer instead of full parameter-wise matrices, and they rely on expected empirical loss (Eq. 5) to obtain gradients without labels; this method improves brain extraction performance across ages and pathologies. Ash et al. further simplify the approach by computing the FI matrix only for the last layer, and their gradient computation matches the BADGE framework, which uses last-layer gradient embeddings. These approximations retain much of FI’s informativeness while avoiding full quadratic complexity.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Influence function-based sample selection
topic_metadata.description: Liu et al. apply influence functions to choose unlabeled samples expected to most positively affect model performance when labeled. The influence of a sample is computed using gradients of the loss on the labeled set and the inverse Hessian of the empirical risk (Eq. 9), capturing how upweighting that sample would perturb model parameters and downstream loss. Because unlabeled samples lack ground-truth, their gradients in the influence expression are approximated using gradients of the expected empirical loss. This yields an AL criterion grounded in classical robust statistics but adapted to deep models in medical imaging.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Surrogate metrics via prediction agreement
topic_metadata.description: Surrogate metrics approximate performance by exploiting prediction agreement or intermediate representations, serving as upper or lower bounds of loss or evaluation scores. Examples include computing the intersection over union (IoU) across multiple MC dropout predictions and correlating it with the true Dice coefficient, and averaging Dice scores between intermediate and final layers under deep supervision. These surrogates show strong linear correlations with real task metrics, making them effective proxies for performance in medical image segmentation.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) as loss surrogate
topic_metadata.description: Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) measures the norm of the change in network outputs between two consecutive annotation rounds. Within limited training iterations, sample loss is shown to be bounded by this output difference, making COD a surrogate for both loss and downstream evaluation metrics. Samples with high COD are preferentially selected, as empirical results demonstrate that higher COD is associated with higher loss and poorer performance.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Combining loss prediction with diversity and disagreement
topic_metadata.description: Some methods enhance learnable loss estimation by integrating it with other active learning criteria such as model disagreement and sample diversity. In COVID diagnosis and colonoscopy polyp analysis under federated active learning, predicted loss is combined with prediction disagreements and diversity measures to select informative and diverse samples across distributed clients. This composite strategy aims to improve both uncertainty targeting and coverage of the data space.

topic_metadata.title: Loss ranking prediction instead of regression
topic_metadata.description: Recognizing that active learning primarily needs an uncertainty ordering rather than exact loss values, loss regression is relaxed to predicting relative loss ranks. Kim et al. (2021) replace the loss regressor in LLAL with a ranking module derived from RankCGAN, directly optimizing for correct ordering of sample uncertainties. This rank-based estimation empirically surpasses exact loss regression for sample selection.
