topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Mistake-driven perceptron updates with selective labels
topic_metadata.description: When a label is queried and the prediction is incorrect, the model is updated via the standard perceptron rule w_t = w_{t−1} + M_t y_t x_t, where M_t is an indicator of a prediction mistake. If the label is not requested, the weight vector remains unchanged, so learning occurs only on queried examples where errors are observed. This couples label querying with mistake-driven updates, reducing annotation cost while maintaining an online learning process.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences around Eq. (2), from 'If the learner queries the label yt...' through '...we have wt = wt−1.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Smoothing-based sampling probability function
topic_metadata.description: The section introduces a sampling probability Pt defined as Pt = δ / (δ + |pt|), where δ ≥ 1 is a smoothing parameter. This formulation yields a sampling distribution equivalent to a previously defined one (Eq. 3), but restricts the smoothing parameter to values not smaller than 1. The sampling probability modulates how likely an example is queried based on a score pt, affecting the shape of the sampling distributions illustrated for b-sampling and logistic sampling.
topic_metadata.text_span: early part of the section, lines around the definition of Eq. (5) starting with “Pt =” and the discussion of δ and the sampling distribution

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Minimax gradient-based conservative selection
topic_metadata.description: To mitigate the risks of aggressively focusing on misclassified examples under label noise, Bordes et al. propose a more conservative selection strategy based on a minimax gradient criterion. Instead of directly choosing the most misclassified points, examples are selected for updating wt according to how they influence a worst-case (minimax) gradient objective. This aims to provide more robust updates that are less sensitive to noisy labels and erroneous boundary estimates.
topic_metadata.text_span: same Bordes et al. (2005) paragraph, specifically the sentences starting with “To address this, they suggested a more conservative approach…” and mentioning a minimax gradient strategy

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Role of model confidence in sampling
topic_metadata.description: Beyond label reliability, the section stresses that confidence in the model itself must be considered when sampling is based solely on model predictions. Hao et al. (2018b) argue that margin-based sampling may be suboptimal when the model is not sufficiently confident, implying that query strategies should account for model uncertainty in addition to prediction margins. This connects active sampling quality directly to the model’s calibration and stability over time.
topic_metadata.text_span: final sentences of the excerpt, starting with “In addition to confidence in the labels…” and mentioning Hao et al. (2018b) and margin-based sampling

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Variance-aware soft margin querying strategy
topic_metadata.description: The sampling decision uses a variance-adjusted soft margin that combines the absolute margin with a correction term ct depending on the margin variance νt. The correction term ct = −(η/2)(1/(νt + 1/γ)) is designed so that high variance (low confidence) increases the incentive to query labels, while low variance reduces it. A composite quantity ρt = |pt| + ct is computed: if ρt ≤ 0 the label is always queried; if ρt > 0, the label is queried with probability Pt = δ / (δ + ρt), introducing a Bernoulli sampling mechanism that smoothly trades off uncertainty and labeling cost.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'The sampling decision uses an additional parameter to the margin ˜pt, which is defined as ct = ...' through the definitions of ρt and Pt up to 'where δ > 0 is a smoothing parameter.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Cost-sensitive loss for imbalanced data streams
topic_metadata.description: To handle class-imbalanced streaming applications, a cost-sensitive variant of the loss function is introduced. This modification assigns different costs to errors from different classes, biasing the learner to pay more attention to minority or more critical classes. The approach is positioned within the broader context of imbalanced data stream analysis.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'Finally, Hao et al. (2018b) also introduced a cost-sensitive variant of the loss function...' to 'For a comprehensive discussion on imbalanced data stream analysis, please see Aguiar et al. (2023).'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Cold-start with imbalanced multiclass ELMs
topic_metadata.description: Qin et al. (2021) highlight the cold-start issue specifically in imbalanced multiclass settings using extreme learning machines (ELMs). In such datasets, some classes have very few instances, severely degrading the model’s predictive ability for those classes, especially early on. They extend an existing active learning framework to multiclass classification and propose a sampling strategy that jointly considers instance uncertainty and diversity, using pairwise diversity measures to avoid redundant queries and to better represent under-represented classes.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'The cold-start issue related to the application of active learning to imbalanced datasets has also been highlighted by Qin et al. (2021)...' to 'To address this issue, they propose a sampling strategy that considers both diversity and uncertainty. The diversity is calculated by computing pairwise...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Differentially private online SVM active learning
topic_metadata.description: A differentially private online active learning method based on SVMs randomizes the classical margin-based querying strategy of Tong and Koller. The informativeness of a point x_t is modeled as c(t) = exp(−d(x_t, w_t)), where d(x_t, w_t) = |⟨w_t, x_t⟩| / ||w_t|| is its distance to the current SVM hyperplane. In the non-private setting, labels are queried for points within a margin band around the hyperplane (c(t) > τ, equivalently d(x_t, w_t) ≤ log 1/τ), but to ensure privacy the method replaces this deterministic rule with randomized decisions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Third paragraph, from 'SVMs have also been used by Ghassemi et al. (2016)...' down to 'around wt.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Mini-batch strategies for private SGD training
topic_metadata.description: For training under differential privacy, the method introduces two mini-batch strategies to mitigate the slow convergence that can result from adding noise in private stochastic gradient descent. By grouping streaming instances into mini-batches before applying noisy updates, the approach aims to balance privacy guarantees with optimization efficiency. This is contextualized with references to prior work on private SGD algorithms.
topic_metadata.text_span: Third paragraph, from 'To tackle the privacy concerns while training...' to the end of the paragraph mentioning Bassily et al., Song et al., and Duchi et al.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online active learning with reject option
topic_metadata.description: Reject option classifiers allow the learner to abstain from making a prediction when instances are highly ambiguous, mitigating the high cost of misclassification errors, as in medical diagnosis tasks. Shah and Manwani study online active learning for such classifiers, where deciding to reject versus predict is integral to the model’s operation. The framework is tailored to streaming data where each new instance may be predicted, rejected, or queried for a label.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences from 'Shah and Manwani (2020) investigated the online active learning problem for reject option classifiers.' to '...but suggest further tests instead.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Double ramp loss for label querying
topic_metadata.description: The reject option classifier uses a non-convex double ramp loss ℓ_dr, where parameter updates occur only in a specific linear region of the loss. The label of the current example xt is queried only if |f_t(xt)| lies within [ρ_t − 1, ρ_t + 1], the interval where the loss is linear and informative for updating. The parameter ρ defines the bandwidth of the rejection region, controlling which instances fall into the 'reject' versus 'predict' zones.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences from 'They proposed an approach based on a non-convex double ramp loss function ℓdr...' to '...determines the rejection region.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Bayesian online active learning framework
topic_metadata.description: Fujii and Kashima propose a Bayesian online active learning framework based on policy-adaptive submodularity to handle data streams. It distinguishes between a stream setting, where labeling decisions can be delayed within a time window, and a secretary setting, where decisions must be taken immediately upon arrival. The framework is general enough to cover tasks such as active classification, active clustering, and active feature selection under streaming conditions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences from 'Fujii and Kashima (2016) investigated the problem of Bayesian online active learning.' to '...active feature selection.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Adaptive submodular maximization in streams
topic_metadata.description: The Bayesian framework is grounded in adaptive submodular maximization, extending classical submodular maximization characterized by diminishing returns of adding elements to a set. By updating the set function as new observations arrive, the method adapts to the evolving data distribution and current state of knowledge. This adaptivity aims to exploit streaming data more efficiently, improving model performance under limited labeling budgets.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences from 'The framework is based on the concept of adaptive submodular maximization...' to '...improved performance.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Disagreement-based online active learning theory
topic_metadata.description: Huang et al. introduce a disagreement-based active learning framework for online settings, formalized over a hypothesis space H with VC dimension d and a Tsybakov noise model. Each classifier h ∈ H maps observations xt to binary labels yt ∈ {0,1}, and pairwise disagreement is quantified by d(h1, h2) = P[h1(x) ≠ h2(x)]. The induced disagreement region, where committee members predict differently, underpins sampling strategies that query labels only on informative, contentious instances.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences from 'Among this class of methods, a common sampling strategy...' to the end of the excerpt starting 'The disagreement among two classifiers is given by d (h1, h2)...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Label complexity and regret objectives
topic_metadata.description: Online active learning is formalized as a policy π = ({v_t}, {λ_t}), where v_t encodes whether a label is queried and λ_t is the prediction rule at time t. The performance over a time horizon T is evaluated via label complexity, defined as the expected number of queried labels E[Q(T)], and regret, defined as the expected excess number of classification errors with respect to an optimal hypothesis h*. The algorithm’s goal is to minimize label complexity subject to a constraint on regret, balancing labeling cost and predictive performance.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'The online active learning strategy is represented by the policy π = ({vt} , {λt})' through the paragraph ending with 'The objective of the algorithm is to minimize the label complexity with a constraint on the regret.' including equations (17) and (18)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Disagreement-based query region in online learning
topic_metadata.description: The learner maintains a version space H_t of candidate hypotheses and defines a region of disagreement D(H_t) as points where at least two hypotheses in H_t predict different labels. Initially, the version space is the full hypothesis class H and the disagreement region is the whole input space X. At each time t, if the current instance x_t falls inside D(H_t), the learner queries its label; otherwise, it predicts with an arbitrary classifier from H_t. This mechanism drives selective querying based on current model uncertainty.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'At the first round, the initial version space is the entire hypothesis space H...' through the definition of D(Ht) in equation (19) and the sentence 'If xt ∈D (Ht), then the label of the current data point is queried, otherwise a prediction is produced...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Version space pruning via empirical error thresholds
topic_metadata.description: After each iteration t, the learner uses the collected labeled set Z_t of size M to estimate the empirical error ε_{Z_t}(h) for all classifiers in H and identify the current best classifier h*_t. The version space is then updated by removing hypotheses whose empirical error exceeds that of h*_t by more than a threshold ε_{Z_t}(h, h*_t). This threshold controls how aggressively the version space is pruned, mediating a trade-off between reducing label complexity (by shrinking the disagreement region) and limiting regret (by avoiding elimination of good classifiers.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'At the end of the iteration t, the set Zt of M collected labeled examples is used...' through 'The threshold regulates the trade-off between reducing label complexity by narrowing the region of disagreement and increasing the regret by eliminating good classifiers.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Surrogate-loss active learning with pseudo-labels
topic_metadata.description: Desalvo et al. (2021) extend disagreement-based online active learning to a framework using surrogate losses and weak labels. At each time step, the learner may either query the true label y_t or assign a pseudo-label ŷ_t, and both true and pseudo-labeled instances form a set S_t that combines Z_t and Ŷ_t. The empirical risk ε_{S_t}(h) is computed over this mixed set, effectively integrating active learning with semi-supervised learning to optimize the sampling and learning strategy.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'The disagreement concept was also used by Desalvo et al. (2021)...' through 'St is obtained by combining the collected labeled examples Zt with the pseudo-labeled ones Ẑt. This represents an example of combining active learning and semi-supervised learning...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Bayesian active learning for activity recognition
topic_metadata.description: For online human activity recognition with sensor data, a semi-supervised active learning strategy leverages a pre-trained conditional restricted Boltzmann machine to extract generic features robust to different sensor layouts. Instance selection follows a Bayesian approach aimed at minimizing uncertainty over model parameters by comparing current model uncertainty (from data up to time t) with the expected risk conditioned on the potential label y_t. The discrepancy between these quantities indicates the impact of acquiring the current label on model uncertainty. A dynamically adaptive threshold is used to decide whether the expected risk justifies querying the label.
topic_metadata.text_span: second paragraph, from 'The DPMM has also been used by Mohamad et al. (2020)...' to 'used to the determine whether the current expected risk is greater than the current risk.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Decay-weighted expert loss and potential
topic_metadata.description: The section discusses how expert advice algorithms maintain a cumulative loss Ri,t−1 for each expert, updated with an exponential decay factor η so that recent mistakes are weighted more heavily than older ones. It explains that the Generalized Forecaster (GF) operates by minimizing, at each time step, the worst-case increase in a potential function over all possible label outcomes. This potential function assigns a value to each expert that reflects the quality of its advice based on its decay-weighted past performance. These mechanisms underpin how expert weights and influence are adapted over time in online prediction.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'where η is a positive decay factor and Ri,t−1 is the cumulative loss...' through '...captures the quality of an expert advice based on its past performance.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Active multiple kernel learning with random features
topic_metadata.description: A related framework applies online active learning to multiple kernel learning (MKL) using random feature approximation. The Active MKL (AMKL) algorithm employs an ensemble of N kernel functions within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), where each kernel-based function 1fi,t(xt) is optimized independently in a local step. In a subsequent global step, the learner combines these N kernel functions to construct a best-approximation function ft(xt) for prediction on sequentially arriving data. This setup leverages MKL’s ability to capture diverse data characteristics while maintaining online, incremental updates suitable for streaming and active settings.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'A similar framework, in conjunction with multiple kernel learning (MKL), has been investigated...' through the description of online MKL, RKHS, and the local and global steps of AMKL at the end of the section.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Regret-minimizing kernel ensemble weighting
topic_metadata.description: The method constructs a learned kernel-based predictor f̃t(xt) as a weighted combination of N kernel functions fi,t, with weights vi,t chosen to minimize regret over the time horizon T. Weights are computed via exponential weighting of past losses on labeled instances: ωi,t = exp(−ηg ∑_{τ∈A_{t−1}} ℓ(f̂i,τ(xτ), yτ)), where A_{t−1} indexes queried points and ηg is a tunable parameter. Normalizing ωi,t yields vi,t, which balance the contribution of each kernel according to historical performance relative to the best kernel function f*i,t. This framework ties instance labeling decisions to an adaptive ensemble of kernel predictors optimized on previous labeled data.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph containing Equations (26), (27), and (28) discussing f̃t(xt), ωi,t, vi,t, regret, and the role of A_{t−1} and ηg

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Confidence-based instance selection via kernel agreement
topic_metadata.description: Instance selection relies on a confidence condition that measures the similarity of predictions among the weighted kernel ensemble, controlled by a tolerance threshold δ > 0. The criterion max_{1≤j≤N} ∑_{i=1}^N vi,t ℓ(f̃i,t(xt), f̃j,t(xt)) ≤ δ enforces that, for an unlabeled instance, all kernels’ predictions are sufficiently close under the loss ℓ, indicating high agreement. When this condition holds, the system can refrain from querying the label, interpreting high consensus as high confidence. This selection rule is analogous to the condition used in AEWAF by Hao et al. (2018a), adapting expert agreement to a kernel-based ensemble.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences introducing the instance selection criterion and Equation (29), including the mention of δ and similarity of the learned kernel function

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Distribution shifts in drifting data streams
topic_metadata.description: Active learning strategies in this category address online classification in time-varying data streams where the underlying data distribution changes over time. The text distinguishes distribution shifts based on whether they affect the feature distribution p(x) or the conditional distribution p(y|x). A covariate shift is defined as a change that only impacts p(x) while leaving p(y|x) unchanged. This categorization sets the stage for analyzing and designing active learning methods tailored to different types of drift.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening sentences of subsection 3.2, from “Active learning strategies belonging to this category…” through the definition of covariate shift

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Limitations of unsupervised drift detection
topic_metadata.description: The text explains that purely unsupervised drift detection struggles to capture true concept drifts when the input distribution p(x) remains unchanged but the conditional relationship between x and y changes. In such cases, labels are necessary to recognize that the mapping from features to labels has shifted. This highlights a fundamental limitation of relying only on unlabeled data for detecting concept drift in active learning scenarios. It motivates combining limited supervised signals with unsupervised detectors.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section where the difficulty of detecting concept drift when p(x) is fixed but the x–y relationship changes is discussed.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Pseudo-label propagation using k-nearest neighbors
topic_metadata.description: The section describes augmenting active learning decisions with pseudo-labels inferred from already labeled neighbors. For an unlabeled queried point, its label is estimated through a weighted majority vote among its k-nearest neighbors, propagating known labels through the feature space. Both true labels and these pseudo-labels are then used to assess the utility of incoming data points. This semi-supervised mechanism enriches label information under latency and sparsity, improving utility estimation in streaming active learning.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final sentences of the section discussing use of real and pseudo-labels, k-nearest neighbors, and weighted majority voting.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Drift-aware dual-classifier management
topic_metadata.description: The algorithm maintains a primary classifier and conditionally spawns a new classifier when the drift detector raises a warning. During a warning phase, the new classifier is trained in the background with labeled examples while the original classifier remains in use. Upon confirmed drift detection, the new classifier replaces the old one, and its training continues, enabling smoother adaptation to concept drift while avoiding abrupt model changes.
topic_metadata.text_span: Within Algorithm 3, the parts beginning 'if drift warning = True then / Start to train a new classifier Cnew' through 'if Cnew exists then / Update classifier Cnew ... end if'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Simulated labeling via bagging and fuzziness
topic_metadata.description: To avoid redundant queries when labels are delayed, the method identifies a region Dn+ = Dn\Wn where queried labels are not yet available. Instead of re-querying similar instances, it simulates incoming labels by using a bagging approach that averages utility estimates over multiple simulated labelings, thus approximating the effect of future supervision. An alternative simulation based on fuzzy labeling is also considered to represent label uncertainty more explicitly.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, discussion of Dn+, bagging-based simulation and fuzzy labeling

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Class-imbalance-aware uncertainty thresholds
topic_metadata.description: Instance selection is based on predictive uncertainty measured by the best-versus-second-best margin for multi-class classification. After a passive initialization pool, a per-class threshold θi is computed (Eq. 31) as a function of class-specific sample counts and a constant m controlling threshold size, so that querying behavior can differ across classes. Class imbalance is further addressed through class-specific training weights and dynamic adjustment of these thresholds to bias selection toward minority-class instances.
topic_metadata.text_span: second paragraph, from mention of best-versus-second-best margin through Eq. (31) and class imbalance handling

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Chunk-based drift detection and selection
topic_metadata.description: A data stream S is partitioned into fixed-length chunks whose adjacent distributions are compared to detect concept drift. After a drift is identified, a multi-objective optimization problem is formulated to select query candidates from the current batch that are both relevant and diverse. Relevance is defined as a point’s contribution to the emerging concept, while diversity is quantified via the Pearson correlation coefficient among instances in the same region, encouraging informative yet non-redundant labeling.
topic_metadata.text_span: third paragraph, description of Cheng et al. (2023) including chunking, drift detection, and relevance/diversity criteria

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Meta-learned uncertainty thresholds per window
topic_metadata.description: Another approach samples the most uncertain instances from each chunk but uses a meta-learning framework to fine-tune the uncertainty threshold for each window. By adapting this threshold based on meta-level information, the method aims to reduce the number of labels requested while preserving effective adaptation to new concepts. This window-wise tuning balances exploration of changing regions of the feature space with labeling cost constraints.
topic_metadata.text_span: third paragraph, sentences describing Martins et al. (2023) and meta-learning for threshold tuning

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Damped sliding window weight decay
topic_metadata.description: Dynamic classifiers are assigned gradually decaying weights based on a damped sliding window mechanism. Each dynamic classifier weight is initialized at 1/D and then updated according to its creation time using the recurrence in Eq. (34). More recent dynamic classifiers receive higher weights to emphasize detection of sudden concept drifts, while older ones have smaller weights and contribute to identifying gradual drifts. This temporal weighting scheme encodes recency into the ensemble’s decision process.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'Conversely, the dynamic classifiers have gradually decaying weights...' through Eq. (34) and the explanation that recent classifiers have highest weights and older ones lower weights.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Hybrid random–uncertainty instance selection
topic_metadata.description: The instance selection strategy combines uncertainty sampling with random sampling to choose which data points in the stream should be labeled. Uncertainty is based on the margin of ensemble predictions, while random sampling ensures coverage of regions far from the current decision boundary. This hybrid design addresses the limitation of pure uncertainty sampling, which may miss concept changes that occur away from the boundary. Similar ideas are reused in chunk-based ensemble active learning, where Zyblewski’s budget labeling strategy selects both random and informative examples measured via a support function threshold (interpreted as distance to the decision boundary in binary problems).
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'The instance selection approach combines random sampling and uncertainty sampling...' through the discussion of hybrid strategies and the description of Woźniak et al. (2023) and Zyblewski et al. (2020) budget labeling with support function threshold.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Clustering-based active learning with stable classifiers
topic_metadata.description: Halder et al. (2023) extend a framework with stable and dynamic classifiers by inserting a clustering step on each data block. The goal is to train a new stable classifier on instances that are simultaneously informative and representative, selected from clusters formed in each incoming block. This integrates cluster structure into the design of online active learning for time-varying data streams.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph beginning 'Another way to perform online active learning...' through '...instances from each data block.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Density-peak clustering for representative sample selection
topic_metadata.description: Zhang et al. (2023) employ density-peak clustering to identify the most representative data points in each batch of a data stream. They detect incomplete clusters in the dynamic feature space via the 'altitude' of data points and then query labels from those regions in subsequent iterations. This targets areas that are underrepresented or poorly formed in the current clustering structure.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences beginning 'To sample the most representative data points...' through '...in the following iterations.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Bi-criteria GGMM-based active learning with drift handling
topic_metadata.description: Mohamad et al. (2018) introduce a bi-criteria active learning algorithm that combines input-space density and label uncertainty. Density is modeled with a growing Gaussian mixture model (GGMM) that forms clusters and estimates data density, creating a new cluster when a point’s Mahalanobis distance to its nearest cluster exceeds a closeness threshold. Label uncertainty and concept drift are handled via a Bayesian logistic regression model whose parameters evolve over time, linking evolving class boundaries with the streaming data’s cluster structure.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences beginning 'Another approach that tries to exploit the clustering nature...' through 'As the classifier parameters wt are assumed to evolve over time, the'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Discrepancy-based incremental model updating
topic_metadata.description: The model is updated incrementally using a discrepancy measure defined as the difference between the model’s uncertainty on an instance xt before and after its true label yt is added to the training set. The query strategy uses a b-sampling approach to preferentially select instances that are expected to contribute most to the current error. This couples an uncertainty-change metric with error-focused sampling for online active learning in data streams.
topic_metadata.text_span: First paragraph, sentences about discrepancy measure and b-sampling (from 'model is incrementally updated using a discrepancy measure' to 'sample, with high probability, the observations that contribute the most to the current error')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Cognitive dual density-uncertainty query strategy
topic_metadata.description: Liu et al. (2021) propose an online active learning strategy that combines local density and classifier uncertainty to select informative and representative instances under concept drift and noise. Local density is defined as the number of times an observation is the nearest neighbor of other instances, computed within a sliding 'cognition window' over the stream. Inspired by Ebbinghaus’s law of human memory, the method uses a memory-strength-based policy to decide when the cognition window is refreshed, addressing both gradual and abrupt drifts. Labeling decisions are controlled by two thresholds, one on local density and one on classifier uncertainty.
topic_metadata.text_span: First paragraph, middle to end (from 'The combination of density and uncertainty is also employed by Liu et al. (2021)' down to 'using two thresholds, one for the local density and one for the classifier uncertainty')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Time-decay Bayesian probit framework for streams
topic_metadata.description: Chu et al. (2011) propose an online framework based on a Bayesian probit model with time-decay to handle evolving data streams. Online Bayesian learning maintains a posterior distribution over the linear classifier’s weight vector wt, while time-decay strategies downweight older examples to cope with concept drift and emphasize recent data. An online approximation technique supports weighted examples, following Minka (2001), and various sampling strategies are explored using entropy-based, function-value-based, and random selection criteria. This integrates probabilistic modeling, temporal weighting, and multiple query heuristics for streaming active learning.
topic_metadata.text_span: Third paragraph about Chu et al. (2011) (from 'A simpler approach for taking into account the time-varying aspect' to 'The instance selection criteria are based on entropy, function-value, and random sampling.')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Conflict and ignorance for stream active learning
topic_metadata.description: In single-pass active learning for evolving classification models, query decisions are based on conflict and ignorance. Conflict captures when an incoming instance lies near the decision boundary between classes, indicating label ambiguity, while ignorance measures the distance of the instance from the labeled training data in feature space, indicating unexplored regions. These two criteria guide which streaming instances should be labeled to most effectively improve the classifier.
topic_metadata.text_span: ‘The first single-pass active learning approach…’ through ‘This suggests that the data point falls within a region that has not been thoroughly explored by the learner.’

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-driven active learning for evolving regression
topic_metadata.description: For evolving regression models, online active learning combines ignorance in the input space with uncertainty in model outputs and parameters. Predictive uncertainty is quantified using confidence intervals via locally adaptive error bars, and overlapping fuzzy rules are merged with a dedicated approach to refine the rule base. Parameter uncertainty is assessed using the A-optimality criterion, an alphabetic optimality measure that aims to minimize the average variance of parameter estimates.
topic_metadata.text_span: ‘Later on, Lughofer and Pratama (2018) also proposed…’ through ‘…which will be discussed in Sect.3.4 together with other alphabetic optimality criteria.’

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Variable uncertainty thresholds and low-support rules
topic_metadata.description: An alternative active learning strategy for recurrent fuzzy classifiers uses a dynamic threshold based on the variable uncertainty strategy. Instead of directly exploiting output uncertainty, the method adaptively adjusts the threshold that determines when to query labels, focusing updates on rules with low support formed from few observations. This emphasizes improving underrepresented regions of the rule base and addresses the what-to-learn question in recurrent fuzzy model training.
topic_metadata.text_span: ‘Instead of leveraging the uncertainty about the output, Pratama et al. (2015)…’ through ‘…rules with low support, which were formed using the smallest amount of observations.’

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: D-optimality for fuzzy model parameter selection
topic_metadata.description: A recent online active learning strategy for fuzzy models introduces criteria based on D-optimality in the consequent space. D-optimality is used to reduce parameter uncertainty by selecting instances that maximize the determinant of the information matrix, thereby improving the precision of parameter estimates in the consequents of fuzzy rules. This embeds classical optimal experimental design principles into active learning for evolving fuzzy systems.
topic_metadata.text_span: ‘Recently, Lughofer and Škrjanc (2023) proposed an online active learning strategy…’ and the bullet ‘• D-optimality in the consequent space to reduce parameter uncertainty, as in Cacciarelli et al. (2022b).’

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Spherical potential-based novelty thresholds
topic_metadata.description: Subramanian et al. propose a meta-cognitive component that evaluates the novelty of incoming data points using a knowledge measure called spherical potential, a concept studied in kernel-based methods. This spherical potential is used to set a threshold deciding whether a new fuzzy rule should be added to capture the knowledge in the current sample. The work contrasts this label-efficient novelty criterion with a prediction-error-based threshold relying on hinge loss, which is less suitable under label scarcity.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'A different kind of threshold, based on the spherical potential theory...' through discussion of hinge loss error

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Certainty-based querying in visual inspection streams
topic_metadata.description: For visual inspection quality control, images are evaluated in a single pass and those selected for querying are stored in a buffer to be labeled later by an oracle. The buffer size defines a trade-off between promptly updating the classifier and limiting frequent human interventions. An active learning strategy is used that queries samples when model certainty, computed differently for a random forest (best-versus-second-best margin) and an evolving fuzzy classifier (conflict and ignorance measures), falls below a threshold.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'Fuzzy models have also been used to solve computer vision tasks...' through description of certainty computation for random forest and evolving fuzzy classifiers

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Hotelling T² and SPE for AL sampling
topic_metadata.description: Cernuda et al. employ a latent-structure-based query strategy using Hotelling T² and squared prediction error (SPE) statistics, classical tools from multivariate statistical process control and anomaly detection. These statistics measure the distance between the current labeled training set and a new unlabeled data point; high values indicate that the observation violates the current model and is thus informative to query. Implementations combine these criteria with principal component regression or partial least squares, and newly labeled samples trigger retraining of a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model using a sliding window over the data stream.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph beginning 'Finally, Cernuda et al. (2014) combine the use of fuzzy models...' through 'they retrain a TS fuzzy model using a sliding window approach.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Optimal experimental design and active learning
topic_metadata.description: Optimal experimental design is presented as a closely related field to active learning, focusing on designing experiments that enable efficient parameter estimation or improved prediction while minimizing the number of labeled runs N. It develops optimality criteria that balance resource efficiency with model performance. The traditional framework considered here is based on linear regression models, connecting classical design of experiments with active learning objectives.
topic_metadata.text_span: Section 3.4 opening lines starting 'Optimal experimental design (Karlin & Studden, 1966) is a research field...' through the sentence mentioning linear regression models

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Linear regression and OLS estimation
topic_metadata.description: The section defines a linear regression model y = Xβ + ε with N observations and d input variables, where ε is Gaussian noise with covariance σ²I. It explains that if XᵀX is full rank, the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator for the regression coefficients β is given by (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. This sets the foundation for later discussion of design properties and parameter uncertainty.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening equations and explanation around (36)–(37)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Moment matrix and design geometry
topic_metadata.description: The moment matrix M = XᵀX / N is introduced as a key object in design optimality criteria, encapsulating information about the design geometry. Since XᵀX governs the estimation of β, its structure (eigenvalues, determinant) reflects how informative the design is for parameter estimation. Optimal design methods exploit these properties to evaluate and compare experimental designs.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph introducing M = X⊤X/N and its role, after equation (37)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Confidence ellipsoid for regression parameters
topic_metadata.description: Assuming Gaussian noise, the estimator β̂ has a Normal distribution with covariance σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹, which induces a confidence ellipsoid for the true parameter vector β. The ellipsoid is defined via quadratic forms in (b − β̂) involving XᵀX, and its volume is inversely proportional to √det(XᵀX), while the axis lengths scale with 1/λᵢ, the eigenvalues of XᵀX. This geometric interpretation underlies how optimality criteria assess designs via ellipsoid size and shape.
topic_metadata.text_span: Equations (38)–(39) and the following explanation about ellipsoid volume and eigenvalues

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: From offline to streaming optimal design
topic_metadata.description: Traditional optimal design methods are used in offline experimental settings, where all design points can be pre-determined before data collection. In streaming scenarios, data points arrive sequentially and the design must be adapted online, requiring modifications of classical optimality-based approaches. This motivates strategies that incrementally select which incoming observations to label to approximate an optimal design.
topic_metadata.text_span: paragraph starting with 'The use of optimality criteria has proven to be highly beneficial in offline experimental design... However, these methods require modification to be applied in a stream-based scenario...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online A-optimal design under heteroskedasticity
topic_metadata.description: Fontaine et al. extend online optimal design to settings with heteroskedastic noise, where the variance of the response depends on the covariates. Their objective is to optimally allocate a fixed labeling budget across covariates so that the variances of the estimated regression coefficients are balanced, in line with A-optimality principles. This results in adaptive selection policies that consider both design geometry and non-constant error variance.
topic_metadata.text_span: sentence starting 'Another approach related to the A-optimality criterion was proposed by Fontaine et al. (2021)...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Conditional D-optimality for streaming selection
topic_metadata.description: Cacciarelli et al. propose a Conditional D-optimality (CDO) algorithm that extends norm-thresholding ideas to D-optimal design in streaming settings. The design is made marginally D-optimal given an initial labeled set, and incoming observations are selected by applying a D-optimality-based thresholding rule to augment this set. The method exploits the link between D-optimality and prediction variance, yielding a sequential selection strategy that improves the determinant of the information matrix as new data arrive.
topic_metadata.text_span: paragraph describing Cacciarelli et al. (2022b), the Conditional D-optimality (CDO) algorithm, and its relation to D-optimality and prediction variance

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Warm-up set and KDE threshold estimation
topic_metadata.description: Before starting active querying, the learner passively collects a warm-up set of j unlabeled observations from the stream to estimate the covariance structure of the data. Using eigendecomposition and whitening of both the initial design X and warm-up set W, the algorithm computes representations Z and V in a normalized space. Kernel density estimation (KDE) over V is then used to select a threshold τ such that the norm-thresholding rule achieves the desired sampling rate α. This procedure initializes τ and is periodically updated as the labeled design grows.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph describing warm-up set and KDE, and the middle block of Algorithm 5 (estimation of covariance, whitening, and KDE-based τ estimation)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Outlier-robust double-threshold sampling region
topic_metadata.description: To mitigate the tendency of design-optimality sampling to focus on outliers, the authors describe bounding the selection region with two thresholds τ1 and τ2. Only points whose leverage x_t^T (X^T X)^{-1} x_t falls between these bounds are eligible for labeling, defining an annular region in the transformed feature space. The upper threshold τ2 controls a trade-off between avoiding high-leverage outliers and still exploring uncertain regions of the input space. This modification aims to preserve predictive performance in the presence of outliers.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting with “Cacciarelli et al. (2023) also investigated…” and Equation (44)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: MAB as sequential experimental design
topic_metadata.description: Multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems are framed as a special case of sequential experimental design, where each arm pull is an experiment chosen to maximize an outcome over time. The learner must identify the arm with the highest expected reward among several arms with different reward distributions. This setting parallels active learning, as both involve sequential decisions (arm pulls or label queries) with feedback guiding future choices to optimize reward or model accuracy.
topic_metadata.text_span: second paragraph, description of MAB as optimization and relation to active learning

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Regret minimization in bandits
topic_metadata.description: Regret minimization in MAB focuses on maximizing cumulative reward across many trials, equivalently minimizing the loss relative to always playing the best arm. Algorithms must carefully balance exploration of lesser-known arms to improve reward estimates with exploitation of the currently best-estimated arm. This paradigm is suited to applications such as treatment design, online advertising, and recommender systems, where ongoing rewards are critical.
topic_metadata.text_span: bullet list, first bullet labeled 'Regret minimization'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Pure exploration bandit strategies
topic_metadata.description: Pure exploration methods aim to identify the best arm with high confidence or under a fixed budget of arm pulls, rather than maximizing cumulative reward. The main objective is to learn an accurate model of the reward structure while minimizing the number of measurements or labels, often motivated by safety or cost constraints on interventions. This setting is relevant to domains such as drug discovery and soft sensor development, where safe and efficient experimentation is crucial.
topic_metadata.text_span: bullet list, second bullet labeled 'Pure exploration'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: G-optimality and XY-allocation for bandits
topic_metadata.description: In the offline pure exploration setting for linear bandits, Soare et al. analyze the problem using the G-optimality criterion from experimental design, which seeks to minimize the maximum prediction variance over a design space. They introduce the XY-allocation algorithm, a specific strategy for allocating pulls across arms to achieve near G-optimal experimental designs. This connects classical optimal design theory with sample-efficient bandit exploration.
topic_metadata.text_span: sentences discussing Soare et al. (2014), G-optimality criterion and XY-allocation algorithm

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: LSTM-based policy for label vs. predict
topic_metadata.description: Woodward and Finn (2017) propose a reinforcement learning approach in which, at each time step, the learner must choose between predicting a label for xt or paying to query its true label yt. The policy π*(st) is optimized over states st to balance the cost of label requests versus the cost of incorrect predictions, with rewards assigned for requesting a label (Rreq), making a correct prediction (Rcorr), or an incorrect prediction (Rinc), where Rcorr and Rinc are modeled as negative due to associated costs. The action-value function is approximated using an LSTM neural network with a linear output layer, enabling the policy to exploit temporal dependencies in the sequence of decisions.
topic_metadata.text_span: last paragraph, from 'Another reinforcement learning-based approach has been proposed by Woodward and Finn (2017).' to 'as they are associated with costly actions.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Learning-curve evaluation of active learning
topic_metadata.description: Active learning strategies are evaluated by comparing them to passive random sampling through learning curves that track model performance versus the number of labeled examples. Metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, or root mean square error on a holdout test set are plotted. The curve’s asymptote and slope capture overall performance and sample efficiency, with steeper slopes indicating faster performance gains per labeled example.
topic_metadata.text_span: Early part of the section discussing learning curves and comparison to passive random sampling (paragraph starting 'The use of active learning approaches...').

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Non-parametric tests for strategy comparison
topic_metadata.description: To rigorously compare multiple active learning sampling strategies, non-parametric statistical tests are recommended. For pairwise comparisons, the sign test and the Wilcoxon signed-ranks test are proposed, while for more than two strategies, Friedman tests (including aligned-ranks and Iman–Davenport correction) and the Quade test are suggested. These tests assess whether observed performance differences between active and passive strategies are statistically significant across tasks or datasets.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section describing Reyes et al. (2018) and listing sign, Wilcoxon, Friedman, aligned-ranks, Iman–Davenport, and Quade tests.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: MOA framework for stream evaluation
topic_metadata.description: MOA (Massive Online Analysis) is an open-source software suite for data stream mining that implements both holdout and prequential evaluation strategies. It provides infrastructure to run and compare online learning and active learning algorithms on streaming data. Many studies in the survey use MOA as their experimental platform for evaluating online active learning strategies. Its inclusion of multiple evaluation protocols makes it a de facto standard tool in this research area.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences 'From an implementation perspective, Bifet et al. (2010) developed an open source software suite called MOA... This framework has found widespread application...'.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Train-on-queried, test-on-full-dataset protocol
topic_metadata.description: Some works adopt a non-standard protocol where models are trained only on queried (labeled) data but evaluated on the entire dataset, including instances seen during training. This differs from strict prequential test-then-train, where each instance is tested before becoming part of the training set. Such a protocol can lead to partial overlap between training and test data, which may bias performance estimates. It reflects a batch-style evaluation layered on top of an active querying process.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences describing Fujii and Kashima (2016): 'their evaluation strategy involved training models on the queried data and subsequently testing them with the entire dataset... differs from the conventional test-then-train paradigm...'.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Window-based batch evaluation in streams
topic_metadata.description: Window-based evaluation assesses prediction accuracy over all observations within the current batch or window of a data stream. Models are evaluated on each window as a unit, reflecting performance over recent data rather than on a per-instance basis. This approach can smooth short-term fluctuations and is useful when data naturally arrive in batches. It diverges from strictly online, instance-level prequential evaluation while still respecting temporal structure.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentence 'Another example is found in Zhu et al. (2007), who utilized a window-based approach, assessing prediction accuracy across all observations in the current batch.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Network protocol identification with AL
topic_metadata.description: Online active learning is used for network protocol identification, where traffic data streams must be classified into protocol types under changing conditions. Zhang et al. (2020a) propose a method to select the most representative instances on the fly, focusing labeling effort where it most benefits the model. This approach enables continual adaptation of the protocol classifier to dynamic data distributions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences beginning 'Another application of online active learning in the field of IT...' through 'adapt the model to dynamic data distributions.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Limits of deep AL in stream settings
topic_metadata.description: Many effective deep active learning strategies for computer vision rely on clustering or computing pairwise similarities between image embeddings to select diverse or informative samples. Such operations typically require multiple passes over the dataset or substantial storage, making them ill-suited to single-pass, stream-based scenarios. Consequently, these deep AL methods are not easily adaptable to online learning from data streams.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'Computer vision is another interesting area...' focusing on sentences about deep active learning methods, clustering, pairwise similarity, and single-pass limitations.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-based AL for 3D objects
topic_metadata.description: For stream-based classification of 3D objects, online active learning can rely on traditional models combined with uncertainty sampling. Narr et al. (2016) employ a Mondrian forest classifier, an efficient online alternative to random forests, and query labels for images with high classification uncertainty. This design balances computational efficiency with focused labeling of the most ambiguous 3D object instances.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences starting 'Narr et al. (2016) analyze the stream-based active learning problem...' through their use of a Mondrian forest and uncertainty-based selection.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Vision-based process monitoring with AL
topic_metadata.description: Online active learning is applied to vision-based process monitoring to reduce the effort required for manual image labeling while tracking industrial or operational processes. Rožanec et al. (2022) first extract visual features using a pre-trained ResNet-18 model, then employ online active learning to decide which images should be annotated. This combination leverages deep feature representations with selective labeling to make process monitoring more scalable.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final sentences mentioning 'Rožanec et al. (2022) used online active learning...' and the use of pre-trained ResNet-18 for feature extraction.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Feature-filtered streaming active learning
topic_metadata.description: A mutual-information-based feature selection step retains only √n of the original features to train an online classifier, where n is the number of observations in the training set. This reduced feature set is then used with a simple uncertainty-based active learning strategy. The approach is combined with several streaming classification algorithms, including Hoeffding trees, Hoeffding adaptive trees, stochastic gradient trees, streaming logistic regression, and streaming k-nearest neighbors.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening paragraph up to the list of five streaming classification algorithms.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Gradient-based diversity sampling for DNNs
topic_metadata.description: For deep streaming active learning, each incoming example is represented by the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the last-layer parameters, using the model’s argmax prediction as a pseudo-label. The selection probability of a point is made proportional to the determinant of the updated covariance matrix of gradient representations, favoring examples that contribute novel information. This determinant-based criterion encourages diversity and coverage in the gradient space of the selected batch.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting with 'Recently, Saran et al. (2023)' including equations (46) and (47).

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Slice-aware budgeting in streaming object detection
topic_metadata.description: In autonomous driving scenarios, streaming camera data includes heterogeneous and imbalanced conditions such as clear, foggy, and rainy weather. A streamline approach is proposed to actively allocate labeling budget across these slices, prioritizing those where the model underperforms rather than sampling proportionally to their frequency. This counters the tendency of passive sampling to under-represent rare but critical conditions in the training data.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph on Beck et al. (2023) describing varying weather scenarios and budget allocation to under-performing slices.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Diversity-based online AL for vehicle faults
topic_metadata.description: For autonomous cars, a diversity-based online active learning strategy is used to improve fault detection. The method focuses on selecting diverse informative examples to reduce the false alarm rate while enabling the system to learn about previously unseen faults. This tailors active sampling to safety-critical anomaly and fault detection in automotive systems.
topic_metadata.text_span: Short passage mentioning Yan et al. (2023) and their diversity-based online active learning strategy for autonomous cars.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Active learning in compressor optimization loops
topic_metadata.description: An industrial framework is introduced that couples a thermodynamics-based simulator of a centrifugal compressor with a Gaussian Process surrogate model and an online active learning module. The goal is to minimize the power absorbed during the boil-off process by adaptively selecting new experimental operating points. Simulator, surrogate, and optimizer interact in real time, with active learning guiding which experiments to run to efficiently explore and optimize compressor behavior.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final paragraph describing Ghiasi et al. (2023) and the compressor optimization framework.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: SBAD framework single-pass sampling
topic_metadata.description: The SBAD framework (Manjah et al., 2023) structures online active learning for data streams into sampling, fine-tuning, and evaluation phases. Sampling is performed in a single pass over the stream using a thresholding mechanism to decide which instances to query. This design aims to respect streaming constraints while still selecting informative examples.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentence referring to Fig. 14: 'SBAD framework (Manjah et al., 2023): sampling, fine-tuning and evaluation. The sampling is performed in a single-pass manner via thresholding.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Scalability of online active learning
topic_metadata.description: Online active learning algorithms must remain computationally efficient and scalable to cope with large datasets and high-velocity data streams. The time to make sampling decisions must be lower than the process feed rate; otherwise, buffers are required, which undermines the benefits of true online operation. As data volume and speed increase, computational demands can become prohibitive, limiting real-world deployment.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point 'Algorithm scalability' under section 5.2 Challenges.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Model interpretability in active querying
topic_metadata.description: Beyond selecting the most informative instances, it can be important to explain why particular samples are queried, especially in high-stakes domains. Providing interpretable rationales for query choices helps practitioners in areas like healthcare and manufacturing better understand both the model behavior and the underlying problem. This links active learning with explainability and user trust requirements.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point 'Model interpretability' under section 5.2 Challenges, including examples from healthcare and manufacturing.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.section_heading: Real-time annotation. In most of the presented works, it is assumed that labels are
topic_metadata.title: Real-time label availability in streams
topic_metadata.description: The section assumes that queried data points from a stream receive labels immediately. This real-time label availability is treated as a foundational condition for many active learning methods in streaming settings. It directly influences how quickly the model can adapt to incoming data and support subsequent querying decisions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening sentences of the section ('it is assumed that labels are immediately available...')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.section_heading: Real-time annotation. In most of the presented works, it is assumed that labels are
topic_metadata.title: Implementation challenges and annotation tools
topic_metadata.description: Despite its advantages, real-time annotation introduces practical implementation challenges, such as coordinating timely human or system responses and integrating them seamlessly into the learning pipeline. The section notes that these issues need to be addressed through advanced data annotation tools, which can support efficient labeling workflows in streaming environments.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final sentences of the section ('However, this approach poses some implementation challenges...')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.section_heading: Postponed annotation. There are cases where we must allow for a delay between
topic_metadata.title: Batch-mode active learning with streamed sampling
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses training deep neural networks from data streams under memory constraints, where instances are sampled in real time but labels and model updates are deferred until a batch is formed. The approach combines streaming data acquisition with batch-mode active learning, in which queried instances are accumulated and then labeled and used for model updates in batches. This design balances computational and memory limitations with the need for timely sampling decisions in streaming environments.
topic_metadata.text_span: sentences on 'training of deep neural networks' with 'real-time sampling from a data stream' and 'batch-mode active learning strategy (Ren et al., 2022)'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Active learning on data streams
topic_metadata.description: The section emphasizes the specific challenge of performing active learning when data arrive as a continuous stream and decisions must be made in real-time. Methods must select the most informative data points on-the-fly, under constraints such as limited labeling budgets and evolving data distributions. This contrasts with pool-based active learning where the full dataset is available in advance.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, sentences 1–3 ('This survey outlines the challenge...in real-time. Table 2 provides a summary...settings.')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Nonlinear regression and Bayesian optimization
topic_metadata.description: A key future direction is to develop online active learning strategies tailored to regression models, especially beyond linear models and linear bandits. The section notes growing interest in using Bayesian optimization techniques for active learning in nonlinear regression problems, where the goal is to select query points that improve function estimates efficiently. These methods can exploit probabilistic surrogate models to balance exploration and exploitation in streaming contexts.
topic_metadata.text_span: second paragraph, middle sentences ('First, we recommend further investigation...linear bandits. For example, there has been a recent spark of interest toward the use of Bayesian optimization...')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Object detection in data stream AL
topic_metadata.description: Object detection appears as a specialized task within online active learning for data streams, treated with single-model strategies. Both stationary and batch-processed settings are represented, suggesting interest in selectively labeling complex structured outputs (e.g., bounding boxes) under streaming constraints. This indicates an extension of AL for streams beyond standard classification and regression to more complex computer vision tasks.
topic_metadata.text_span: Rows labeled 'Object detection' under 'Single-pass' / 'Stationary' and 'Batch' / 'Stationary' in Table 2

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Limits of ensemble and batch online methods
topic_metadata.description: This topic highlights that ensemble models and batch-based approaches, although dominant in online classification, rely on assumptions that may break in real-world streaming applications. When data arrive continuously and resources are constrained, forming batches or maintaining multiple models may be infeasible. This motivates investigation into alternative online learning and sampling paradigms better suited to strict temporal or memory budgets.
topic_metadata.text_span: sentences 'Ensemble models and batch-based approaches have been the dominant methods in online classification...' through 'it may not be possible to divide it into batches due to time or memory constraints.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Query strategies for online active learning
topic_metadata.description: The survey reviews strategies for selecting the most informative data points in an online setting, where instances arrive sequentially. Key query mechanisms include uncertainty sampling, diversity sampling, query by committee, and reinforcement learning-based approaches. These methods aim to optimize which instances are labeled under limited annotation budgets while the data stream evolves. The topic concerns query selection criteria, model informativeness measures, and sequential decision-making policies.
topic_metadata.text_span: Main conclusion paragraph, sentence 6 (from 'We reviewed a wide range of strategies...' to 'among others.')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Reinforcement-based weight adjustment with DCIR
topic_metadata.description: Zhang et al. (2022) introduce a reinforcement mechanism to adapt dynamic classifier weights ω_d after each labeled instance, with a focus on class imbalance. The adjustment is triggered once the true label y_t is known and only if the sample belongs to a minority class according to the damped class imbalance ratio (DCIR). For such samples, each dynamic classifier’s weight is multiplicatively increased if it predicts correctly and decreased if it predicts incorrectly, as formalized in Algorithm 4. This strategy reinforces classifiers that perform well on minority classes, thereby improving performance under imbalance.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'They modified the original strategy by introducing a reinforcement mechanism...' through the description of DCIR and the full pseudocode of Algorithm 4.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Damped Class Imbalance Ratio (DCIR)
topic_metadata.description: The DCIR metric quantifies class imbalance in a data stream by considering the number of observations collected so far for each class. For each class κ, DCIR_κ summarizes its relative frequency in a damped manner, and a class is treated as minority when DCIR[y_t] < 1/K. This condition is used to decide when to apply special weight updates in Algorithm 4, focusing learning effort on underrepresented classes. DCIR thus operates as a streaming-aware imbalance indicator guiding active adaptation of the ensemble.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'The damped class imbalance ratio (DCIR) value is obtained...' through the condition 'if DCIR[yt] < 1/K then' in Algorithm 4.

topic_metadata.title: ProxyRank for CT segmentation cold-start
topic_metadata.description: ProxyRank designs specialized self-supervised pretext tasks tailored to CT segmentation to improve cold-start performance. The model is trained to learn threshold segmentation using an abdominal soft-tissue window, producing proxy labels that shape meaningful representations before any manual annotation. topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Empirical class probability from committee votes
topic_metadata.description: The class membership probabilities are estimated empirically from committee predictions using the pBAG function. For each pixel and class ω, pBAG is computed as the relative frequency with which committee members assign that class, implemented via the Kronecker delta operator δ to count votes. The numerator counts how many times a pixel is classified as ω across k models, normalized by the total number of predictions across all Ni predicted classes. This provides an empirical probability distribution over classes for each unlabeled sample.
topic_metadata.text_span: Equations defining pBAG and the accompanying explanation: 'where pBAG(y∗i = ω|xi) = ... The δ(y∗i,m, ω) operator returns the value 1 if the classifier using the m-th bag classifies the sample xi into class ω and 0 otherwise.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Normalized entropy query-by-bagging heuristic
topic_metadata.description: The normalized entropy query-by-bagging (nEQB) heuristic selects unlabeled pixels by maximizing a normalized entropy measure of committee predictions. First, HBAG(xi) is computed as the Shannon entropy of the empirical class probability distribution pBAG for pixel xi. This entropy is then normalized by log(Ni), where Ni is the number of distinct classes predicted for that pixel, to bound the uncertainty score and mitigate hotspots in regions where many classes overlap. The selection rule is ˆx_nEQB = arg max_{xi∈U} HBAG(xi) / log(Ni), making the method naturally suited to multiclass settings.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: G-optimality for predictive performance
topic_metadata.description: G-optimality is presented as an optimality criterion focused on predictive quality rather than solely parameter estimation. It seeks to minimize the maximum prediction variance v(x) over a region of interest R, solving min_D max_{x∈R} v(x). This provides protection against worst-case prediction uncertainty within the specified input domain.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final paragraph introducing predictive criteria and equation (40)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: G-, I-, and V-optimality via prediction variance
topic_metadata.description: G-optimality focuses on minimizing the maximum prediction variance over a region R, using the scaled prediction variance v(x) that depends on the information matrix (X⊤X)⁻¹ and the model-expanded point x(m). Because it protects against the highest possible variance, G-optimality can be heavily influenced by anomalous observations. I- and V-optimality address this by integrating or averaging prediction variance over R, targeting overall rather than worst-case prediction accuracy.
topic_metadata.text_span: paragraph containing equation (41) for v(x) and discussion of G-optimality, I-optimality, and V-optimality

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: A-optimality for parameter variance minimization
topic_metadata.description: A-optimality is defined as minimizing the sum of the variances of the regression coefficients, which correspond to the diagonal elements of (XᵀX)⁻¹. In terms of the moment matrix M(D), an A-optimal design D* minimizes tr[M(D)]⁻¹. This focuses on improving average precision of parameter estimates across all coefficients.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point labeled “A-optimality”

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: D-optimality and ellipsoid volume reduction
topic_metadata.description: D-optimality considers both variances and covariances of the regression coefficients by maximizing the determinant of the moment matrix M(D). Equivalently, it minimizes the total volume of the confidence ellipsoid for β, leading to designs that are highly informative in a joint, multivariate sense. A D-optimal design D* satisfies max_D |M(D)| = |M(D*)|.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point labeled “D-optimality” and the prior discussion of ellipsoid volume

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: E-optimality via eigenvalue control
topic_metadata.description: E-optimality aims to shrink the confidence ellipsoid by minimizing the maximum eigenvalue of the covariance matrix of β̂. By controlling this worst-case eigenvalue, E-optimal designs reduce the largest principal axis of the ellipsoid, improving the least well-estimated linear combination of parameters. This yields a more balanced precision across directions in parameter space.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet point labeled “E-optimality” and reference to eigenvalues of X⊤X

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: A-, D-, and E-optimality criteria
topic_metadata.description: A-, D-, and E-optimality are optimal design criteria expressed in terms of a confidence ellipsoid around model parameters. A-optimality seeks to shrink the hyper-rectangle enclosing the ellipsoid (minimizing average parameter variance), D-optimality minimizes the ellipsoid volume (maximizing determinant of information), and E-optimality reduces the length of the longest axis (minimizing worst-case parameter variance). These criteria guide where to place design points to optimally reduce parameter uncertainty.
