topic_metadata.title: Evolving fuzzy systems for adaptation
topic_metadata.description: Evolving fuzzy systems are a class of fuzzy systems that can adapt and change over time in response to new data or environmental changes. They dynamically modify their internal structure, particularly rules and membership functions, to maintain performance in non-stationary settings. This adaptability makes them suitable for streaming and continually changing data scenarios.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening sentences of the section describing 'evolving fuzzy system approaches' and their ability to adapt and change over time

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.section_heading: Evolving fuzzy system approaches. These approaches are based on a type of fuzzy system
topic_metadata.title: Contrast with traditional fixed fuzzy systems
topic_metadata.description: Traditional fuzzy systems rely on fixed rules and membership functions that do not change once defined, limiting their ability to cope with evolving data distributions. In contrast, evolving fuzzy systems explicitly adjust these components based on incoming data, enabling continual learning. This comparison highlights the key structural and behavioral differences between static and adaptive fuzzy paradigms.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section comparing traditional fuzzy systems with evolving fuzzy systems ('In traditional fuzzy systems... On the other hand...')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.section_heading: Evolving fuzzy system approaches. These approaches are based on a type of fuzzy system
topic_metadata.title: Handling non-stationary environments and applications
topic_metadata.description: Evolving fuzzy systems are positioned as particularly useful in non-stationary environments where data characteristics change over time. Example applications include control systems for autonomous vehicles that must adapt to varying traffic patterns, road conditions, and weather. The systems’ ability to update their rule base and membership functions allows robust performance under such dynamic operating conditions.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Evolving fuzzy systems for streaming data
topic_metadata.description: Evolving fuzzy systems (EFS) are presented as soft-computing models tailored to time-varying data streams, capable of dealing with novelty and ongoing knowledge expansion. They are self-developing, self-learning fuzzy rule-based or neuro-fuzzy systems that adapt both their parameters and structure on the fly as new data arrive. By dynamically growing and updating fuzzy rule bases, EFS aim to mimic human-like reasoning over data streams through a formal learning process. This provides an alternative paradigm for handling evolving concepts compared to traditional parametric models.
topic_metadata.text_span: Beginning of Section 3.3 Evolving fuzzy systems approaches (from 'An alternative way to take into account the time-varying nature' to 'implementing it utilizing data streams using a formal learning process.')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Evolving Fuzzy Systems architecture
topic_metadata.description: Evolving Fuzzy Systems (EFS) use fuzzy rules of the form mapping input variables to outputs via parametric consequents, with each rule associated to prototypes (focal points) and parameters. Their architecture includes a structure-evolving scheme and a parameter-updating scheme that together maintain and adapt the rule base. With every new labeled example, these learning modules update both structure and parameters to track the evolution of the data stream in an online manner.
topic_metadata.text_span: from the rule definition (Eq. 35) through 'These learning modules are used to update the EFS every time a new labeled example (xt, yt) is made available.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Rule generation, merging, and pruning in EFS
topic_metadata.description: The structure-evolving scheme in an EFS decides when to add new fuzzy rules, based on criteria indicating that the current rule base is insufficient to model new data. It also merges rules whose similarity exceeds a threshold and prunes redundant rules, thereby simplifying the model while preserving performance. This process controls model complexity in streaming settings where concepts and data distributions change over time.
topic_metadata.text_span: ‘The two key components of an EFS are the structure evolving scheme…’ through ‘The rule merging and pruning steps simplify the models by removing redundant rules and combining two rules when their similarity is larger than a given threshold.’

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Overlap and novelty in fuzzy rule antecedents
topic_metadata.description: In evolving fuzzy rule-based models, the overlap degree in the antecedent space is used to reduce the number of data points that fall into regions where two rules overlap, thereby improving rule distinctiveness and reducing ambiguity. Novelty content in the antecedent space quantifies how much new information incoming data bring, guiding when rule evolution or knowledge expansion is needed. Together, these measures steer the adaptive refinement of the fuzzy rule base in data streams.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Sliding-window forgetting strategy
topic_metadata.description: A sliding-window-based strategy discards labeled instances that will not belong to the future training window when their labels arrive. The current window Wn at time tx_n and the future training window Dn at time ty_n are compared, and all labeled instances (ai = 1) that lie in Wn but not in Dn form the forgetting set On. This prevents the learner from training on soon-to-be outdated observations, better aligning the model with the temporally relevant portion of the data stream.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Sliding-window kNN active learning with dual distance criteria
topic_metadata.description: Kurlej and Woźniak (2011) introduce a sliding-window active learning approach built on a k-nearest neighbors classifier whose reference set is a moving window. The window is updated either in a FIFO manner or by retaining examples selected through active learning, enabling adaptation to concept drift and time-varying data streams. The sampling strategy uses two distance-based criteria: a margin-like rule that queries instances close to neighbors from different classes, and a greedy-diversity rule that targets instances with large minimum distance to the current reference set. Both criteria are enforced via thresholds on pairwise distances.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Bayesian committee framework for unknown-class discovery
topic_metadata.description: Loy et al. (2012) propose a Bayesian online active learning framework that uses committee consensus to balance exploration and exploitation. Exploration aims to discover new, previously unknown classes, while exploitation refines decision boundaries for known classes. The model employs a Pitman–Yor process (PYP) prior together with a Dirichlet process mixture model (DPMM), a non-parametric clustering and classification approach that flexibly models the data-generating process and supports the emergence of new classes.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'Loy et al. (2012) presented a Bayesian framework that leverages the principle of committee consensus...' to the end of the provided text describing the use of Pitman-Yor Processes and Dirichlet process mixture models

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Dirichlet process mixture active querying
topic_metadata.description: A Dirichlet process mixture model (DPMM) is used to cluster streaming data, where each cluster defines a class probability distribution and the number of clusters is governed by a Dirichlet process allowing a potentially infinite, but effectively finite, number of clusters. At each time step, two hypotheses are sampled from the model and their posterior class predictions for the current point are compared. The label is queried when the two hypotheses disagree (disagreement-based querying) or when both predict a new class index K+1, enabling novel-class detection. This integrates nonparametric Bayesian clustering with selective labeling in a data stream setting.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Photointerpretation and redundancy in VHR imagery
topic_metadata.description: In very high resolution imagery, labels are often obtained through visual inspection or photo-interpretation directly on the image, making data collection easier. However, mass selection of neighboring pixels with similar appearance leads to highly redundant training sets, which slows model training and may include many pixels carrying nearly identical information.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: On-screen photointerpretation with small batches
topic_metadata.description: When labels are acquired by on-screen photointerpretation in very high resolution (VHR) imagery, users can perform many iterations with relatively small query batches. In this regime, complex active learning heuristics that promote spectral diversity among selected samples are preferred, because they effectively reduce redundancy and better explore the feature space. The text notes that the computational complexity of diversity-enforcing heuristics grows quickly with batch size, reinforcing the small-batch setting.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Breaking Ties uncertainty sampling strategy
topic_metadata.description: The Breaking Ties (BT) strategy is an uncertainty-based active learning heuristic that exploits conditional label probabilities p(y*i = ω|xi) for each unlabeled candidate xi. It uses the predicted label y*i = arg maxω f(xi, ω) and the associated class probabilities, analogous in spirit to the EQB method mentioned earlier. Such probabilities can be produced by probabilistic neural networks, maximum likelihood classifiers, or other models that output calibrated class likelihoods. BT focuses on candidates where the classifier is most ambiguous between top classes, effectively targeting decision-boundary regions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Second paragraph, from 'B. Breaking ties (BT)' through 'Such estimates are provided by several methods, including probabilistic neural networks or maximum likelihood classifiers.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Breaking Ties uncertainty sampling heuristic
topic_metadata.description: The Breaking Ties (BT) heuristic selects unlabeled samples for which a classifier is most uncertain, quantified as the smallest difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities. In both binary and multi-class settings, a small gap between these top probabilities indicates that the classifier is nearly indifferent between competing labels. The heuristic thus prioritizes samples that lie near decision boundaries, where model confidence is lowest.

topic_metadata.title: BT method using single probabilistic model
topic_metadata.description: The BT method is an active learning strategy that relies on a single probabilistic classifier providing p(y|x) for sample selection. Instead of an ensemble, it exploits uncertainty or related criteria derived from the model’s posterior distribution to choose informative unlabeled samples. This simplifies computation while still leveraging probabilistic confidence information for query decisions.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Dominant labeling and class-balanced sampling
topic_metadata.description: Dominant labeling assigns to each superpixel the majority class label of its pixels, then propagates this label to every pixel in the region, avoiding detailed boundary delineation. Cai et al. (2021) combine this with a class-balanced sampling strategy to preferentially select superpixels that contain minority classes, improving class balance in queried data. Their results show that dominant labeling with superpixels significantly outperforms precise patch-level labeling under the same number of annotation clicks, highlighting gains in annotation efficiency.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Adaptive merging and splitting of superpixels
topic_metadata.description: Building on dominant labeling, Kim et al. (2023) propose adaptively merging spatially adjacent and similar superpixels, while splitting those that are complex. This dynamic adjustment produces region units that better match underlying structures, potentially improving both label consistency and uncertainty estimation. The adaptive scheme achieves better performance than the fixed superpixel approach of Cai et al. (2021).

topic_metadata.title: Historical development and survey gap in AL for NLP
topic_metadata.description: Active learning has been researched for over two decades, with foundational work in the 1990s and multiple subsequent literature surveys. However, existing surveys, especially those focused on NLP such as Settles (2009) and Olsson (2009), are now outdated relative to recent advances in the field. The text highlights a current gap: the lack of a contemporary, comprehensive survey of active learning specifically tailored to modern NLP developments.

topic_metadata.title: Multi-planar 2D and 3D segmentation framework
topic_metadata.description: The method trains three separate 2D segmentation networks, each operating on slices from a different plane (axial, sagittal, coronal), alongside a 3D segmentation network. These networks generate four sets of pseudo-labels that are then used to train a final 3D segmentation model, effectively fusing information from multiple views. Experimental results indicate that this slice-based training pipeline surpasses uniform slice sampling in segmentation performance.

topic_metadata.title: Segmentation training, loss, and augmentation
topic_metadata.description: The segmentation model is trained with a composite loss combining cross-entropy and Dice loss, capturing both per-pixel accuracy and overlap-based region similarity. Training uses the Adam optimizer for 4,000 iterations with a batch size of 32, a base learning rate of 0.001, and a polynomial learning rate decay schedule. Data augmentation includes random flips and rotations by fixed 90 degrees and arbitrary angles to increase spatial robustness of the model.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Fixed-confidence and fixed-budget linear bandits
topic_metadata.description: Subsequent work on pure exploration linear bandits distinguishes fixed-confidence and fixed-budget settings. Jedra and Proutiere propose algorithms that, given a target confidence level, adaptively sample arms until the best arm can be identified with that confidence. Azizi et al. study the complementary fixed-budget case, determining how to optimally use a given number of pulls, and extend the framework to generalized linear models, broadening the class of reward-generating processes beyond simple linearity.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Fixed-confidence evaluation in bandit algorithms
topic_metadata.description: In the fixed-confidence setting for bandit algorithms, the goal is typically to identify the best arm with a guaranteed confidence level under a limited budget. Performance is assessed by relating label complexity—the number of labeled observations required—to factors such as problem dimensionality or the number of arms pulled. This framing emphasizes sample efficiency and theoretical bounds on how many interactions are needed to reach a target confidence.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the excerpt: 'bandit algorithms employed a distinct evaluation approach... In the ﬁxed conﬁdence setting, performance typically hinges on comparing label complexity to problem dimensionality or the number of arms pulled, as observed in Fiez et al. (2019).'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Norm-thresholding extension to multi-model MAB
topic_metadata.description: The norm-thresholding approach is extended to scenarios where a learner must estimate multiple models uniformly well under a shared labeling budget. This is cast as a multi-armed bandit–like setting, where each model (or arm) has an unknown difficulty and pulls correspond to acquiring labels. Riquelme et al. propose a trace upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm that uses a trace-based uncertainty measure to guide budget allocation across models. The method jointly estimates model difficulty and decides how to distribute limited label queries.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Upper Confidence Bound in bandits
topic_metadata.description: The Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm is used in multi-armed bandit problems to trade off exploration and exploitation by combining the predicted mean reward and its uncertainty (standard deviation), scaled by a tunable parameter. By assigning higher scores to arms with either high estimated reward or high uncertainty, UCB guides the sequential selection of arms to maximize long-term reward. It operationalizes exploration–exploitation balance via confidence intervals on expected rewards.

This structure-aware design aims to improve multi-label predictions by exploiting label co-occurrence patterns.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Linear margin-based online prediction
topic_metadata.description: The learner uses a linear predictor parameterized by a weight vector w ∈ R^d to classify each incoming instance in a data stream. At time t, after observing xt, the predicted label is the sign of the inner product wᵀ_{t−1} xt, and this inner product defines the margin p_t. The margin quantifies the confidence of the current model on xt and later serves as a key quantity in the querying rule.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences describing the linear predictor and Eq. (1), including the definition of the margin pt.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Second-order online active learning
topic_metadata.description: Second-order online active learning augments traditional margin-based (first-order) strategies by explicitly modeling the classifier’s parameter uncertainty. The weight vector w ∈ R^d is assumed to follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution w ~ N(μ, Σ), where μ encodes the current estimate and the variances and covariances in Σ encode confidence about each feature weight and their dependencies. This allows the method to consider both the margin value and the associated uncertainty when deciding whether to query a label and update the model.

topic_metadata.title: Pre-training effects on DAL and spurious correlations
topic_metadata.description: The paper examines how pre-training a ResNet18 backbone on ImageNet-1K (ResNet18P) influences DAL performance on datasets with different characteristics, focusing on Waterbird and MNIST. Waterbird contains spurious correlations between object class and background, causing non pre-trained models to over-rely on background cues (e.g., misclassifying landbirds as waterbirds when the background is water). Pre-trained models offer richer feature representations and improved object semantics, which help DAL methods focus on relevant object information rather than spurious backgrounds.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Effect of pretraining on DAL for easy vs. hard tasks
topic_metadata.description: Pretraining is analyzed on both an easy, well-studied dataset (MNIST) and a harder, spurious-correlation dataset (Waterbird). On MNIST, pretraining consistently boosts overall accuracy across DAL methods without largely changing their relative ranking, except for a notable improvement of LPL when using better features from ResNet18P. This setup isolates how pretraining interacts with DAL strategies under different task difficulties, showing that gains can be substantial yet method ordering remains mostly stable.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Backbone quality, bias, and DAL selection on Waterbird
topic_metadata.description: On the Waterbird dataset, DAL methods such as Entropy, EntropyD, CEAL, and KMeans are found to be highly sensitive to the quality of the backbone network. With a non-pretrained ResNet18, low-quality features lead to poor query choices, and acquiring more labels can even amplify biases due to group imbalance, degrading performance (including mismatch and worst-group accuracy). When switching to a pretrained ResNet18P, these methods ‘return to normal’ because predictions better reflect object semantics rather than spurious background cues.

topic_metadata.description: The text highlights the scenario where the model used during querying differs from the final model used at deployment, termed query–successor model mismatch. This mismatch can arise when a lightweight model guides selection for a heavier successor model, potentially harming downstream performance if their inductive biases differ. The survey examines methods to mitigate or account for this mismatch when designing AL strategies.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Model mismatch in active learning
topic_metadata.description: Model mismatch refers to using different models for querying and for final deployment (successor models), or reusing data collected by one model to train another. The section highlights that while it is natural to keep a single best-performing model, practical constraints (efficiency, model evolution over time) often lead to mismatches. Empirical studies show that such mismatch can significantly reduce or even negate the performance gains of active learning, raising concerns about the long-term utility of AL-collected datasets.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Adaptive Maximum Disagreement query rule
topic_metadata.description: The Adaptive Maximum Disagreement (AMD) heuristic selects unlabeled samples whose predictions across views are most uncertain according to a multiview entropy criterion. Formally, given a partition of the d-dimensional input space into V views, AMD selects the candidate ˆxAMD in the unlabeled pool U that maximizes HMV(xi). This aligns active learning with areas where committee members (views) disagree the most, focusing labeling effort on the most informative pixels. AMD thus operationalizes disagreement in a principled, entropy-based way.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Candidate subset selection to reduce computation
topic_metadata.description: To alleviate computational cost, the AMD approach restricts selection to a subset of the unlabeled pool containing only the most uncertain pixels. Specifically, candidate pixels are those for which the committee (the set of view-based classifiers) has predicted the largest number of distinct classes, indicating high disagreement. AMD is then applied within this reduced subset, maintaining informativeness while lowering processing effort. This strategy balances query quality and scalability for large remote sensing datasets.

topic_metadata.title: Regional consistency and combined uncertainty metrics
topic_metadata.description: Li et al. (2023) use superpixels to compute a regional consistency measure, defined as the difference between the model prediction and the dominant class within each superpixel. This regional consistency is combined with other metrics such as entropy and diversity to identify the most uncertain foreground and background superpixels. By focusing queries on these regions, their approach aims to reduce annotation cost while targeting areas where model predictions are least aligned with local dominant labels.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: IoU-Based Quality Prediction for 3D Segmentation
topic_metadata.description: In 3D medical image interactive segmentation, a quality predictor network is used to estimate the reliability of current segmentations. This predictor outputs a predicted Intersection-over-Union (IoU) score for each slice relative to an ideal segmentation. Slices with lower predicted IoU are automatically suggested for expert annotation, where users can provide corrections via scribbles, bounding boxes, or extreme clicks. This mechanism focuses expert effort on low-quality slices, integrating prediction quality assessment with interactive refinement.

topic_metadata.title: Training paradigms and fine-tuning regimes
topic_metadata.description: The text contrasts earlier deep learning paradigms, such as training from scratch, with pre-train–finetune strategies using supervised or self-supervised pre-trained models. It then introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and prompt tuning, where only a small fraction of model parameters (e.g., 5%) are updated for downstream tasks. This evolution in training regimes forms the technical backdrop for how AL strategies might need to adapt.

topic_metadata.title: Active learning under PEFT and prompt tuning

topic_metadata.title: CNN-based DeepAL for Text Classification
topic_metadata.description: [251] proposes an active learning strategy for CNN-based sentence and text classification that selects instances expected to induce the largest updates in word embeddings. The method targets samples whose embeddings are likely to change with the greatest magnitude, rapidly learning discriminative, task-specific representations. This approach outperforms traditional AL baselines on both sentence and document-level text classification tasks.

topic_metadata.title: RNN-Based Acquisition in Text DeepAL
topic_metadata.description: [7] introduces a DeepAL framework for text classification that uses an RNN as the acquisition function to drive sample selection. By learning which text instances are most informative, the method reduces the number of labeled examples needed while maintaining accuracy. topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online active learning with expert forecasters
topic_metadata.description: A committee-based framework is proposed where an online learner follows predictions from a pool of N experts and aims to minimize the number of label queries while maintaining strong predictive performance. The learner adapts forecaster algorithms such as the exponentially weighted average forecaster (EWAF) and the greedy forecaster, forming its prediction as a weighted average of expert predictions and updating expert weights based on incurred loss. Performance is analyzed via cumulative regret, defined as the difference between the learner’s cumulative loss and that of each expert over time. In EWAF, expert weights are set proportional to the exponential of their cumulative regret, emphasizing experts with better historical performance.
topic_metadata.text_span: remaining paragraphs, from 'A different kind of committee has been considered by Hao et al. (2018a)...' through equations (20)–(22)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Active EWAF and GF with limited labels
topic_metadata.description: Hao et al. extend the Exponentially Weighted Average Forecaster (EWAF) and the Generalized Forecaster (GF) to an online active learning setting where the true label yt is not always observed. They introduce a binary variable Zt ∈ {0,1} to decide whether to request a label at round t, and define the cumulative loss Li,T of each expert only over the queried instances. The active forecaster’s prediction pt is obtained by projecting an underlying prediction pt into [0,1], and is designed to approximate what would be obtained in a fully supervised setup. This framework formalizes how expert-advice forecasters operate under label budget constraints.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'Hao et al. (2018a) extended the EWAF and GF...' through the definition of Li,T in equation (23) and the explanation of pt and pt.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Confidence-based querying in AEWAF and AGF
topic_metadata.description: The sampling strategy for active expert-advice forecasters is based on confidence conditions that bound the difference between the fully supervised prediction pt and the active prediction pt. In AEWAF, a label is considered unnecessary if the maximum pairwise disagreement between any two experts’ outputs is below a tolerance δ, which guarantees |pt − pt| ≤ δ; a robust variant is proposed to handle noisy or bad experts violating this assumption. In AGF, the confidence condition is instead defined via the maximum deviation of each expert’s prediction from pt, again ensuring |pt − pt| ≤ δ when this deviation is small. These criteria operationalize when the forecaster is confident enough to skip querying a label while keeping the active prediction close to the fully supervised one.
topic_metadata.text_span: From 'The sampling strategy is based on the determination of a confidence condition...' through equations (24) and (25) and the discussion of the robust AEWAF and AGF conditions.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Per-round regret as evaluation metric
topic_metadata.description: Per-round regret measures the difference in loss between a forecaster (or learning algorithm) and the best expert at each iteration of the active learning process. It originates from online learning and bandit theory and focuses on cumulative or step-wise suboptimality rather than classification accuracy alone. Using per-round regret emphasizes how quickly an active learner approaches the performance of the best possible strategy. This metric is particularly suited to decision-making scenarios framed as expert advice or bandit problems.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentence 'On a different note, Hao et al. (2018a) employed the per-round regret metric, which quantifies the loss difference between the forecaster and the best expert at each iteration of the active learning process.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Regret and error metrics vs trial budget
topic_metadata.description: An alternative evaluation approach for bandit algorithms focuses on regret or prediction error as functions of the number of trials. Here, performance is measured by how quickly an algorithm reduces regret or error given a specified trial budget, reflecting its learning speed and efficiency over time. Studies such as those by Riquelme et al. (2017a), Sudarsanam and Ravindran (2018), and Fontaine et al. (2021) exemplify this trial-based evaluation methodology.
topic_metadata.text_span: Later sentences of the excerpt: 'Alternatively, regret or error metrics were evaluated against the required number of trials, as demonstrated in the studies by Riquelme et al. (2017a), Sudarsanam and Ravindran (2018), Fontaine et al. (2021).'

topic_metadata.title: Hyperspectral dataset preprocessing and sampling

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Multiclass level uncertainty criterion
topic_metadata.description: Multiclass level uncertainty (MCLU) extends margin sampling from binary to multiclass SVM classification by considering the distance to the margin for the two most probable classes. The criterion f(x_i)^MC is defined as the difference between the maximum per-class decision value and the maximum decision value among all remaining classes. Samples with small f(x_i)^MC are considered unreliable and are selected for labeling, formalized by x̂_MCLU = argmin_{x_i∈U} f(x_i)^MC. This provides an uncertainty measure that directly leverages all SVM decision values across classes.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 'B. Multiclass level uncertainty (MCLU)', including equations (8) and (9)

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: MCLU versus margin sampling in mixed regions
topic_metadata.description: MCLU is contrasted with standard margin sampling (MS) in areas of the feature space where three classes overlap. Because MCLU is computed from all per-class decision values, it yields maximal uncertainty in highly mixed regions, whereas MS yields uncertainty values slightly lower than along two-class decision boundaries. This leads to better identification of ambiguous samples in complex multiclass regions, particularly in the illustrated top-right area of the feature space. The comparison emphasizes MCLU's advantage when more than two classes interact locally.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Pairwise stable–dynamic classifier strategy
topic_metadata.description: The pairwise strategy uses two models: a stable classifier Cs trained on all labeled data seen so far (L1, …, Lt−1) and a dynamic classifier Cd trained only on the most recent batch Lt−1. Predictions for an incoming instance xt are obtained via a weighted combination fE(xt) = ωs fCs(xt) + ωd fCd(xt). When the dynamic classifier outperforms the stable one, Cs is replaced by Cd, enabling rapid adaptation to concept drift by emphasizing recent data and discarding older, potentially obsolete information. However, this hard replacement leads to forgetting older patterns and is ineffective for gradual drifts that require longer-term memory.
topic_metadata.text_span: second paragraph, from 'Shan et al. (2019) and Zhang et al. (2018) developed' through 'makes the learner forget about observations away from the current window.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Ensemble reactive models for mixed drifts
topic_metadata.description: To better handle both gradual and abrupt drifts, Shan et al. extend the pairwise approach by replacing the single reactive classifier with an ensemble of dynamic classifiers. In this variant, the stable classifier continues to learn from all labeled instances, while multiple dynamic classifiers are trained on multilevel recent windows of the stream. This ensemble of reactive models provides a richer representation of recent concepts over different temporal scales, enabling simultaneous responsiveness to sudden changes and robustness to slow, gradual shifts.
topic_metadata.text_span: end of section, from 'Hence, similarly to the approach of Zhu et al. (2007)' to 'trained on multilevel'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Stable–dynamic ensemble for concept drift
topic_metadata.description: The method uses an ensemble composed of one stable classifier and multiple dynamic classifiers to handle concept drift in data streams. The final prediction fE(x_t) is a weighted combination of the stable classifier output and the outputs of D dynamic classifiers. This structure enables both long-term stability and short-term adaptability to changing concepts.

topic_metadata.title: Multiview entropy uncertainty measure
topic_metadata.description: The multiview entropy HMV(xi) quantifies uncertainty over class labels by aggregating predictions from classifiers built on each view. It is defined as the Shannon entropy of a multiview class probability distribution pMV(y*i = ω | x_i^v), summing over all classes ω. High entropy indicates strong disagreement or uncertainty among the views’ predictions, making the corresponding sample a prime candidate for querying. This measure directly drives sample selection in the AMD heuristic.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: View-class weighting matrix for prediction fusion
topic_metadata.description: The probability pMV(y*i = ω | x_i^v) used in multiview entropy is computed via a weighting matrix W^ε−1 that encodes each view’s ability to discriminate each class. An indicator δ(y*i,v, ω) counts when a classifier built on view v predicts class ω, and these counts are weighted and normalized over views and classes using W^ε−1. At each iteration ε, W is updated based on the true labels of newly sampled pixels, then its columns are normalized to sum to one. This adaptive weighting increases the influence of views that prove more reliable for specific classes over the course of active learning.

topic_metadata.title: Chunk-based ensemble active learning
topic_metadata.description: The data stream is divided into chunks St, each used to train a current classifier Ct, while an ensemble retains the k−1 most recent past classifiers Ct−k+1, …, Ct−1 trained on labeled subsets Lt−k+1, …, Lt−1. At each time t, the ensemble is used to predict labels for the unlabeled instances Ut in the current chunk. Classifier predictions are combined via weights ωt−k+1, …, ωt−1, and a weight updating rule adapts the ensemble to evolving data streams. This framework allows reuse of past models even when raw historical data are no longer available.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: MAO: Most Ambiguous and Orthogonal heuristic
topic_metadata.description: The MAO (Most Ambiguous and Orthogonal) heuristic introduces an explicit diversity notion by constraining margin sampling with an angular distance in feature space. It starts from a subset of samples selected by pure margin sampling (UMS) and iteratively chooses new samples that are both ambiguous (high uncertainty) and as orthogonal as possible to the already selected ones. Orthogonality is quantified via the angle between feature vectors, which acts as a diversity metric to spread labeled points across the feature space. This leads to iterative batch selection where each new pixel maximizes angular diversity relative to the current batch.

By computing these metrics during selection, the algorithm can favor samples that expand the coverage of the feature space or decision boundary. topic_metadata.title: Challenges of high-dimensional density estimation
topic_metadata.description: Density-based AL relies on accurate density estimation, which becomes difficult in high-dimensional feature spaces. Common density estimators like kernel density estimation and Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) struggle with scalability and accuracy as dimensionality increases. This limitation constrains the effectiveness of density-based representativeness measures in modern high-dimensional medical image representations.

topic_metadata.title: General diversity-based batch selection algorithm
topic_metadata.description: Algorithm 2 formalizes a generic procedure for diversity-based selection in a single active learning iteration. Starting from a reduced candidate set U* (already filtered by a base heuristic like margin sampling), the algorithm first picks the best candidate under the base criterion, then repeatedly adds samples that maximize a user-defined diversity measure with respect to the current batch S. After q pixels are selected, the batch is labeled, added to the training set, and removed from the candidate pool. This process operationalizes batch-mode active learning where exploitation (uncertainty) and exploration (diversity) are explicitly balanced.

topic_metadata.title: TypiClust and typical-sample querying
topic_metadata.description: TypiClust is based on a theoretical result that querying 'typical' samples is especially beneficial when annotation budgets are low. Using self-supervised features, it performs k-Means clustering and then selects samples from high-density regions of each cluster, effectively choosing prototypical points. This typicality-driven strategy aims to maximize the representativeness of the initial labeled set, improving label efficiency in the cold-start phase. It contrasts with purely uncertainty-based selection by prioritizing data density and coverage.

topic_metadata.description: Several AL approaches show strong performance within narrowly defined medical imaging domains but may fail to generalize to broader or different clinical applications. This domain specificity questions whether methods tuned to particular organs, modalities, or tasks can be reliably transferred to other medical imaging problems. The generalization issue becomes a central concern for deploying AL in diverse clinical environments.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section where the text notes AL works focused on a specific domain of medical imaging with excellent performance but questionable generalization.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Diversity, Distance, and Density Metrics
topic_metadata.description: Representative samples in AL should be spread across the data distribution to avoid redundancy and preserve the original distribution, implying a strong emphasis on diversity. This necessitates robust metrics for sample-wise or distribution-wise distances and sample density to characterize the dataset landscape. The unique properties of medical images may demand specialized distance metrics distinct from those used for natural images.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences starting 'Besides, representative samples should also be widely distributed...' through 'may require different distance metrics than that of natural images.'

topic_metadata.title: Improved discrepancy metrics for medical images
topic_metadata.description: Discrepancy-based AL depends critically on how distance between probability distributions is measured. Because discrepancy-based AL has seen limited use in medical image analysis, designing appropriate distribution-distance metrics could significantly advance its applicability in this domain.

topic_metadata.title: Performance prediction via expected loss reduction
topic_metadata.description: Performance-prediction strategies aim to select instances that most reduce future test error if labeled and added to training. Expected Loss Reduction (ELR) explicitly evaluates instances by their expected decrease in error after retraining, though it can be computationally expensive. Recent refinements introduce more efficient or refined metrics such as predicted error decay on groups, mean objective cost of uncertainty, and measures based on strictly proper scoring rules.

topic_metadata.title: Expected model change strategies
topic_metadata.description: Expected model change methods select samples whose labeling is predicted to induce the largest change in the model parameters or predictions. These strategies explicitly estimate how much the model would update if a candidate sample’s label were known, and prioritize those that most influence learning. They aim to directly link the query to anticipated model improvement rather than only uncertainty or diversity.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Expected error or variance minimization
topic_metadata.description: These strategies estimate how the model’s future generalization error or prediction variance would change if a candidate instance were labeled and added to the training set. The learner selects instances that are expected to most reduce this error or variance, directly optimizing a performance-related objective. This often requires modeling uncertainty over labels or parameters to compute expected outcomes of potential queries.

topic_metadata.title: Expected model change maximization
topic_metadata.description: Expected model change approaches select instances whose labeling would produce the largest update to the model parameters. The underlying assumption is that examples causing a strong change to the current hypothesis are most informative for learning. This requires estimating how gradient updates or parameter shifts depend on the unknown labels of candidate instances.

topic_metadata.title: Effect of training epochs on DAL performance
topic_metadata.description: An ablation study investigates how the number of training epochs in each active learning (AL) iteration affects deep learning-based DAL performance. Increasing epochs generally improves AUBC (area under the budget curve) for both Random and Entropy strategies, with Entropy especially benefiting from more epochs (e.g., a boost of about 1.5 AUBC at 30 epochs). However, the performance gains exhibit diminishing returns, and prior work suggests excessive epochs may harm generalization, highlighting the need to select an optimal epoch count that balances computation cost and test performance.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Human-computer interaction in streaming AL
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses the interaction between human labelers and active learning systems in data stream scenarios. It highlights the pivotal role of human-computer synergy in the labeling process while most online methods emphasize querying the most informative data points in real-time. The text also alludes to multiple distinct labeling scenarios, suggesting that different human-in-the-loop configurations may affect how queries are presented and labels are acquired over time.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Drift detector categories in streams
topic_metadata.description: The section distinguishes three macro-categories of drift detectors for data streams: error-based, data distribution-based, and multiple hypothesis testing methods. Error-based detectors monitor online changes in the classifier’s error rate (e.g., DDM, ADWIN), while the other two focus on detecting changes in data distributions or use statistical testing. The text emphasizes that error-based methods usually require full label availability, whereas the latter two can be implemented in an unsupervised way. This classification frames which detectors are suitable under label-scarce active learning conditions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Early part of the section discussing drift detectors and their three macro-categories, including DDM and ADWIN.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Error-based drift detection with sparse labels
topic_metadata.description: To address the need for labels in detecting concept drift, Krawczyk et al. propose applying an error-based drift detector to the few labeled instances obtained during online active learning. They employ ADWIN to monitor changes in performance on this sparse labeled subset and decide when to update or replace the current model. This yields a general framework that fuses active query selection with incremental model adaptation under drift. The approach leverages limited supervision efficiently instead of assuming labels for all instances.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section describing Krawczyk et al. (2018) and the use of ADWIN on actively collected labels.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: ADWIN-driven ensemble adaptation under drift
topic_metadata.description: An ensemble of N classifiers is maintained for online active learning in non-stationary data streams. The ADWIN drift detector monitors performance and, upon detecting concept drift, the classifier with the highest error is replaced by a newly trained model, enabling continual adaptation. This ensemble replacement mechanism allows the active learner to track evolving concepts while operating under streaming constraints.
topic_metadata.text_span: second paragraph, sentences describing ensemble of N classifiers and ADWIN-based replacement

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Time-variable uncertainty thresholds for budgeting
topic_metadata.description: The section presents a time-variable thresholding scheme to adapt the labeling budget around detected drifts. Given a base uncertainty threshold and an adjustment parameter r, the threshold is progressively reduced when ADWIN signals a warning or a confirmed drift, making the classifier request more labels in those periods. This ensures the labeling rate during drift is strictly higher than in static conditions, so the model can quickly gather representative samples of the new concept. The mechanism explicitly connects drift signals to dynamic budget allocation in online active learning.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting with “Moreover, the authors proposed the use of a time-variable threshold…” describing threshold changes on warnings and drifts.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Piecewise constant labeling rate control
topic_metadata.description: A related strategy by Castellani et al. introduces a piecewise constant budget function for non-stationary data streams with verification latency. The labeling rate is raised from its nominal value α to a higher rate α_high when a drift is detected, then lowered to α_low, and finally restored to α. The durations of these phases are chosen so that the long-term average labeling rate equals the original α. This method offers a simple, interpretable control policy linking drift events to temporary budget boosts and reductions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section where Castellani et al. (2022) and the α, α_high, α_low scheme and time segments are described.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Adaptive labeling rate around drift events
topic_metadata.description: The labeling rate α is dynamically adjusted to focus annotation effort around suspected drift periods. When a drift warning or detection occurs, α is increased (to αhigh) to collect more labels and better characterize the new concept; it is later reduced (to αlow) and eventually restored to its nominal value as stability returns. This behavior is formalized as a piece-wise constant budget function that modulates the sampling rate over time relative to drift detection and recovery intervals.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Intra- and extra-cluster sampling for batch streams
topic_metadata.description: Ienco et al. (2013) adapt a pre-clustering-based active learning method from pool-based to stream-based batch scenarios where only part of each block can be labeled. Their sampling strategy uses an extra-cluster metric to rank clusters and an intra-cluster metric to rank instances, relying on cluster homogeneity (number of predicted classes) to detect uncertain clusters and on representativeness (distance to centroid) and posterior-class probabilities to measure instance certainty. The learner alternates label queries across ranked clusters and their top-ranked instances.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Micro-cluster based adaptive stream classification
topic_metadata.description: Yin et al. (2023) propose a data stream classification method that maintains and updates micro-clusters built from initial training data. Labels for new instances are acquired using a mixed querying strategy that combines random sampling with a class-weighted margin score, and the micro-cluster model is dynamically updated. This enables adaptation to concept drift while controlling labeling effort.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: WI-DL and stage-wise hybrid querying
topic_metadata.description: WI-DL (Weighted Incremental Dictionary Learning) applies a two-stage hybrid query strategy within a Deep Belief Network framework. In the unsupervised feature learning stage, it emphasizes data representativeness, while in the supervised fine-tuning stage it emphasizes uncertainty; both indicators are integrated and optimized via a weighted incremental dictionary learning algorithm. This design reflects how different learning phases can prioritize distinct selection criteria.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Unsupervised pretraining with WI-DL in AL
topic_metadata.description: WI-DL addresses the impracticality of fully training Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) on limited labeled data in active learning by combining unsupervised feature learning on all (labeled and unlabeled) datasets with supervised fine-tuning only on labeled data. This improves DBN training efficiency under annotation constraints by leveraging unlabeled data to learn representations before task-specific supervised refinement. The process exemplifies a broader strategy of unsupervised pretraining plus supervised tuning within AL cycles.

topic_metadata.title: Posterior probability based active learning
topic_metadata.description: This topic covers a class of active learning methods that rank candidate samples using estimated posterior class probabilities p(y|x). The posterior values quantify classifier confidence, and heuristics are built by examining how adding a labeled candidate would change the overall or per-class posterior distribution. By focusing on samples that induce large changes or lie in regions of high uncertainty, these methods guide labeling effort to the most informative parts of the input space. The section introduces this family and indicates that specific heuristics like KL-max and Breaking Ties instantiate this principle.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: KL-max heuristic using KL divergence
topic_metadata.description: The KL-max heuristic selects candidates whose inclusion in the training set maximizes the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between posterior distributions before and after labeling. For each candidate, one estimates how much the posterior p(y|x) over the data would change if the candidate were added with its most likely label, and then chooses the sample producing the largest KL divergence. This strategy has been applied in remote sensing with probabilistic classifiers, including Maximum Likelihood classifiers, to prioritize pixels expected to induce the greatest model update. It formalizes informativeness in terms of distributional change rather than local uncertainty alone.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection A. KL-max, from “The first idea is to sample the pixels whose inclusion in the training set would maximize the changes in the posterior distribution.” through the description of applications in [47] and [48]

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: KL-divergence active learning criterion
topic_metadata.description: A Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence-based criterion selects the next pixel to label by comparing posterior class distributions with and without including a candidate sample. For each candidate xi, a new posterior p+(ω|x) is computed using an augmented training set X+ that includes xi labeled with its most probable class y*i. The KL divergence between p+(ω|x) and the original posterior p(ω|x) is accumulated over all other unlabeled pixels, and the pixel that maximizes this expected divergence (equations (17) and (18)) is chosen. This approach explicitly targets samples that most change the model’s predictive distribution over the unlabeled pool.
topic_metadata.text_span: First paragraph, from 'its posterior probability. The Kullbach-Leibler divergence KL is then computed...' through definition of equations (17) and (18) and the description of p+(ω|x) and X+.

topic_metadata.title: Posterior KL-max with multiple models
topic_metadata.description: Posterior KL-max is an active sampling heuristic that uses posterior class probabilities p(y|x) from multiple models and selects samples by maximizing a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence-related criterion. The notation '(q − 1) models' suggests an ensemble of probabilistic classifiers, each providing p(y|x), whose disagreement or divergence is exploited to measure informativeness. This approach targets samples where model posteriors differ most, aiming to reduce model uncertainty efficiently.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: KL-divergence-based Gaussian model update
topic_metadata.description: When a label yt for instance xt is queried, the Gaussian distribution over the classifier weights is updated by minimizing an objective based on the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. This constrains the posterior distribution to remain close to the previous one while incorporating the new labeled information, effectively performing a conservative update of μ and Σ. The KL-based formulation formalizes the trade-off between adapting to new data and preserving previous model knowledge in the streaming setting.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Linear contextual bandits and active regression
topic_metadata.description: Linear bandits, a form of contextual bandit, assume that the expected reward of each arm is a linear function of its feature vector and an unknown parameter vector, with observed rewards modeled as r(x) = xᵀθ* + ε. The learner interactively chooses arms x to best estimate θ* under noise, closely mirroring active linear regression where informative data points are selected to learn an underlying linear system. This establishes a tight conceptual link between pure exploration in linear bandits and active learning for regression.
topic_metadata.text_span: paragraph starting 'The pure exploration approach is particularly useful...' through the equation (45) and surrounding explanation

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Contextual-bandit ensemble for query selection
topic_metadata.description: Wassermann et al. (2019) model the sampling routine in online active learning as a contextual bandit problem where rewards measure the usefulness of query decisions. The learner receives positive reward ρ+ when requesting a label prevents a misclassification and negative reward ρ− when a query was unnecessary, thus penalizing ex-post useless label requests. An ensemble of models (experts) each decides whether to query based on prediction certainty exceeding a threshold, and experts are weighted by how past suggestions were rewarded and their agreement with others. The objective is to maximize cumulative reward over a time horizon T while adaptively allocating decision power across experts.
topic_metadata.text_span: second paragraph, from 'One approach to combining active learning and reinforcement learning' to 'objective function of the learner is to maximize the total reward over a time horizon T .'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Informative hierarchical margin cluster sampling (hMCS-i)
topic_metadata.description: hMCS-i extends margin-based cluster sampling by hierarchically partitioning candidate data while explicitly handling bounded support vectors to reduce redundancy. At each iteration, a dataset composed of MCLU-optimized candidates (U_MCLU) and bounded support vectors from the previous iteration is recursively split in a binary fashion, always subdividing the largest current cluster. The process continues until q clusters that contain no bounded support vector are obtained, and then selection is restricted to candidates within those clusters, again minimizing the margin-based objective. This design controls overlap between iterations and maximizes informativeness by avoiding repeatedly sampling points near existing bounded support vectors.

topic_metadata.title: M-SVM with nonlinear candidate clustering
topic_metadata.description: This topic refers to an active learning strategy built on a single multi-class SVM (M-SVM) combined with nonlinear clustering of candidate unlabeled samples. The clustering step groups candidates in feature space, and the SVM then guides which cluster representatives are queried to balance informativeness and diversity. This reduces redundancy in sampled points while exploiting the SVM decision structure.

topic_metadata.title: hMCS-i: clustering candidates and support vectors
topic_metadata.description: The hMCS-i method extends SVM-based active learning by performing nonlinear clustering not only on unlabeled candidates but also on current support vectors (SVs). By jointly considering candidates and SVs, it aims to maintain diversity in queried points while explicitly focusing on regions critical to the current decision boundary. This hybrid clustering enhances exploration near informative margins while avoiding oversampling similar SV neighborhoods.

topic_metadata.title: Criterion-switching SVM sampling for imbalance
topic_metadata.description: To address class imbalance in active learning, a method with linear SVMs dynamically switches among multiple instance selection criteria during online operation. topic_metadata.title: Pneumonia vs normal chest X-ray classification
topic_metadata.description: This topic involves binary classification of chest X-ray images into pneumonia vs normal categories, using the PneumoniaMNIST dataset. topic_metadata.title: Pathological WSIs and patch-based processing
topic_metadata.description: Pathological whole-slide images (WSIs) provide cellular-level microscopic detail for tasks like cancer staging and prognostic prediction but are extremely large (up to 100,000 × 100,000 pixels). To make them tractable for deep learning, WSIs are divided into many smaller patches that can be processed by CNNs or other models. Fully supervised approaches require patch- or cell-level labels, leading to very high annotation costs that motivate the use of active learning. This setup defines the basic data structure (WSI → patches) and cost constraints under which subsequent methods operate.

topic_metadata.title: Weakly supervised WSI classification via MIL
topic_metadata.description: When only WSI-level labels are available, the problem is framed as weakly supervised multi-instance learning (MIL), where each WSI is a bag and its patches are instances. A MIL model learns to identify task-relevant patches (e.g., cancerous regions) using only bag-level labels, drastically reducing the need for dense annotations. However, relevant instances are often heavily outnumbered by irrelevant patches (fat, stroma, debris, etc.), which makes optimization and convergence more challenging. This MIL formulation underlies subsequent AL strategies aimed at filtering out uninformative instances.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Holdout-based evaluation for stationary streams
topic_metadata.description: One evaluation scheme repeatedly measures model performance on a fixed holdout test set at each learning step. This approach is appropriate when dealing with stationary data streams whose distribution does not evolve over time. Under these conditions, using the same test set enables clearer assessment of prediction improvements as more labeled examples are incorporated into the model.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Holdout test set evaluation
topic_metadata.description: Holdout evaluation in data stream active learning uses a fixed, separate test set that is not involved in training to assess model performance. Various works adopt this strategy to measure prediction accuracy or error after the active sampling and training processes. This approach is more traditional and is often preferred when methods are not designed to cope with concept drift. It contrasts with online, instance-by-instance evaluation schemes such as prequential testing.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Prequential evaluation with forgetting mechanisms
topic_metadata.description: For non-stationary data streams, prequential evaluation can be combined with forgetting mechanisms to better reflect current performance under concept drift. Forgetting is typically implemented via sliding windows or fading factors that downweight older instances in the evaluation statistics. Gama et al. advocate this approach as more appropriate than simple static holdout schemes for evolving streams. It enables the performance estimate to adapt as the underlying data distribution changes over time.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences 'An in-depth analysis and discussion between the use of a holdout test set and the prequential evaluation scheme... suggested the use of a prequential evaluation scheme with forgetting mechanisms.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Choosing evaluation protocols under concept drift
topic_metadata.description: The survey distinguishes between evaluation protocols based on their suitability for drifting versus stationary or ill-suited methods. For active learning methods targeting drifting data streams, prequential evaluation is usually preferred because it naturally tracks performance over time. When algorithms are not designed to handle drift, static holdout test sets are more commonly used. This reflects a methodological choice linking the assumed data dynamics to the evaluation strategy.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences 'In most cases, when assessing active learning methods in the context of drifting data streams, a prequential approach is favored. Conversely, for scenarios where the methods are ill-suited to handle concept drifts, holdout test sets tend to be the preferred choice.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Purely theoretical evaluation of active learning
topic_metadata.description: Some works in active learning for data streams focus on theoretical analysis without employing empirical evaluation strategies like holdout or prequential testing. These studies analyze sample complexity, label complexity, or regret bounds under specific probabilistic or adversarial assumptions. As a result, they do not rely on concrete experimental protocols or metrics applied to datasets. Their contribution lies in formal guarantees and insights rather than empirical performance comparisons.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences 'In some instances, none of the previously mentioned methods were employed, as the analysis took a more theoretical perspective. This is exemplified by the works of Dasgupta et al. (2005), Chae and Hong (2021), Huang et al. (2022).'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Query-while-learning for decision trees
topic_metadata.description: A query-while-learning strategy for decision tree classifiers uses entropy intervals derived from evidential likelihood to guide label queries. The idea is to assess the uncertainty or ambiguity in the current tree's predictions via these entropy-based intervals and decide in real time whether to request a label for an incoming instance. This tailors active learning to tree-based models within a streaming context.

topic_metadata.title: Query-while-learning using dominant attributes
topic_metadata.description: This approach orders attributes by information gain ratio and defines 'dominant attributes' that guide label querying for new instances in a streaming scenario. A label for a new point xt is only requested if no dominant attribute exists, which helps identify one and narrow the entropy interval. It is particularly aimed at monitoring performance where minority class detection is critical, such as rare event detection. The adaptation ensures that evaluation remains meaningful despite class skew over time.

topic_metadata.title: Limitations of misclassification-based sampling under noise
topic_metadata.description: The text highlights that always selecting the most misclassified examples is only a reasonable sampling strategy when training labels are highly reliable. In the presence of noisy labels, this approach can preferentially pick examples that are mislabeled or lie on the wrong side of the optimal decision boundary. Such behavior can misguide model updates and degrade performance in an active learning setting.

topic_metadata.description: Transductive experimental design considers a setting where arms are pulled from a set X in order to improve predictions on a separate set of points Z. topic_metadata.title: Active distillation and teacher-student bias
topic_metadata.description: Active distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger pre-trained teacher model while actively selecting informative samples. Confirmation bias here arises when the student overfits to the teacher’s predictions, reproducing incorrect outputs instead of correcting them. To mitigate this, sample selection focuses on instances where the teacher is likely to err, encouraging the student to learn from discrepancies rather than blindly copying.

topic_metadata.description: The SBAD framework combines active learning with self-supervision to perform online active learning for object detection without relying on human annotators. Knowledge is distilled from a large teacher model to a lightweight student while explicitly accounting for the teacher’s imperfections. A confidence threshold, determined in a warm-up phase, is used to only query high-confidence images in order to mitigate confirmation bias in the distillation process.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty as Distance to Hyperplane
topic_metadata.description: This topic captures the common notion of uncertainty used across the described active learning strategies, defined as the distance of an instance from the prediction hyperplane. Both the b-sampling and logistic margin approaches derive the query probability P_t from |p_t|, the absolute perceptron margin, making points near the decision boundary much more likely to be labeled. This shared representation of uncertainty governs how selectively labels are requested in streaming scenarios.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Best-versus-second-best margin uncertainty
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty of an unlabeled instance x_t is quantified as the difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities, margin(x_t) = p(y = c_b | x_t) − p(y = c_sb | x_t). This "best-versus-second-best" margin is highlighted as an effective uncertainty measure when many classes are present. The approach combines this with a Manhattan-distance-based similarity between unlabeled observations, but requires computing similarity and uncertainty for all unlabeled samples in a batch, making it unsuitable for single-pass streaming active learning.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Active palmprint recognition via core-set matching
topic_metadata.description: Active Palmprint Recognition applies deep active learning to high-dimensional palmprint data by recasting AL as a binary classification problem distinguishing labeled from unlabeled samples. The goal is to obtain a labeled core subset whose distribution matches that of the full dataset, making the two sets hard to distinguish. Since generative modeling is difficult in this setting, the method instead selects samples that can be clearly distinguished from either labeled or unlabeled sets and iteratively adds them, correcting distributional mismatches caused by earlier core-set methods that ignored density.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Domain-adaptation-inspired palmprint DeepAL
topic_metadata.description: Active Palmprint Recognition proposes a DeepAL framework where active learning is formulated as a binary classification task inspired by domain adaptation. The goal is to make labeled and unlabeled sample sets share a similar data distribution so that they become hard to distinguish, effectively reducing domain shift between them. Supervised training is then carried out under this setting, using deep models and AL to jointly adapt features and queries for palmprint recognition.
