topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Bernoulli b-sampling query strategy
topic_metadata.description: The b-sampling method casts the query decision as a Bernoulli random variable whose parameter controls the probability of requesting a label. Proposed in early online active learning work by Cesa-Bianchi et al., this approach adjusts the Bernoulli parameter dynamically based on properties of the current instance. It provides a probabilistic alternative to hard thresholding, allowing stochastic control of labeling effort.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences starting with 'Another method, sometimes referred to as b-sampling...' through the mention of Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2004, 2006).

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Margin-dependent query probability function
topic_metadata.description: The probability of querying the label at time t is defined as P_t = b / (b + |p_t|), where p_t is the current margin and b is a tuning parameter. This Bernoulli parameter decreases as the absolute margin increases, meaning that points near the decision boundary (low |p_t|) are more likely to be queried. The mechanism formalizes uncertainty sampling in a probabilistic way, linking model confidence directly to labeling probability.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final sentences introducing Zt ∈ {0,1} and Eq. (3), defining Pt in terms of b and |pt|.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Logistic Margin Sampling Probability
topic_metadata.description: This topic focuses on the logistic margin sampling rule where the label-query decision is modeled as a Bernoulli variable Z_t with parameter P_t = e^{−γ|p_t|}. The probability of querying decreases exponentially with the absolute margin, again interpreting uncertainty as distance from the decision hyperplane. Compared to the traditional b-sampling P_t = b / (b + |p_t|), the logistic form yields a different sampling distribution over margins, affecting how sharply the querying probability decays as confidence increases.
topic_metadata.text_span: Equations and discussion around “According to the logistic margin sampling strategy, the sampling decision is taken by drawing a Bernoulli random variable Zt… Pt = e−γ |pt| … The main difference between the two strategies is the shape of the resulting sampling distribution”

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Randomized querying via Bernoulli and exponential mechanism
topic_metadata.description: To privatize the querying process, labeling decisions are modeled either as a Bernoulli random variable with parameter p (or 1−p) depending on whether c(t) is below or above a threshold τ, with p < 1/2, or via the exponential mechanism. In the latter, a Bernoulli with parameter q(t) assigns a constant labeling probability to points within a sampling region of radius α and an exponentially decaying probability to points outside, with q(t) defined using ε and Δ = (1 − α/M)^M under the assumption ||x_t|| ≤ M. These constructions inject controlled randomness while still favoring informative, near-boundary instances in the data stream.
topic_metadata.text_span: Third paragraph, from 'However, to avoid a deterministic decision process...' through equation (15) and the sentence about the bounded norm assumption.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Label delay and verification latency
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses the impact of label delay (verification latency) in online active learning, defined as the time between a query and the oracle’s provision of the label. If latency is not considered, the learner may issue redundant label requests for similar instances while earlier queries are still unresolved. Latency is categorized into null, intermediate, and extreme latency, with null latency corresponding to the common but idealized case of immediate label availability. Sampling strategies must explicitly account for these latency regimes to manage queries and model updates effectively in streaming scenarios.
topic_metadata.text_span: Latter part of the section starting from 'Another important property to consider when designing an active learning strategy is the label delay or verification latency' through the description of latency types.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Label latency in online active learning
topic_metadata.description: The text distinguishes different regimes of label latency in data streams, ranging from extreme latency (labels never arrive) to intermediate latency, where labels are delayed by a finite but non-zero time L. Extreme latency pushes the problem toward unsupervised learning, as no oracle feedback is ever obtained. Intermediate latency settings must explicitly handle delayed supervision, affecting how and when models can be updated using oracle-provided labels.
topic_metadata.text_span: early lines of the section, from 'Extreme latency, where labels are never made available...' to 'Intermediate latency assumes a delay 0 < L < ∞...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Handling verification latency via spatial information
topic_metadata.description: To cope with verification latency, the authors leverage the spatial locations of queried but not yet labeled points to guide future sampling. By recognizing regions where many nearby instances already have high utility (low confidence), the method avoids oversampling in those areas while labels are pending. This spatial awareness helps distribute queries more effectively across the input space under delayed feedback. It adapts active learning decisions to the structure of unlabeled regions and ongoing queries.
topic_metadata.text_span: Later part of the section beginning “The authors also tackled the verification latency issue…” up to avoiding oversampling in high-utility regions.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Verification latency in streaming active learning
topic_metadata.description: Verification latency refers to the delay between querying a label for a selected instance and receiving it from the oracle (tyi > txi). During this delay, the learner continues to process new instances without being able to update its utility function or decision threshold, which can lead to redundant label requests for similar instances and policy updates based on outdated information. This latency critically affects methods whose querying decisions depend on recently labeled neighbors or timely classifier updates in drifting data streams.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph beginning 'each nearest neighbor depends on the arrival time of the labels' through the description of txi, tyi, and the consequences before and after the requested label arrives

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Label quality and imperfect oracles
topic_metadata.description: The effectiveness of online active learning heavily depends on the quality of labels obtained from human annotators or other oracles. Real-world annotators may introduce errors, biases, or inconsistent interpretations of labeling instructions, and oracle imperfections must be considered, including cases like knowledge distillation where the oracle itself is a model. Additionally, label delays or latency complicate learning from streams, as highlighted earlier in the survey.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Stopping Criteria for Active Learning
topic_metadata.description: Determining when to stop querying is treated as a key component of the AL process, balancing further performance gains against additional annotation cost. Stopping criteria can be based on model confidence, validation performance, stability of predictions, or budget limits. The survey devotes a subsection to summarizing and comparing these stopping methods in NLP applications.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Need for and heuristics of AL stopping
topic_metadata.description: In practical applications, it is important to know when to stop active learning so that annotation is halted once model performance approaches its upper bound, before the labeling budget is exhausted. This requires stopping criteria that monitor appropriate metrics during AL. Simple heuristic criteria include stopping when all unlabeled instances lie farther from an SVM’s support vectors than labeled ones, or when no new n-grams are present in the unlabeled pool for machine translation.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 5.2, opening discussion on the desirability of knowing when to stop AL and examples of heuristic rules (sentences starting 'When adopting AL in practice...' through 'no new n-grams remain in the unlabeled set for MT').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Metrics for active learning stopping decisions
topic_metadata.description: Designing stopping criteria involves choosing appropriate metrics, which may include performance on a development set, cross-validation estimates, or query-strategy-derived measures. Standard dev sets can be too small and cross-validation may be biased due to AL’s non-uniform sampling. Alternative metrics include uncertainty or confidence scores, disagreement among models, estimated performance, expected error, confidence variation, actual performance on queried instances, and stability of predictions between consecutive AL iterations.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 5.2, paragraph on the 'metric' aspect of stopping criteria (sentences beginning 'For the metric, measuring performance...' through 'comparing the predictions between consecutive AL iterations is another reasonable option').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Threshold and trend-based stopping conditions
topic_metadata.description: Stopping conditions typically compare metric values against thresholds, but directly thresholding a single iteration’s metric (e.g., uncertainty or error below a fixed level) is sensitive to the specific model and task. To improve robustness, some approaches cascade multiple criteria, while others track metric trends over several AL iterations. Trend-based strategies stop when confidence consistently drops, the rate of performance change flattens, or prediction outputs stabilize across iterations.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 5.2, paragraph on the 'condition' aspect (sentences beginning 'The condition to stop AL is usually comparing the metrics...' through 'the predictions stabilize across iterations').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Relation to performance prediction and early stopping
topic_metadata.description: Stopping active learning is related to broader tasks such as predicting final model performance and performing early stopping during training. This connection is particularly important in early AL stages, which correspond to low-resource learning scenarios where data are scarce. Determining when to halt learning in these stages may require specialized early-stopping considerations aligned with AL’s incremental annotation process.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection 5.2, closing remarks (sentences starting 'Pullar-Strecker et al. (2021) provide an empirical comparison...' through the end of the section discussing performance prediction and early stopping).

These criteria determine when to stop querying labels from the oracle. However, the survey notes that such simple heuristics can lead to suboptimal performance through either premature stopping or unnecessary labeling.

topic_metadata.description: This topic covers criteria and algorithms for deciding when to stop querying additional labels in DeepAL. topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Norm-thresholding for online active regression
topic_metadata.description: Riquelme’s norm-thresholding algorithm applies A-optimality ideas to online active linear regression in data streams. Only observations whose (scaled) norms exceed a threshold τ are selected for labeling, where τ is set so that P(∥x∥ ≥ τ) = α, with α representing the desired fraction of labeled points in the stream. This yields a near A-optimal design by preferentially including more informative, high-norm covariate vectors.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Norm-thresholding for online active regression
topic_metadata.description: The section presents a norm-thresholding criterion for selecting which streaming data points to label in online active linear regression. A point xt is queried if its leverage score x_t^T (X^T X)^{-1} x_t exceeds a threshold τ, approximating a target sampling rate α. This design-optimality-based rule aims to prioritize points that most reduce prediction variance by using the current labeled design matrix X. The criterion is formalized in Equation (43) and operationalized within Algorithm 5.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Selective Sampling Perceptron with b-sampling
topic_metadata.description: This topic describes an online active learning algorithm that processes a data stream using a linear perceptron model under a labeling budget. At each time step, the model computes the margin p_t = wᵗx_t, predicts the label via the sign of the margin, and draws a Bernoulli random variable Z_t with parameter P_t = b / (b + |p_t|) to decide whether to query the true label. Label requests are thus more likely when the margin is small (high uncertainty), causing the sampling probability to approach 1 as |p_t| → 0, and the algorithm tracks and constrains labeling cost c ≤ B over a time horizon T. This embodies a probabilistic uncertainty-based sampling strategy tailored for data streams.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online Active Learning for Real-time Spam Filtering
topic_metadata.description: This topic describes an application-focused comparison of online active learning models—perceptron and SVM—in the context of real-time spam filtering. The study evaluates three instance selection criteria: fixed margin thresholding (Dasgupta et al., 2005), Bernoulli-based b-sampling (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004), and a newly proposed logistic margin sampling strategy. The perceptron is updated with Dasgupta-style reflection updates, while the SVM is retrained on all labeled data whenever new labels are acquired, enabling a comparative analysis of model-update regimes and querying policies for streaming spam data.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Passive-Aggressive Variant of Selective Sampling
topic_metadata.description: This topic refers to an extension of the selective sampling perceptron where a passive-aggressive learning rule is used in an online active learning setting. At each time step, a Bernoulli random variable Z_t is again drawn to decide whether to query the label of the current instance x_t, but the parameterization of Z_t and the subsequent model update follow a passive-aggressive scheme rather than a standard perceptron update. This integrates margin-based selective querying with more aggressive corrective updates when misclassifications occur.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Passive-aggressive updates for online learning
topic_metadata.description: Instead of the traditional perceptron rule that updates only on misclassified examples, passive-aggressive learning updates the weight vector wt ∈ R^d whenever the current loss ℓt(wt−1; (xt, yt)) is nonzero. The new parameter vector is given by wt = wt−1 + τt yt xt, where the step size τt is computed according to different policies involving the loss, the norm of xt, and a penalty cost parameter κ. This aggressive update strategy ensures that even correctly classified but low-confidence examples can influence the model, reducing the risk of wasting informative data points.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online active learning with expert advice
topic_metadata.description: This algorithm processes a data stream sequentially, using the predictions of N experts fi,t(xt) to form a combined prediction pt for each incoming instance xt under a labeling budget B and time horizon T. A Bernoulli random variable Zt with parameter Pt = b / (b + |pt̃|) governs whether the instance is considered for labeling, and Equations 24 or 25 (referenced but not shown) determine the final sampling decision. If the condition is not met, the true label yt is queried and the labeling cost counter c is incremented. This setup formalizes online querying decisions driven by expert advice and a probabilistic sampling mechanism.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Incremental training across AL cycles
topic_metadata.description: Incremental training, where a deep model is updated rather than retrained from scratch in each active learning cycle, is highlighted as an important research direction. Training from scratch every cycle is computationally prohibitive, but naïve incremental updates can lead to parameter drift and degraded performance. Despite limited existing work, the potential resource savings make improved incremental training schemes highly attractive.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Incremental training in active data streams
topic_metadata.description: Incremental training updates model parameters using small batches of new labeled data without restarting training from scratch. This allows the model to incorporate new information while preserving previously acquired knowledge, often via fine-tuning or techniques such as elastic weight consolidation to prevent catastrophic forgetting. It is particularly suited to streaming and online active learning scenarios where data arrive continuously and queries are limited.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Complete retraining for evolving data streams
topic_metadata.description: Complete re-training creates a new model from scratch using all labeled data accumulated so far, discarding the previous model’s parameters. This strategy is typically chosen when a substantial amount of new data arrives, concept drift makes the previous model obsolete, or architectural changes are required. While potentially more accurate in such situations, it can lose previously encoded structure and is computationally more expensive, directly impacting online active learning efficiency.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Fine-grained partial-structure querying
topic_metadata.description: Partial-structure active learning decomposes structured outputs into fine-grained annotation units and queries only some of them, such as individual tokens, word boundaries, syntactic-unit pairs, or mention pairs. Query strategies at this level resemble classification AL but typically require inference to compute marginal probabilities for sub-structures. When full structured labels are ultimately needed, semi-supervised methods like self-training are used to automatically fill in unannotated parts with pseudo-labels.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.1.2, first part ('Factorizing full structures into the finest-grained sub-structures... individual tokens for sequence labeling... word boundaries for segmentation... syntactic-unit pairs... mention pairs... querying strategy... marginal probabilities... semi-supervised techniques such as self-training could be utilized to assign pseudo labels to the unannotated parts').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Learning models from partial annotations
topic_metadata.description: Under partial-structure AL, output modeling must accommodate incomplete labels. Local discriminative models that treat each sub-structure independently can use partial labels directly, while global structured models require specialized algorithms to learn from incomplete annotations. Global models exploit constraints and label interactions so that annotated parts reduce the uncertainty of unannotated parts, enabling better query selection, efficient batch-mode selection via cheap re-inference, and interactive correction where annotator edits propagate through the structure.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.1.2, later paragraphs ('For AL with partial structures, output modeling is of particular interest... local discriminative models... more complex models that consider interactions among output sub-structures... combining the annotated parts and the constraints may reduce the output space... the annotation of one label can intermediately influence others with cheap re-inference, which can help batch-mode selection and interactive correction').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Partial feedback for large-label classification
topic_metadata.description: Classification tasks with many possible labels can be reframed as structured prediction with partially observed outputs to simplify annotation. Instead of requiring a full label choice, annotators provide partial feedback such as answering yes/no queries about specific labels or eliminating clearly incorrect classes. This reduces per-instance annotation difficulty while still providing informative supervision for active learning.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.1.2, final paragraph ('In addition to classical structured-prediction tasks, classification tasks can also be cast as structured predictions with partial labeling... Partial feedback is an example... annotators may find it much easier to answer yes/no questions or rule out negative classes than to identify the correct one').

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Submodular information measures and SMI-based selection
topic_metadata.description: An active learning framework based on submodular information measures addresses challenges like rare classes, redundancy, and out-of-distribution samples by carefully designing submodular objectives. In object detection, a reference set of minority-class examples is used and unlabeled samples are selected according to their submodular mutual information (SMI) with this reference, thereby prioritizing labels that resemble the classes of interest. SMI between two sets A and B is defined from an underlying submodular function g as ISMI = g(A) + g(B) − g(A ∪ B), quantifying their shared information. This approach generalizes representativeness-based selection to set-level similarity and supports targeted querying for specific classes.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Margin sampling heuristic for SVMs
topic_metadata.description: Margin sampling (MS) exploits the geometric properties of SVMs, particularly that unbounded support vectors lie exactly on the margin with decision function value equal to one. The heuristic selects unlabeled samples whose minimum absolute distance to any class hyperplane is smallest, i.e., they are closest to some decision boundary. Formally, it chooses the unlabeled point minimizing the inner minimum over classes of |f(x_i, ω)|, where f(x_i, ω) is the SVM decision function (distance) for class ω. This operationalizes the idea of querying the most uncertain instances near the margin.

topic_metadata.title: Multiclass one-against-all distance modeling
topic_metadata.description: In a multiclass SVM setting, the method adopts a one-against-all decomposition, learning one hyperplane per class. For each candidate sample, its distance to each class-specific hyperplane is represented, as illustrated in Figs. 1(d–f). The margin sampling heuristic then operates over this set of per-class distances to determine which unlabeled sample lies closest to some decision boundary. This connects the geometric SVM view with multiclass active query selection.

topic_metadata.title: Over-confidence in deep neural uncertainty
topic_metadata.description: The section highlights that straightforward probability-based uncertainty metrics using a single forward pass are problematic for deep neural networks due to their tendency toward over-confidence. Over-confidence means assigning very high probabilities (e.g., 0.99) to incorrect predictions and extreme probabilities to inherently uncertain cases, which distorts the true uncertainty structure of the data. This miscalibration affects all class probabilities and undermines the reliability of uncertainty-based active learning strategies built solely on raw softmax scores.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Task-independent deep active learning
topic_metadata.description: Task independence aims to develop DeepAL models that generalize well across different tasks without extensive task-specific tailoring. Current task-independent methods are still few and primarily rely on uncertainty-based selection, which naturally aligns with deep learning models. While uncertainty methods are expected to dominate, incorporating diversity-based criteria into task-agnostic frameworks is suggested as a challenging but valuable extension.

topic_metadata.title: Outlier Selection in Uncertainty-Based AL
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty-based active learning (AL) selects samples that the current model finds hard, but this can inadvertently prioritize outliers that harm model training. These outliers are chosen because the selection criterion focuses solely on prediction uncertainty and ignores intrinsic sample characteristics. This leads to inefficient use of labeling budget and degraded performance.

topic_metadata.title: Redundancy and class imbalance in medical images
topic_metadata.description: In medical image analysis, informativeness metrics are challenged by redundancy and severe class imbalance. Due to high intra-class similarity, images from the same region of interest can be grouped into a few clusters, making many highly informative samples visually and semantically redundant. Additionally, healthy cases typically far outnumber diseased ones, causing skewed label distributions that standard selection strategies fail to correct, which can degrade model performance on rare but clinically important classes.

topic_metadata.title: Class Imbalance in Medical Image Analysis
topic_metadata.description: Class imbalance arises when some diagnostic categories have many labeled images while others have very few, a frequent situation in medical image analysis. This imbalance is highlighted as particularly common in deep learning pipelines for medical tasks, where label distributions are skewed across classes. Such imbalance is a fundamental challenge that must be addressed to build reliable models.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Evidential Deep Learning with Dirichlet outputs
topic_metadata.description: Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) replaces the standard Softmax-based categorical output with a Dirichlet distribution whose parameters are produced by the network. The sharpness or flatness of this Dirichlet distribution encodes model confidence, with sharp distributions indicating confident predictions and flat ones indicating uncertainty. This representation makes it straightforward to derive aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty measures for active learning sample selection.

topic_metadata.title: Evidential uncertainty in object detection
topic_metadata.description: For object detection, a model evidence head is introduced to adaptively scale Dirichlet parameters, stabilizing EDL-based training. Epistemic uncertainty is first computed for each detection box, and then aggregated hierarchically to estimate sample-level uncertainty for active learning. This enables fine-grained uncertainty estimation at both box and image levels in detection tasks.

topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-aware models via evidential deep learning
topic_metadata.description: Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) outputs evidence parameters of a Dirichlet distribution instead of point probability estimates, enabling the model to represent both predictions and associated uncertainty. This framework explicitly distinguishes confidence from uncertainty, making it naturally suited for active learning, where uncertain cases should be prioritized for labeling. In medical image analysis, an uncertainty-aware model with EDL can better identify ambiguous cases such as atypical lesions or poor-quality scans.

topic_metadata.title: Label-free gradient computation with pseudo labels
topic_metadata.description: Since true labels are unavailable for unlabeled samples in active learning, the described methods compute gradients without using ground truth. Instead, they rely on supervised losses with pseudo-labels (e.g., cross-entropy with pseudo-labels) or unsupervised losses (e.g., entropy loss), making gradient computation independent of true labels. This enables gradient-based uncertainty estimation directly on unlabeled data.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Label-free gradient-norm sampling strategy
topic_metadata.description: This topic covers an active learning strategy where sample selection is based on gradient norms computed without ground-truth labels. Wang et al. (2022b) show mathematically that larger gradient norms correspond to a lower upper bound on test loss, motivating the use of such norms as an informativeness measure. They compute gradients using the expected empirical loss (a probability-weighted sum over class losses) and the entropy loss, both relying only on predicted class probabilities (Eqs. 5 and 6). This approach is applied to cryo-electron tomography subtomogram classification and shown to outperform competing methods.

topic_metadata.title: Gradient-based uncertainty in deep AL
topic_metadata.description: The section introduces gradient-based uncertainty as a key idea in deep learning–based medical image analysis, where a sample’s gradient indicates its contribution to model parameter changes. Larger gradient lengths correspond to larger parameter updates and thus higher uncertainty, while being independent of predictive probabilities and therefore less prone to over-confidence. Three commonly used gradient-based uncertainty metrics are mentioned: raw gradients, Fisher information, and influence functions.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Fisher information-driven active learning objective
topic_metadata.description: This topic describes using Fisher information (FI) to quantify how data influence uncertainty in model parameters for active learning. FI is defined as the expectation of the squared gradients (or Hessian) of the loss with respect to model parameters (Eq. 7), capturing sensitivity of the model to data. The AL objective minimizes the trace of the inverse FI for a queried subset relative to the unlabeled pool (Eq. 8), so that selected samples accelerate convergence to optimal parameters. However, computing FI exactly scales quadratically with the number of parameters, making naive FI-based methods impractical for deep networks.

topic_metadata.title: Gradient-based uncertainty via Fisher Information
topic_metadata.description: This topic refers to using gradient information, often summarized through Fisher Information, to quantify model uncertainty in deep active learning. Samples that induce large parameter gradients or high Fisher Information are considered more informative and are prioritized for annotation. This approach directly links the acquisition function to the model’s sensitivity to individual training points, which is particularly relevant in deep neural networks.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Drift change rate and drift types
topic_metadata.description: The section introduces change rate as a key characteristic of distribution shifts, distinguishing how quickly new concepts enter the data stream. Four drift types are defined: abrupt drift, where the distribution changes sharply between consecutive time steps and requires immediate model updating; gradual drift, where overlapping distributions make detection and adaptation more difficult; incremental drift, where extremely slow and small-step changes in the data-generating process hinder detection; and recurring concepts, where previously seen concepts reappear cyclically, such as seasonal product popularity. These patterns inform the design of drift detection and adaptive learning strategies in streaming environments.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Handling data drift in streams
topic_metadata.description: In streaming environments, underlying data distributions can shift over time, causing models to degrade if they cannot adapt. Such drift also affects which instances are considered informative, potentially invalidating previously effective query criteria. The text points to methods discussed in earlier sections that explicitly deal with dynamic, ever-changing behaviors as necessary tools in these scenarios.

In the t-th round (1 ≤ t ≤ T), the system operates on the current unlabeled pool and model state from the previous round. This iterative process allows gradual refinement of the model while controlling labeling cost over multiple cycles.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Disagreement-based query-by-committee methods
topic_metadata.description: Disagreement-based strategies use multiple models (a committee) and query instances where these models disagree most, exemplified by query-by-committee (QBC). Disagreement can be quantified via vote entropy, KL-divergence between predictive distributions, or variation ratio. Committees can be built from distinct models or via Bayesian treatments of a single model’s parameters, and dropout in neural networks provides a practical deep Bayesian approximation for estimating uncertainty.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Committee-based uncertainty via learner disagreement
topic_metadata.description: Committee-based active learning quantifies the uncertainty of a pixel by assembling a committee of learners, each based on different hypotheses about the classification problem. Each committee member independently labels candidate pixels in the pool, and the algorithm selects those samples that exhibit maximal disagreement among the committee’s predictions. This disagreement serves as the acquisition criterion for querying new labels. The approach is highlighted as the first major family of methods in the survey.

topic_metadata.title: Committee-based batch active learning
topic_metadata.description: Several methods, such as EQB and AMD, are characterized as batch-mode active learning algorithms that rely on a committee of learners. They operate on multiclass problems (M), consider all candidates for selection, and require training k models, indicating that multiple classifiers jointly decide which samples to label. The absence of classifier diversity (marked ×) suggests that the committee members may be similar or identically parameterized models.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Disagreement-based active learning
topic_metadata.description: Disagreement-based strategies rely on multiple models or experts and focus on instances where their predictions diverge. By querying labels for points with high disagreement, the learner targets regions of hypothesis space that are poorly constrained by current data. Query by committee is a canonical method, using an ensemble of models to identify and score conflicting predictions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Bullet beginning 'Disagreement-based query strategies. topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Entropy-based disagreement and informativeness
topic_metadata.description: Entropy of committee predictions is used as a measure of disagreement and thus informativeness of unlabeled samples. If all classifiers in the committee agree on a label for a candidate pixel, the entropy is zero, indicating that querying this sample would add little information to the training set. Conversely, when there is maximum disagreement among the classifiers, the entropy is high, and adding that pixel’s label is expected to be highly beneficial for the model. This links the nEQB criterion directly to the active learning objective of prioritizing uncertain and informative instances.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final explanatory sentences: 'HBAG(xi) is an empirical measure of entropy... A candidate for which all the classifiers in the committee agree is associated with null entropy... On the contrary, a candidate with maximum disagreement between the classifiers results in maximum entropy, and its inclusion will be highly beneficial.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Model disagreement and vote entropy
topic_metadata.description: This topic focuses on committee-based active learning where multiple inferences from a model (or models) are used to measure disagreement. Vote Entropy quantifies how diverse the predictions are across the committee, with higher entropy indicating more informative, uncertain samples. Selection is often done at the patch level, choosing Top-k patches whose predictions show the greatest disagreement for annotation in dense prediction tasks.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Model disagreement with entropy-weighted Dice
topic_metadata.description: Multiple inference or ensemble-based active learning measures the disagreement between several segmentation predictions on the same medical image. Entropy-weighted Dice distance combines predictive uncertainty (via entropy) with segmentation overlap (Dice coefficient) to quantify how inconsistent and uncertain the predictions are. Samples with high entropy-weighted Dice distance are prioritized for annotation, as they are likely to be challenging and informative for improving the model.

topic_metadata.title: Active learning for multiple domains and languages
topic_metadata.description: In multi-target scenarios, active learning may need to select examples across multiple domains or multiple languages rather than a single setting. Strategies that consider all targets jointly, often via a single shared model, tend to outperform naively splitting budgets or focusing only on high-resource settings followed by transfer. This raises questions of how to optimally allocate annotation effort across heterogeneous but related targets.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Interaction of active learning and multi-task learning
topic_metadata.description: When there are multiple target tasks, multi-task learning (MTL) can be combined with active learning so that queried instances benefit several tasks simultaneously. Query strategies that consider all target tasks jointly can yield better overall performance than task-specific selection. This setting involves designing acquisition functions that exploit shared representations while balancing the needs of different tasks.

topic_metadata.title: Membership query synthesis and generative AL
topic_metadata.description: Membership query synthesis allows a learner to query any point in the input space for annotation, including synthetic samples generated by models, and is referred to in this survey as generative active learning. It is generally suitable for low-dimensional spaces, but in high-dimensional domains like images, generated instances may be unrecognizable to human annotators. This raises practical challenges when integrating generative models with human-in-the-loop labeling.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Membership query synthesis scenario
topic_metadata.description: Membership query synthesis is an active learning scenario where the learner can request labels for any point in the input space, including synthetically generated instances not present in an existing unlabeled pool. This gives maximal flexibility to probe specific regions of the space, for example by generating adversarial or boundary-centered points. It is particularly relevant when the cost or feasibility of evaluating arbitrary queries is acceptable for the oracle.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection '2.2.1 Membership query synthesis active learning' and its first sentence: 'This scenario represents the case when the learner is given complete freedom to ask for the label of any data point...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Membership query synthesis active learning
topic_metadata.description: Membership query synthesis is an active learning strategy where the learner generates new synthetic instances and asks an oracle (e.g., a human annotator) for their labels. Instances can be created by modifying, combining, or transforming existing data to explore regions of the input space that have not yet been observed. A key drawback is that some generated samples may be unnatural or uninterpretable, making it impossible for annotators to assign meaningful labels. The process is typically iterated until a labeling budget is exhausted or a performance-based stopping criterion is met.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Synthetic query generation across domains
topic_metadata.description: Membership query synthesis is illustrated across several domains, each using domain-specific transformations to create informative synthetic data. In image classification and object detection, the learner generates modified or composite images from existing ones, while in NLP tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis, it creates synthetic sentences or paragraphs to cover a wider range of linguistic variations. In speech recognition, the system generates speech samples with different accents, pronunciations, and speaking styles to better model acoustic variability and improve recognition accuracy. These examples show how synthetic query design is tightly coupled to the structure and variability of the target domain.

Weighted-sum approaches jointly optimize a composite objective that balances, for example, uncertainty and diversity, while two-stage methods apply different criteria sequentially. topic_metadata.title: Combined querying and uncertainty–diversity trade-off

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Families of active learning heuristics
topic_metadata.description: The section explains that successful active learning for remote sensing requires strategies to rank pixels in the unlabeled pool U according to their utility for labeling. It groups these strategies into three main families—committee-based, large margin-based, and posterior probability-based heuristics—each relying on different underlying models of uncertainty. A fourth, more recent family, cluster-based heuristics, is mentioned as conceptually distinct and therefore excluded from detailed treatment. This taxonomy structures the subsequent survey of algorithms.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Cluster-based active learning via clustering trees
topic_metadata.description: Cluster-based heuristics are described as an alternative family of active learning methods that operate by pruning a hierarchical clustering tree. The goal is to refine clusters until they become consistent with the labels provided by the user, effectively guiding exploration of the data space. These methods rely on an unsupervised model of the data distribution rather than on a predictive classifier, making their aim different from the other families. Because of this differing objective, they are mentioned but not detailed further in the survey.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Four families of active learning heuristics
topic_metadata.description: The survey organizes diverse active learning algorithms into four main heuristic families based on their characteristics. For each family, specific selection strategies have been detailed and systematically compared. This taxonomy structures the variety of methods and enables a clearer analysis of their relative behaviors and design principles.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Probabilistic view of distribution shift
topic_metadata.description: The section formalizes distribution shifts in data streams through time-dependent probability distributions p_t(x), p_t(y|x), and p_t(y). It explains that shifts can affect the input distribution, the conditional label distribution, or the marginal label distribution, each with different consequences for the underlying predictive model. This probabilistic framing underpins later distinctions between virtual drift, real concept drift, and label distribution shift, and motivates the need for model updates when these distributions change.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, sentences describing p_ti(x), p_ti(y|x), and p_ti(y)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Virtual drift affecting input distribution
topic_metadata.description: Virtual drift (also referred to as covariate shift) is defined as a situation where the input distribution p_t(x) changes over time while the conditional distribution p_t(y|x) remains stable. This implies that the relationship between features and labels does not change, but the regions of the input space that are frequently observed do, as in seasonal or environmental changes that alter observed features. The model’s mapping from x to y is still valid, but its performance may be affected due to mismatches between training and current input frequencies.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, discussion of virtual drift where p_ti(x) ≠ p_ti+ε(x) and p_ti(y|x) = p_ti+ε(y|x)

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Real concept drift and model degradation
topic_metadata.description: Real concept drift occurs when the conditional distribution p_t(y|x) changes over time, meaning that the underlying relationship between inputs and labels evolves. This leads to a severe deterioration in predictive performance because the learned model no longer reflects the true mapping from features to labels, necessitating model updates or replacement. Examples include shifts in consumer behavior after major events like the COVID-19 pandemic.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, sentences defining real concept drift and its impact (p_ti(y|x) ≠ p_ti+ε(y|x))

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Combined virtual and real concept drift
topic_metadata.description: The text highlights that in many practical scenarios, virtual drift and real concept drift co-occur, leading to simultaneous changes in both the input distribution p_t(x) and the conditional distribution p_t(y|x). This compound shift creates a more challenging adaptation problem, as models must cope with changing feature frequencies and evolving label relationships at the same time. Such situations are typical in complex, non-stationary environments.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, sentences noting that virtual and real drifts often occur together (p_ti(x) ≠ p_ti+ε(x) and p_ti(y|x) ≠ p_ti+ε(y|x))

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Label distribution shift over time
topic_metadata.description: Label distribution shift is described as a change that affects only the marginal distribution of labels p_t(y), while p_t(x) and p_t(y|x) may remain stable. This phenomenon is common in real-world settings where the prevalence of certain classes varies over time, such as seasonal patterns in disease incidence (e.g., influenza) or sudden outbreaks. It alters class priors and can significantly impact model calibration and performance if not properly handled.
topic_metadata.text_span: first paragraph, sentences defining label distribution shift where p_ti(y) ≠ p_ti+ε(y)

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Neural network-based learnable sampling
topic_metadata.description: Recent deep AL work employs neural networks directly to perform sample selection, moving beyond explicit informativeness evaluation. In this learnable sampling paradigm, a model is trained to predict which unlabeled samples are most beneficial for annotation, effectively learning a selection policy from data or from proxy signals. This contrasts with handcrafted metrics by allowing the selection mechanism itself to be parameterized and optimized as part of the learning pipeline.
topic_metadata.text_span: later part of section, sentences 'Furthermore, with the recent development of deep AL, more and more studies directly employ neural networks for sample selection. In this context, we no longer evaluate informativeness but directly choose informative samples with neural networks.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Learnable sampling with neural selectors
topic_metadata.description: Learnable sampling replaces the traditional two-step active learning paradigm—informativeness evaluation followed by heuristic selection—with a single, end-to-end trainable process. A neural network, termed a neural selector, directly outputs which samples to query without explicitly computing informativeness scores. This shifts sample selection from hand-crafted criteria to learned, data-driven policies.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Set-cover-based Core-Set and variants
topic_metadata.description: Set-cover-based methods like Core-Set formulate active learning as a k-center location problem, solved via farthest-first traversal to select representative samples that minimize the maximum distance to all points. Similarity between samples is originally measured by L2 distance in deep feature space, and later extended by contextual diversity metrics that fuse uncertainty and spatial/semantic diversity. Graph convolutional networks are also introduced to model relations between labeled and unlabeled data, improving feature representations before Core-Set sampling. These methods embody a set-cover constraint aiming for complete coverage, but can be prone to selecting outliers when the labeled set is small.

Methods such as those inspired by Sener and Savarese (2018, ICLR) frame sample selection as a covering or core-set optimization problem in feature space, often using L2 distances. The goal is to select a subset of samples that well-cover the data manifold, reducing redundancy in the labeled set.

topic_metadata.description: Cover-based methods aim to select unlabeled samples so that they well 'cover' the representation space of the data, reducing redundancy while maintaining representativeness. In deep active learning for medical images, this typically involves selecting images or slices that span the feature manifold learned by a network. Such strategies help ensure that annotated data provide broad coverage of anatomical and pathological variations.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Core-set k-center formulation and scalability
topic_metadata.description: The Core-set approach formulates active learning as a k-center problem, seeking a subset such that a model trained on it performs competitively with one trained on the full dataset. It constructs a core subset by maximizing coverage in feature space, effectively trying to minimize the maximum distance from any unlabeled point to the selected set. However, building the required distance matrix over all unlabeled samples is computationally expensive, making this strategy challenging for large-scale unlabeled datasets.

topic_metadata.title: Cold-start problem in active learning
topic_metadata.description: The cold-start problem arises when active learning (AL) methods have little or no initial labeled data, causing informativeness estimates to be unreliable and performance to degrade, sometimes below random sampling. Simply combining self-supervised learning with standard AL baselines can also underperform random sampling, showing that naive pretraining is insufficient. This issue is pervasive across domains, including medical image analysis where labeling is expensive. A key mitigation strategy is to deliberately select an optimal initial labeled set using strategies different from conventional AL query policies.

topic_metadata.title: Prequential evaluation for online active learning
topic_metadata.description: Prequential evaluation assesses performance on streaming data by predicting each incoming instance before deciding whether to query its label and update the model. Algorithm 6 formalizes this for online active learning under a labeling budget: for each time step, the model predicts, the active strategy decides whether to request the true label, and the model is updated only when a label is acquired, consuming budget. This scheme is particularly suitable for drifting data streams, where using a static holdout set would not reflect evolving data distributions.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Prequential (test-then-train) evaluation
topic_metadata.description: Prequential evaluation, also called the test-then-train approach, assesses performance in online learning by first predicting on each incoming instance, then optionally querying its label, and finally updating the model with that instance. This method produces a time series of prediction errors, enabling monitoring of performance evolution in data streams. Algorithmically, at each time step t, the model predicts, a query decision is made, and then the model is updated with the instance and its label. It is a natural fit for streaming settings where data arrive sequentially and immediate evaluation is desired.

topic_metadata.title: LLAL loss-prediction-based active learning
topic_metadata.description: LLAL (Learning Loss for Active Learning) introduces a small loss prediction module attached to a target network, using outputs from multiple hidden layers as its input. This auxiliary module is trained to predict the target loss for unlabeled samples, turning predicted loss into a proxy for informativeness. A top-K selection strategy then chooses query samples with the highest predicted loss. With modest parameter overhead, LLAL is designed to be task-agnostic and demonstrates competitive performance on image classification, object detection, and human pose estimation.

topic_metadata.title: LLAL loss-prediction framework
topic_metadata.description: LLAL introduces a framework where a loss prediction module is trained jointly with the deep model to estimate future loss for unlabeled samples. Outputs from multiple hidden layers serve as inputs to this module, and samples with top-K predicted losses are queried from the oracle. The training phase optimizes a combined objective of target loss and loss-prediction loss, while the query phase uses the predicted losses to drive active sampling.

topic_metadata.title: Margin-based uncertainty heuristic
topic_metadata.description: This topic explains the core heuristic that underlies large-margin active learning: samples close to the decision boundary are considered uncertain and informative, while samples far from it are deemed uninteresting for labeling. The process uses the magnitude of the decision function f(xi) as a metric, with low absolute values indicating candidates for querying. This establishes the general uncertainty-sampling principle specialized to margin-based classifiers.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification
topic_metadata.title: Diversity-constrained margin-based heuristics
topic_metadata.description: Margin-based active learning heuristics rank unlabeled samples by their decision margin (e.g., distance between class posteriors), but can still select highly similar points. To counter this, the base margin sampling heuristic is augmented by a diversity constraint that penalizes or filters candidates that are too similar to already selected ones. This combination exploits both uncertainty (small margin) and spatial or spectral diversity in feature space, leading to more representative labeled sets in remote sensing. The process involves computing margins (Equations (7), (8) or (9)) and then applying a diversity measure on the candidate subset.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Measuring annotation cost realistically
topic_metadata.description: Annotation cost in AL is often oversimplified as a uniform per-instance value, despite real efforts varying with factors such as sequence length and instance difficulty. Because AL tends to select hard and ambiguous instances, unit-cost assumptions can distort evaluation and change which strategies appear best. Time-based cost—measuring actual annotation time in user studies—is advocated as the most accurate metric, and regression-based cost models learned from input features are proposed to predict real costs for use in evaluation and querying.

This requires actual annotating exercises... cost measurement can also be used for querying... cast as a regression problem, for which several works learn a linear cost model based on input features').

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

In practice, label scarcity is the very reason for using active learning, which makes comprehensive evaluation of deployed sampling strategies difficult or unrealistic. This gap raises questions about how to reliably measure performance when labels are limited or costly.

topic_metadata.description: This topic covers a threshold-based strategy where unlabeled instances are selected if their margin |p_t| is below a dynamically adjusted threshold ε. topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Single-pass vs window-based sampling
topic_metadata.description: This topic contrasts single-pass online active learning algorithms, which must decide on querying immediately for each arriving instance, with window- or batch-based methods that process fixed-size chunks of data. Window-based approaches perform best-out-of-window sampling by evaluating an entire buffer and selecting the top k most informative observations for labeling, with k and buffer size constrained by storage and computation. Window-based strategies suit high-volume streams without strict time constraints, whereas single-pass methods are required when decisions must be made instantly on each data point.

topic_metadata.title: Single-pass online sampling for streams
topic_metadata.description: This topic concerns sampling strategies that process each instance from a dynamic data stream only once, without revisiting or storing large portions of the stream. Such single-pass methods avoid maintaining or updating multiple models, making them more practical in settings with strict time or memory constraints. They are proposed as an alternative to dominant ensemble and batch-based methods in online classification when continuous, high-velocity data cannot be easily batched.

topic_metadata.title: H-divergence and VAAL framework
topic_metadata.description: H-divergence measures the distance between labeled and unlabeled distributions using a discriminator, typically derived from GAN-style architectures, whose ability to distinguish the two sets correlates with the divergence. Variational Adversarial Active Learning (VAAL) combines a VAE that maps samples to a latent space with a discriminator that predicts whether latent codes come from labeled or unlabeled data. Through adversarial training, the VAE tries to fool the discriminator, and the system selects samples the discriminator deems most likely to be unlabeled for annotation.

topic_metadata.description: Adversarial representative methods learn to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data in a latent space and use this signal to guide selection. DiscAL employs a discriminator reminiscent of GANs to separate samples from labeled and unlabeled distributions. VAAL uses a VAE plus adversarial discriminator trained with reconstruction and adversarial losses, and selects points by the discriminator’s probability of being unlabeled (αVAAL). WAAL leverages adversarial training framed via H-divergence to find unlabeled batches that are both diverse and distributionally distinct from labeled data.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: TA-VAAL: task-aware variational adversarial AL
topic_metadata.description: TA-VAAL (Task-Aware Variational Adversarial Active Learning) enhances VAAL by explicitly accounting for both data distribution and task structure. It addresses the limitation that uncertainty-based methods underuse global data distribution and distribution-based methods overlook task structure, by integrating a loss prediction module and RankCGAN into VAAL. This yields a framework that jointly exploits data distribution and model uncertainty, achieving strong performance on balanced and imbalanced benchmarks.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: VAAL adversarial representation learning for AL
topic_metadata.description: VAAL tackles limitations of batch uncertainty sampling (low diversity, outlier sensitivity) and density-based methods (p-norm distance concentration in high dimensions) by learning an adversarial latent representation that distinguishes labeled from unlabeled data. It jointly trains a VAE in a semi-supervised fashion on both labeled and unlabeled datasets while an adversarial discriminator is trained to classify whether latent codes originate from the labeled pool, pushing the encoder to align their distributions. This yields a low-dimensional latent space that supports an effective sampling strategy combining representation learning with uncertainty to reduce outlier influence and distance concentration issues.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: ARAL and TA-VAAL extensions of VAAL
topic_metadata.description: ARAL builds on VAAL and adversarial representation learning to minimize manual annotations while exploiting both real and generated data. The framework uses VAAL to learn the latent feature space of labeled and unlabeled data, selects unlabeled samples with maximal information, and then enhances learning with adversarial representation training on both actual and synthetic samples produced by a deep generative network; its architecture includes an encoder, generator, discriminator, classifier, and sampler trained jointly. TA-VAAL further extends VAAL by combining the global data structure learned by VAAL with local task-related information derived from learning loss for more informed sample querying.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Batch Mode Deep Active Learning concept
topic_metadata.description: Batch Mode Deep Active Learning (BMDAL) replaces classical one-by-one querying with batch-based sample selection to better suit deep model training. One-by-one querying causes frequent retraining with little change in data, leading to inefficiency and potential overfitting. BMDAL instead scores candidate unlabeled batches B ⊆ U using an acquisition function a and a trained deep model f_θ(L), and selects an optimal batch B* that maximizes a_batch(B, f_θ(L)). This reframes acquisition as a batch-level optimization problem aligned with deep learning training dynamics.

topic_metadata.title: Wasserstein-based adversarial active learning
topic_metadata.description: Wasserstein distance is used as a more diversity-preserving distribution metric compared to H-divergence in discrepancy-based active learning. WAAL (Wasserstein Adversarial Active Learning) extends VAAL by adding a sample-selection module trained to minimize the Wasserstein distance between labeled and unlabeled sets. This design encourages querying samples that are both highly uncertain and most likely unlabeled while maintaining representativeness and diversity of the selected subset.

Losses are derived from this formulation, and the method is decomposed into deep neural network parameter optimization and query batch selection stages. This adversarial, distribution-based approach targets alignment between labeled and unlabeled data distributions while maintaining informative selections.

topic_metadata.title: Principle of discrepancy-based active learning
topic_metadata.description: Discrepancy-based active learning selects unlabeled samples that are farthest from the labeled set in distribution space, treating them as most representative. By repeatedly querying such samples, the method aims to reduce the discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled distributions so that a small labeled subset approximates the full dataset. The core technical challenge is defining and computing a distance between two high-dimensional probability distributions.

topic_metadata.title: Discrepancy-based sampling using H-divergence
topic_metadata.description: Discrepancy-based active learning strategies compare distributions between labeled and unlabeled sets to identify regions where the model is poorly supported by annotations. H-divergence is used as a formal measure of distributional discrepancy, guiding the selection of samples that reduce this gap. By repeatedly querying top-scoring examples under this divergence, the learner aims to better align the labeled set with the overall data distribution.

topic_metadata.title: Discrepancy-Based Selection with Statistical Distances
topic_metadata.description: Discrepancy-based methods select unlabeled samples by measuring distributional or prediction discrepancies between models or between labeled and unlabeled sets. Metrics such as Wasserstein distance, H-divergence, and KL divergence quantify how much a candidate sample differs from what the model has already seen or what an ensemble predicts. These criteria are often combined with uncertainty or diversity in hybrid strategies.

topic_metadata.title: Discrepancy-based distribution alignment measures
topic_metadata.description: Some surveyed works measure how well labeled and unlabeled sets align by computing discrepancies between their feature distributions. These include cosine similarity-based discrepancies, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and Wasserstein distance, which quantify gaps between empirical distributions or feature embeddings of candidate samples and the existing labeled pool. Selection then targets samples that maximally reduce such discrepancies, promoting distribution alignment. This perspective treats active learning as minimizing a statistical distance between training and target data distributions.

topic_metadata.title: Superpixel-based pre-segmentation and informativeness
topic_metadata.description: In region-based active learning, images are first pre-segmented into superpixels using color- and texture-based algorithms, and then informativeness is computed at the superpixel level. The informativeness score of a superpixel is defined as the average informativeness of its constituent pixels, turning pixel-wise uncertainty into region-wise measures. This enables querying compact, coherent regions rather than individual pixels, improving annotation efficiency.

In early work on interactive cell segmentation, the most informative superpixels are selected using expected prediction error as the acquisition metric, guiding user interaction to areas that would most improve the model. Later, an approach is described where the most informative foreground and background superpixels are chosen for annotation, refining the segmentation boundary by focusing expert effort on critical regions.

topic_metadata.title: Batch-mode active learning and diversity
topic_metadata.description: Batch-mode active learning selects multiple instances at once, which is more practical than querying a single instance per iteration. This requires controlling redundancy within the selected batch, not just dissimilarity to labeled data, so that each new labeled example contributes distinct information. Batch diversity thus becomes an additional design objective on top of informativeness and representativeness.

topic_metadata.title: Batch-mode vs one-by-one querying
topic_metadata.description: For large neural networks and high-dimensional data, such as image classification or detection tasks, batch-mode active learning is generally more efficient and effective than querying one instance at a time. Retraining a complex model after adding a single high-dimensional data point often yields minimal performance gains relative to the computational cost. Batch-mode querying amortizes the retraining cost over multiple informative instances, improving resource utilization. This motivates preferring larger batches in deep learning scenarios.

topic_metadata.title: BatchBALD and joint mutual information
topic_metadata.description: BatchBALD extends the BALD acquisition function to batch mode by modeling the joint mutual information between the labels of multiple queried samples and the model parameters. It represents a batch of inputs and outputs as joint random variables and defines the batch acquisition score as the difference between the predictive entropy over the batch and the expected conditional entropy given parameters. This explicit joint mutual information mechanism captures correlations between query samples to construct a more informative batch.

topic_metadata.description: BatchBALD extends the BALD acquisition function from single-instance to batch active learning by computing the mutual information between a batch of samples and the model parameters. Instead of scoring points independently, it jointly scores the entire batch to better capture complementary information among queried points. This yields more accurate estimates of the information gain from labeling a batch.

topic_metadata.title: Active learning with crowdsourcing
topic_metadata.description: Crowdsourcing introduces non-expert annotations to lower labeling costs, and can be combined with active learning to further reduce annotation effort. However, the resulting labels are often noisy, which can hurt active learning effectiveness. The combination requires careful handling of crowd label quality when selecting which instances to annotate.

topic_metadata.title: Crowdsourcing to reduce AL annotation cost
topic_metadata.description: Crowdsourcing is proposed as a way to further reduce annotation costs in AL by distributing labeling work across non-expert annotators. Integrating crowdsourcing with AL raises issues of label quality control, aggregation, and cost-aware query selection in order to maximize benefit from limited human effort.

topic_metadata.title: Core methods in active learning
topic_metadata.description: The section defines the core methods of active learning (AL) as the evaluation of sample informativeness and the design of sampling strategies. Informativeness quantifies the value of annotating each unlabeled sample, and sampling strategies use these scores to choose which samples to label under a given annotation budget. Together, they determine how efficiently AL systems query data for labeling.

topic_metadata.title: Informativeness evaluation and sampling strategies
topic_metadata.description: Deep active learning methods rely on metrics and criteria to evaluate the informativeness of unlabeled samples, guiding which instances to query. Sampling strategies operationalize these criteria to select a subset of data points that are expected to most improve the model when labeled. These components are central to designing effective AL pipelines in medical image analysis.

topic_metadata.title: Sampling strategies and top-k selection
topic_metadata.description: Sampling strategies operationalize informativeness scores to select a subset of unlabeled samples for annotation under a specified budget. A common approach is to rank all unlabeled data by their informativeness scores and choose the top-k samples (top-k selection). This procedure is the de facto standard in many AL works for transforming informativeness metrics into concrete query sets.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Top-k selection in deep active learning
topic_metadata.description: Many deep active learning (AL) methods use a simple top-k strategy, selecting the k samples with the highest informativeness scores for annotation. This assumes that the informativeness metric alone is sufficient to drive efficient learning. The process ranks unlabeled samples by an informativeness measure (e.g., uncertainty) and picks the top subset, without further structural constraints on diversity or balance.

topic_metadata.title: Top-k selection for batch querying
topic_metadata.description: Many methods in the table employ a Top-k selection strategy, where the k highest-scoring samples under a chosen acquisition function (e.g., entropy, H-divergence, estimated loss) are queried in each iteration. This defines how batches of images are constructed for annotation and directly impacts the label efficiency of the active learner. The repeated appearance of Top-k highlights its role as a standard mechanism for batch-mode deep active learning.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Adversarial-based uncertainty estimation framework
topic_metadata.description: This topic treats uncertainty in active learning as a function of a sample’s robustness to adversarial perturbations. Adversarial samples are generated by adding carefully designed, visually imperceptible perturbations that move inputs across the model’s decision boundary with minimal cost. The required perturbation magnitude (attack strength) is used as a proxy for the sample’s distance to the decision boundary: smaller perturbations imply closer proximity and therefore higher uncertainty. This links adversarial robustness analysis with sample selection strategies in deep active learning.
topic_metadata.text_span: opening explanation of adversarial samples, decision boundary, and attack strength as distance (first half of section)

topic_metadata.title: Adversarial samples and decision boundary distance
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses active learning methods that use adversarial examples to probe the classifier’s decision boundary. Samples are selected based on their distance to the decision boundary, with closer points considered more informative for labeling. The approach typically ranks unlabeled data by this distance and chooses the Top-k items, exploiting adversarial perturbations to better explore uncertain regions of the feature space.

topic_metadata.title: Adversarial-based uncertainty in medical AL
topic_metadata.description: This topic discusses using adversarial examples to model uncertainty in active learning for medical image analysis. Adversarial samples lie near the decision boundary and are thus inherently uncertain, making them attractive candidates for selection in training to enhance model robustness. The section notes that adversarial-based uncertainty has seen limited application in medical AL so far and suggests exploring it further, particularly within federated learning scenarios where robustness and communication-efficient uncertainty sampling are critical.

The aim is to minimize labeling effort while achieving robust performance under domain shifts common in medical imaging.

topic_metadata.title: Domain Adaptation in Medical Imaging
topic_metadata.description: Domain Adaptation (DA) is used in medical image analysis to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled or sparsely labeled target domain, thereby reducing annotation costs. It leverages relationships between domains (e.g., different scanners or modalities) so that models trained on one domain generalize better to another. DA is framed as a key strategy for handling distribution shift between medical image datasets.

topic_metadata.title: Active learning with weak annotations
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses using weak forms of supervision (e.g., image- or box-level labels instead of full pixel masks) within active learning to reduce annotation burden. It contrasts region-based active learning, which still requires labeling all pixels in a region, with approaches that relax this requirement. The focus is on simplifying tasks for annotators while maintaining model performance, especially in medical image analysis. It is highlighted as a promising direction for future research in active learning.
