topic_metadata.description: For instance segmentation, this topic describes an active learning setup where annotators supply only each object’s class label and bounding box, omitting precise pixel-wise segmentation masks. The model is trained using these weaker annotations, significantly reducing annotation complexity compared to full mask labeling. This exemplifies how active learning can be combined with weak supervision to scale instance-level segmentation tasks.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Concept of Representativeness-Based Active Learning
topic_metadata.description: Representativeness-based AL seeks a subset of samples that collectively approximate or represent the full dataset. Representative samples should capture key visual properties such as imaging style and visual content, ensuring broad coverage of the data manifold. This approach is proposed to overcome the pitfalls of pure uncertainty-based selection.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences starting with 'Representativeness is adopted in AL...' through 'visually distinctive in properties like imaging style or visual content.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Taxonomy of Representativeness-Based AL Methods
topic_metadata.description: The survey categorizes representativeness-based AL into four major method families: clustering-based, cover-based, discrepancy-based, and density-based approaches. These categories reflect different mathematical formalisms—such as set cover, submodular functions, similarity measures, H-divergence, Wasserstein distance, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)—used to operationalize representativeness. This taxonomy structures the design space for representativeness in deep active learning.
topic_metadata.text_span: Final sentences introducing 'four types of representativeness-based AL' and the items listed around Figure 4

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Core concept of density-based AL
topic_metadata.description: Density-based active learning selects samples from densely populated regions of the data distribution by performing density estimation in a high-dimensional feature space. The likelihood value reflects the estimated data density, so samples with higher likelihood are considered more representative. These methods risk redundancy in selected samples, so clustering is often incorporated to increase diversity. They directly estimate data distribution, avoiding complex optimization problems typically required in other AL paradigms.
topic_metadata.text_span: First paragraph beginning with '3.2.4. Density-based Active Learning' through 'which prevents the need to solve complex optimization problems.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Conceptual contrast: cover-based vs density-based AL
topic_metadata.description: Conceptually, cover-based active learning aims to select samples that cover the entire dataset, regardless of whether they lie in dense regions of the distribution. Empirical evidence (e.g., Core-Set) shows cover-based methods may preferentially select outliers in low-budget regimes. In contrast, density-based AL focuses on selecting samples from high-density areas, which may make it more suitable when annotation budgets are very limited. This highlights an opposing behavior between the two paradigms in certain operating regimes.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph beginning with 'It is worth noting that cover-based and density-based AL differ in both concept and methodology.' up to 'may be a better choice in the low-budget regime.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Representativeness-based slice selection in AL
topic_metadata.description: Active learning methods in this context aim to select a subset of 2D slices from 3D volumes that are most representative of the overall data distribution. Representativeness-based criteria are used to prioritize slices whose features capture the semantic diversity of the volume, making them more informative for training. This contrasts with naive uniform sampling of slices.

topic_metadata.title: Representativeness-based active learning categories
topic_metadata.description: Representativeness-based active learning (AL) uses feature representations and data distributions to select informative samples. It comprises cover-based and discrepancy-based methods that implicitly capture the data distribution, and density-based methods that explicitly estimate it. Density-based AL, however, requires additional strategies to maintain diversity among selected samples. This framing highlights different mechanisms for leveraging data representativeness in AL.

topic_metadata.description: Density-based methods aim to select a core subset of samples that represents the overall data distribution, thereby reducing annotation cost while preserving coverage. These strategies evaluate data from the perspective of sample density, preferring points in dense or representative regions. The chosen subset is intended to approximate the full pool’s distributional structure with far fewer labeled instances.

topic_metadata.title: Model initialization and initial labeled pool
topic_metadata.description: Proper initialization of the deep model is emphasized as crucial for meaningful informativeness estimates in active learning. If the initial model f_θ0 is randomly initialized, its uncertainty or acquisition scores may be unreliable; therefore, most works first select a small random set D_l^0 to obtain initial labels and train f_θ0. This seeding step stabilizes the subsequent query strategy and learning dynamics.

topic_metadata.title: Initialization of labeled pool and model
topic_metadata.description: Before starting active learning, an initial labeled pool is formed by randomly selecting samples, with its size equal to the annotation budget. This pool is used to train the initial model, establishing a common starting point for all methods. The randomness is controlled via seeding to ensure experimental reproducibility.

topic_metadata.description: In many medical images, the region of interest (ROI) occupies only a small portion of the full image. Active learning can be combined with region-based annotation by selecting and labeling only informative subregions containing the ROI instead of annotating the entire image. This strategy reduces annotation effort while preserving diagnostic information, thereby increasing label efficiency.

Instead of requiring oracles to annotate whole images, experts focus on informative subregions that can better utilize the annotation budget. This strategy reframes the labeling unit from entire images to localized regions, improving efficiency in complex medical image analysis tasks.

topic_metadata.title: Active Domain Adaptation and Sample Selection
topic_metadata.description: Active Domain Adaptation (ADA) augments domain adaptation by selectively querying and annotating informative target-domain samples to reduce the performance gap with fully supervised target training. It integrates active learning principles into DA, focusing on samples that are both uncertain and representative of the target distribution. This selection aims to maximize the benefit of limited annotation budget for adapting to the target domain.

topic_metadata.title: Image-wise versus Region-wise Active Domain Adaptation
topic_metadata.description: ADA methods in medical image analysis can operate at different granularities, namely image-wise and region-wise. Image-wise ADA selects entire images from the target domain for annotation, while region-wise ADA focuses on specific image regions or segments deemed most informative. This distinction structures how annotation effort is allocated and how fine-grained the adaptation process becomes.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.section_heading: THE NECESSITY AND CHALLENGE OF COMBINING DL AND AL
topic_metadata.title: Data hunger of DL vs AL’s limited labels
topic_metadata.description: Active Learning typically assumes that models are trained and updated with small labeled sets, whereas Deep Learning is highly data-intensive and requires large numbers of labeled examples. Classic AL settings provide too few labeled training samples to adequately train traditional DL models, and the common one-by-one query strategy is ill-suited to DL’s mini-batch training regime. This mismatch creates practical difficulties in directly coupling conventional AL loops with DL training.
topic_metadata.text_span: second bullet point under challenges, discussing “Insufficient data for labeled samples” and one-by-one querying

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.section_heading: THE NECESSITY AND CHALLENGE OF COMBINING DL AND AL
topic_metadata.title: Processing pipeline mismatch between AL and DL
topic_metadata.description: Most traditional Active Learning algorithms assume fixed feature representations and focus on training a classifier on top of them, with query strategies defined in this static feature space. Deep Learning, in contrast, jointly optimizes feature representations and classifier parameters, tightly coupling representation learning and prediction. Simply fine-tuning DL models within a classic AL loop, or treating feature learning and querying as separate problems, can lead to divergence and suboptimal behavior.
topic_metadata.text_span: third bullet point under challenges, discussing “Processing pipeline inconsistency” between AL and DL

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Pipeline inconsistency between AL and DL
topic_metadata.description: This topic describes a common 'split-and-splitting' approach where deep learning models are first trained via conventional supervised learning and only afterward combined with active learning for sample querying. Examples include systems that pretrain on session datasets, DBN-based AL-DL, ADN for sentiment classification, and CNN-based captcha recognition, all treating AL and DL as largely independent problems. The text argues that this processing pipeline inconsistency can cause divergence between AL and DL objectives and motivates the need for a unified, general DeepAL framework that tightly couples model training and querying.

topic_metadata.section_heading: Towards Active Learning with Better Generative Models
topic_metadata.title: GAN-based sample generation in AL
topic_metadata.description: Existing deep active learning work has mainly relied on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) as sample generators. GANs are used to synthesize additional training examples that can be queried or labeled, thereby enriching the pool of informative samples for model improvement. This establishes GANs as the dominant generative backbone in prior AL pipelines discussed in the survey.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening sentences: 'In §4.4, we summarize ... using GANs as sample generators.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Generative Networks for Data Augmentation
topic_metadata.description: To address insufficient labeled data in Deep Active Learning, generative models are used to synthesize additional training samples. These generative networks expand the input space coverage, aiming to improve model robustness and reduce labeling needs by providing diverse, label-efficient augmentations.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentence starting 'To solve the problem of insufficient labelled sample data, researchers have considered using generative networks for data augmentation [223]'.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Generative models for deep active querying
topic_metadata.description: In deep active learning, membership query synthesis can be implemented using generative models that produce informative synthetic instances. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are used for data augmentation by creating diverse, high-quality samples from the input space that are likely to yield useful labels. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) combined with Bayesian data augmentation can generate instances targeted to disagreement regions between multiple models, explicitly modeling the uncertainty of generated data. This allows the learning process to focus on contentious areas of the hypothesis space while accounting for the reliability of synthetic samples.
topic_metadata.text_span: Second paragraph, from 'In the context of deep active learning (Ren et al., 2022)...' through '...in the learning process.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Adversarial representation-based querying
topic_metadata.description: Adversarial learning representations in DAL leverage adversarial examples or adversarially trained feature spaces to guide query selection. The idea is that instances near adversarial decision boundaries reveal model weaknesses and thus are informative when labeled. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) or adversarial perturbation methods may be used to synthesize or identify such borderline samples. This integrates robustness considerations into the active learning loop.
topic_metadata.text_span: Line 'Adversarial learning representations' under 'Uncertainty-based'

topic_metadata.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Adversarial query generation methods
topic_metadata.description: AdvDeepFool, GAAL, and BGADL are adversarially-driven methods that generate or identify challenging samples for labeling in DAL. AdvDeepFool adapts adversarial perturbation techniques (like DeepFool) to locate points near decision boundaries, while GAAL uses GANs to synthesize informative queries. BGADL combines Bayesian modeling with adversarial data generation or selection to exploit both epistemic uncertainty and adversarial vulnerability. These methods exemplify the integration of adversarial learning into active querying.

topic_metadata.title: Generative adversarial query synthesis in DAL
topic_metadata.description: Generative Adversarial Active Learning (GAAL) uses GANs to synthesize query samples instead of selecting from an unlabeled pool, targeting images near the classifier’s decision boundary for annotation. However, such generated boundary samples can be semantically meaningless and hard even for humans to label. Bayesian Generative Active Deep Learning (BGADL) improves this by combining Bayesian acquisition functions (e.g., BALD) with a VAE-ACGAN generator that produces synthetic but informative samples to augment the labeled set.

topic_metadata.title: Data augmentation and adversarial sample generation
topic_metadata.description: Data augmentation within DAL expands the training set using transformed or generated samples, but naive augmentation may waste computation on uninformative data. AdvDeepFool augments training with adversarial examples crafted to be label-changing minimal perturbations, thus targeting informative boundary regions. BGADL uses ACGAN alongside Bayesian Data Augmentation to generate artificial samples that are as informative as those selected by active learning, integrating data synthesis tightly with the acquisition process.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Generative Adversarial Active Learning (GAAL)
topic_metadata.description: GAAL introduces Generative Adversarial Networks into active learning query strategies to synthesize new samples that are expected to be more informative than those in the original dataset. The goal is to use generative learning to augment data for the DL model, but the text notes that random data augmentation may fail to guarantee higher information content and can waste computational resources. GAAL is presented as the first such GAN-based AL query method, motivating more principled generative approaches.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section, discussion starting with 'At the same time, some researchers have considered using GAN...' and describing GAAL and its limitations.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Bayesian Generative Active Deep Learning (BGADL)
topic_metadata.description: BGADL extends GAAL by integrating Bayesian data augmentation, ACGAN, and VAE techniques to generate synthetic samples targeted at disagreement regions between classifiers. This Bayesian generative framework aims to create informative samples from different categories specifically in regions of model uncertainty, thereby improving AL efficiency over random augmentation. The approach combines generative adversarial active learning with probabilistic modeling to guide where and how new data are synthesized.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the section, paragraph beginning 'Accordingly, BGADL (Bayesian Generative Active Deep Learning)...' through the sentence describing combination of GAAL, Bayesian data augmentation, ACGAN, and VAE.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: DeepFool-based query strategy in DAL
topic_metadata.description: This topic focuses on using the DeepFool algorithm to generate adversarial perturbations and drive active learning queries. DeepFool iteratively finds minimal perturbations that change a model’s prediction, thereby approximating the distance from each sample to the decision boundary. In this setting, samples requiring only small adversarial perturbations are considered most uncertain and are prioritized for labeling. The approach operationalizes uncertainty sampling through explicit computation of minimal adversarial noise.
topic_metadata.text_span: description of Ducoffe and Precioso (2018) adopting DeepFool and selecting samples with small perturbations (middle of section)

topic_metadata.title: Adversarial attack-based active learning
topic_metadata.description: Adversarial attack-based DAL methods rank unlabeled samples by their distance to adversarial examples. AdvDeepFool uses DeepFool to compute the minimal perturbation rx required to change a sample’s predicted label and queries points with the smallest such perturbations, interpreting them as closest to the decision boundary. The same idea can be instantiated with other attacks like the Basic Iterative Method (AdvBIM).
topic_metadata.text_span: paragraph starting 'Inspired by recent advances in generating adversarial examples, some DAL methods utilize adversarial attacks...' including the definition of AdvDeepFool and mention of AdvBIM

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: DFAL: adversarial example-based querying
topic_metadata.description: DeepFool Active Learning (DFAL) argues that traditional uncertainty-based DeepAL methods are vulnerable to adversarial examples and instead focuses on samples near the decision boundary. By generating adversarial examples, DFAL exploits information about the input space distribution to approximate each sample’s distance to the decision boundary and uses this to guide queries. This adversarial query strategy accelerates CNN convergence but can reduce batch diversity, limiting how well the queried set reflects the overall data distribution.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph beginning with 'There are many DeepAL...' describing DFAL and its impact on convergence and diversity

topic_metadata.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Bayesian deep active learning
topic_metadata.description: Bayesian DAL uses Bayesian treatments of deep networks to quantify predictive uncertainty more robustly than simple softmax scores. It often relies on approximate Bayesian inference techniques such as Monte Carlo dropout or deep ensembles to estimate posterior distributions over model parameters. Acquisition functions can then target epistemic uncertainty, focusing on regions where the model lacks knowledge. This framework underpins methods like BALD for information-theoretic querying.
topic_metadata.text_span: Line 'Bayesian DAL' under 'Uncertainty-based'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.section_heading: THE NECESSITY AND CHALLENGE OF COMBINING DL AND AL
topic_metadata.title: Bayesian deep learning for DeepAL uncertainty
topic_metadata.description: To mitigate unreliable uncertainty estimates in Deep Learning when used within Active Learning, some works adopt Bayesian Deep Learning. These approaches model parameter or predictive uncertainty in a principled Bayesian manner, enabling more robust uncertainty-based querying for high-dimensional mini-batch samples with fewer labeling queries. This provides a partial solution to the first challenge identified for DeepAL.
topic_metadata.text_span: sentence beginning “To address the first problem, some researchers have applied Bayesian deep learning…”

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Deep Bayesian Active Learning (DBAL)
topic_metadata.description: Deep Bayesian Active Learning refers to active learning methods built on Bayesian convolutional neural networks. By modeling uncertainty through Bayesian treatments of deep network parameters, DBAL leverages posterior distributions to drive query selection. This provides a probabilistic foundation for acquisition functions such as mutual-information-based criteria.
topic_metadata.text_span: Third bullet in the list: '• Deep Bayesian Active Learning (DBAL). Active learning based on Bayesian convolutional neural network [70] is called deep Bayesian active learning.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: HDAL for face recognition
topic_metadata.description: HDAL (Heuristic Deep Active Learning) extends the CEAL-style framework to face recognition tasks by coupling a deep CNN with an active learning query strategy. It integrates feature learning and query model training in one loop, using the deep network both as a feature extractor and classifier while AL selects informative samples. This demonstrates the applicability of CEAL-like DeepAL architectures beyond generic image classification to specialized biometric recognition domains.
topic_metadata.text_span: sentence 'Moreover, HDAL (Heuristic Deep Active Learning) [132] uses a similar framework for face recognition tasks...' immediately following the CEAL description

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: DeepAL for verification codes and faces
topic_metadata.description: Active learning with convolutional neural networks is used to recognize verification codes by exploiting automatically obtained labeled data, thereby avoiding manual intervention and increasing recognition accuracy under limited annotation. HDAL introduces a heuristic deep active learning framework for face recognition, exploiting deep CNN feature extraction and labeling-cost savings from active sampling. These systems typically use model uncertainty or heuristic criteria to select informative samples for annotation, improving performance with fewer labeled examples.

topic_metadata.title: Novel taxonomy of AL and sampling strategies
topic_metadata.description: One contribution is a comprehensive survey accompanied by a novel taxonomy for active learning methods, especially in medical imaging. Beyond traditional focus on informativeness measures, the taxonomy explicitly covers additional sampling strategies such as diversity and class-balance, which aim to improve dataset representativeness and mitigate class imbalance during query selection. This structured view is intended to guide the design and comparison of deep AL methods.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Taxonomy of active learning sampling strategies
topic_metadata.description: The survey introduces a structured taxonomy of sampling strategies in AL, categorizing approaches into diversity sampling, class-balanced sampling, hybrid sampling, and learnable sampling. Diversity sampling focuses on reducing redundancy by selecting varied samples, while class-balanced sampling targets label distribution issues by enforcing or approximating balance across classes. Hybrid strategies integrate multiple criteria or metrics, and learnable strategies use neural networks to adaptively select informative samples, collectively providing a comprehensive framework for designing AL selection mechanisms.
topic_metadata.text_span: final sentences of section, starting 'As one of the contributions of this survey, we systematically summarize different sampling strategies in AL, including diversity sampling, class-balanced sampling, hybrid sampling, and learnable sampling.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Stationary versus drifting data streams
topic_metadata.description: This topic describes the distinction between stationary data streams, where the underlying data-generating distribution and its statistical properties remain stable, and drifting streams, where these properties change over time. It highlights that active learning strategies designed for stationary streams can perform suboptimally on drifting streams because concept drift may modify the scale of informativeness measures or necessitate model replacement and additional labeled observations. Accurately assessing whether a stream is stationary or drifting is thus critical for designing effective online active learning strategies and fully exploiting active learning benefits.
topic_metadata.text_span: Second paragraph, segment describing assumptions about the data stream distribution and the difference between stationary and drifting streams, including concept drift effects.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Assumptions on data stream dynamics
topic_metadata.description: The survey distinguishes active learning strategies by assumptions about the temporal behavior of data streams: stationary, drifting, and evolving. Stationary streams assume fixed data distribution, drifting streams model gradual or abrupt changes (concept drift), and evolving streams allow for structural evolution such as new concepts or classes. These assumptions drive different algorithmic requirements for model updating and query selection.

The process typically involves querying or obtaining labels for a subset of instances and immediately incorporating them into the model, enabling real-time adaptation. The assumption of stationarity allows the incremental model updates to remain valid over extended periods without major re-training.

topic_metadata.title: Model updating with immediate feedback
topic_metadata.description: Immediate access to true labels allows the active learning model to be promptly updated after each query. This enables the system to refine its decision boundary and to recommend exploration of new regions in the input space using the most up-to-date information. Such continual, online updating is presented as an optimization of the active learning routine for data streams.

topic_metadata.title: Stationary data stream classification approaches
topic_metadata.description: This topic covers methods for learning from data streams whose underlying distribution does not change significantly over time (stationary streams). The focus is on online classification tasks where a model continuously receives data but assumes long-term stability in the generative process. Such approaches can exploit stationarity to simplify model adaptation and reduce the need for complex drift detection mechanisms.

topic_metadata.description: This topic concerns data-stream scenarios where the underlying data distribution changes over time, requiring models that can continuously adapt to maintain high classification accuracy. It highlights the need for techniques that track distributional shifts and update decision boundaries or parameters accordingly in streaming environments.

topic_metadata.title: Online classification with stationary and drifting streams
topic_metadata.description: Existing research is reported to focus predominantly on online classification models for data streams. These models are designed to cope with both stationary environments and drifting data streams where the underlying concept may change over time. The emphasis has been on maintaining good predictive performance while updating models incrementally as new labeled examples are acquired.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Cost-sensitive querying and proactive learning
topic_metadata.description: Cost-sensitive querying incorporates annotation cost directly into selection criteria so that instances with high utility per unit cost are preferred, often operationalized as a return-on-investment (ROI) ratio. Variants include imposing per-instance cost caps and combining utility and cost ranks, with empirical evidence that ROI-based strategies can lower total annotation cost. In more realistic settings with multiple annotators of varying expertise and reliability, proactive learning jointly selects both the instance and the oracle, accounting for refusal and error rates and extending to specific tasks such as named entity recognition.
topic_metadata.text_span: §3.2.2 ('Given the goal of reducing actual cost, the querying strategies should also take it into consideration... return-on-investment (ROI)... dividing the original querying utility by cost measure... constraining maximal cost budget per instance and weighted rank combination... ROI can reduce total cost... multiple annotators with different expertise... annotators may refuse to answer or make mistakes... proactive learning to jointly select the optimal oracle and instance... extend proactive learning to NER tasks').

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing
topic_metadata.title: Cost-sensitive annotator and instance selection
topic_metadata.description: Cost-sensitive querying strategies in active learning can jointly select both which instances to label and which annotators to query, based on estimated annotator reliability. Additional mechanisms include collecting multiple labels per instance and consolidating them, as well as automatic crowd consolidation frameworks tailored to sequence labeling tasks. These methods explicitly model noise and cost trade-offs in crowd-based active learning.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Scope and contributions of the survey
topic_metadata.description: The survey aims to comprehensively review recent query strategies for online active learning over data streams, analyzing their strengths and limitations. It also covers evaluation strategies for such algorithms, highlights real-world application domains, and identifies open challenges and future research opportunities. The focus is explicitly on the core problem of selecting the most informative data points to label in an online streaming context.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Gap in online active regression research
topic_metadata.description: The authors highlight a comparative lack of work on online active linear regression and online regression models in general. While classification in streaming settings has been extensively studied, regression-oriented active learning for streams remains underdeveloped. This gap motivates calls for methods that can handle continuous targets in dynamic environments.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Streaming AL for classification tasks
topic_metadata.description: Classification is a primary task for online active learning in data streams, appearing under stationary, drifting, and evolving scenarios. Methods are grouped by whether they maintain a single classifier or an ensemble while actively querying labels, reflecting different strategies for robustness and adaptability to changing distributions. The extensive reference lists under these rows indicate that classification is the most heavily studied task in streaming active learning.

topic_metadata.title: Regression in streaming active learning
topic_metadata.description: Regression tasks in online active learning are treated primarily with single-model approaches for both stationary and evolving data streams. These methods focus on selectively querying continuous-valued labels while the underlying functional relationship may remain stable or gradually evolve. The relatively small set of cited works highlights that regression is less explored than classification in the streaming AL context.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online learning tasks and paradigms
topic_metadata.description: The surveyed active learning strategies are applied across several online learning formulations. These include online classification, where class labels are predicted for streaming instances; online regression, where continuous targets are modeled; and online semi-supervised learning, which leverages both labeled and unlabeled streaming data. The topic covers how active querying is adapted to different predictive tasks in a streaming context.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Data Expansion Strategies for Labeled Sets in DeepAL
topic_metadata.description: DeepAL must reconcile AL’s small labeled set assumption with DL’s need for large labeled datasets, motivating strategies that expand effective training data without proportional manual labeling cost. The text criticizes methods that only train on explicitly labeled samples, overlooking the utility of unlabeled data. It emphasizes the importance of data expansion and training strategies that exploit unlabeled sets to mitigate label scarcity in DeepAL.
topic_metadata.text_span: Subsection '3.2 Data Expansion of Labeled Samples in DeepAL', from 'AL often requires only a small amount of labeled sample data...' through 'Therefore, the study of these strategies is also quite meaningful.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Data expansion for scarce labels
topic_metadata.description: When labeled data are insufficient, DeepAL can be supported by techniques that expand the effective labeled set, such as augmentation, pseudo-labeling, or other label-efficient strategies. Table 1 groups such work under 'Data expansion of labeled samples' as a response to the challenge of insufficient labeled samples. These methods aim to increase model performance without proportionally increasing annotation cost.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Labeled Sample Data Expansion Techniques
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses methods that effectively expand the labeled dataset in deep active learning beyond direct human annotation. It involves data augmentation, semi-supervised learning, pseudo-labeling, or generative approaches that synthesize or infer labels to increase training data diversity and volume. The goal is to amplify the benefit of each queried label while maintaining label quality and improving model performance.
topic_metadata.text_span: summary paragraph, second sentence (phrase: 'labeled sample data expansion')

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Cost-Effective Active Learning (CEAL)
topic_metadata.description: CEAL integrates pseudo-labeling with uncertainty-based active learning to balance label quality and annotation cost. The method forwards the most uncertain unlabeled samples to human experts for annotation while assigning pseudo-labels only to samples for which the model is highly confident. This selective strategy aims to reduce labeling cost while limiting noise from incorrect pseudo-labels, and has inspired many subsequent works in medical imaging.
topic_metadata.text_span: Sentences introducing CEAL and its sample routing strategy (around 'To mitigate this, Wang et al. (2017) proposed cost-effective active learning (CEAL)...')

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: CEAL Pseudo-Labeling for Cost-Effective DeepAL
topic_metadata.description: CEAL (Cost-Effective Active Learning) augments the training set by combining oracle-labeled uncertain samples with pseudo-labeled high-confidence samples. An initialized CNN is fed unlabeled data and outputs a small set of uncertain instances for manual labeling and a large set of high-confidence predictions to which pseudo-labels are automatically assigned. Both types of samples are then used to fine-tune the CNN iteratively, expanding the effective labeled data without increasing annotation cost proportionally.
topic_metadata.text_span: Description around Fig. 5 starting 'Fig. 5. In CEAL [229], the overall framework of DeepAL is utilized...' through 'These two types of samples are then used to fine-tune the CNN, and the updated process is repeated.'

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: CEAL framework with pseudo-labeling
topic_metadata.description: The CEAL framework integrates deep convolutional neural networks with active learning for image classification by jointly leveraging uncertain and high-confidence unlabeled samples. At each iteration, unlabeled data are passed through a CNN, producing a small set of uncertain samples sent to a human oracle and a large set of high-confidence samples that receive pseudo-labels from the model. Both human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data are then used to fine-tune the CNN iteratively, forming a closed-loop DeepAL process that efficiently expands the labeled set.
topic_metadata.text_span: paragraph starting 'CEAL [229] is one of the first works to combine AL and DL' through the detailed description of uncertain and high-confidence samples and iterative fine-tuning

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: CEAL: pseudo-labeling with uncertainty queries
topic_metadata.description: CEAL addresses high labeling costs by assigning pseudo-labels to high-confidence unlabeled samples and adding them to the training set, alongside highly uncertain samples selected via an uncertainty-based AL strategy. This dual use of confident and uncertain examples expands the training data without fully relying on manual annotations. The approach targets efficient DeepAL-based image classification.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph starting 'To solve this problem, CEAL [229] assigns pseudo-labels to samples with high confidence...'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online active learning for streams
topic_metadata.description: Online active learning addresses scenarios where data arrives as a continuous stream and instances cannot be stored in a pool for greedy selection. The learner must decide immediately, for each incoming instance, whether to request its label, similar to the sequential decision structure of the secretary problem. This setting is crucial when real-time sampling decisions are required and latency or storage constraints prohibit batch-based active learning.
topic_metadata.text_span: Paragraph beginning 'In this type of active learning, we cannot greedily select...' through the secretary problem analogy and real-world applications sentence.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online active learning for drifting streams
topic_metadata.description: This topic describes a generic online active learning loop that operates over a data stream under a labeling budget. At each timestamp, a sampling strategy decides whether to query the label of the incoming instance, incurring labeling cost and updating both a classifier and a drift detector. The process is constrained by a global budget and stream length, and includes mechanisms to manage classifier updates continuously as labeled data arrive.
topic_metadata.text_span: Algorithm 3 block at the beginning of the section (from 'Algorithm 3 Online active learning with drifting data streams' down to 't ←t + 1 / end while')

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online active learning for data streams
topic_metadata.description: Online active learning is applied in settings where data arrives at high velocity, labels are expensive, and it is infeasible to store all unlabeled instances prior to selection. The process involves making labeling decisions on-the-fly, querying only the most informative observations to update the model. It is particularly suited to dynamic, evolving environments where models must adapt in real time to new data distributions.
topic_metadata.text_span: Opening paragraph of section 5.1 (description of high-velocity streams, expensive labeling, and dynamic environments).

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Online active learning under distribution shift
topic_metadata.description: This topic calls for online active learning strategies capable of handling a wide variety of distribution shifts in data streams. The goal is to design query and labeling policies that remain effective when underlying data distributions change in different ways, as categorized earlier in the survey (Sect. 3.2). Such methods must detect and adapt to shifting conditions while still judiciously selecting data points for labeling.
topic_metadata.text_span: sentence 'Moreover, it could be beneficial to develop online active learning strategies that are able to tackle all the types of distribution shifts introduced in Sect.3.2.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Practical challenges in active learning
topic_metadata.description: The text highlights that the survey also addresses practical challenges of active learning, such as implementation issues, computational constraints, and interaction with human annotators. topic_metadata.description: Pool-based active learning operates on a closed, static pool of unlabeled data, aiming to select the most informative subset of instances for labeling. It is predominantly used for classification tasks, notably image classification, where manual labeling is costly. Sampling schemes are typically iterative and governed by a parameter k, the number of unlabeled instances queried per round, with k often set to one for traditional models that are relatively cheap to retrain. This framework structures the query process around batch selection from the pool to optimize label efficiency under computational and annotation constraints.

At each iteration, a batch of unlabeled instances is selected via an acquisition function α(x, M) applied to a current model M, labels for these instances are queried from an oracle, and the labeled/unlabeled sets are updated before retraining M. The process continues until a labeling budget is exhausted or a target performance level is reached, and is described for classification tasks but extends to other domains like image segmentation.

topic_metadata.description: Deep active learning (DeepAL) initializes or pre-trains the deep model parameters θ on an initial labeled dataset L₀, then uses the model to extract features from an unlabeled pool U. A query strategy selects informative samples from U, which are labeled and added to an expanded labeled set L, while U is updated to remove queried instances. The deep model is retrained on the evolving L, and this process iterates until the label budget or predefined termination criteria are reached.

This cycle repeats until a label budget is exhausted or stopping criteria are met. topic_metadata.title: Entropy as an active learning acquisition function
topic_metadata.description: Entropy quantifies the randomness or disorder in a probability distribution and is used to measure predictive uncertainty in active learning. Given a model’s predicted class probabilities for a data point, higher entropy indicates greater uncertainty about the correct class label. Acquisition strategies that select examples with maximal entropy prioritize points where the model is most unsure, aiming to improve decision boundaries efficiently. Entropy thus serves as a principled scalar metric derived from the model’s output distribution.

topic_metadata.title: BALD acquisition strategy in DAL
topic_metadata.description: Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreements (BALD) defines an acquisition function that selects data points expected to maximize information gained about the model parameters ω. In deep active learning, this means querying samples that are most informative with respect to the posterior over parameters, rather than merely uncertain predictions. The criterion explicitly links the selection of new data to improving knowledge of the model itself. This approach is formalized as α_BALD(x, M), which is computed for each candidate input x and model M.
topic_metadata.text_span: Entire section text describing BALD and its objective

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: BALD-based naive batch construction
topic_metadata.description: A naive BMDAL approach repeatedly applies a one-by-one acquisition rule, such as BALD (Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement), to select the top-K highest-scoring samples. The BALD acquisition function sums mutual information terms I(yᵢ; ω | xᵢ, D_train) over batch elements, where mutual information is defined as predictive entropy minus expected conditional entropy over model parameters. Here, ω ∼ P(ω | D_train) represents Bayesian model parameters, H(·) is predictive entropy, and E[H(·)] averages entropy under the posterior. This approach treats each sample independently when forming the batch.

The conclusion emphasizes this economic and practical motivation as a core driver for adopting deep active learning in the medical imaging domain.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Fundamentals and objectives of active learning
topic_metadata.description: Active learning is introduced as query learning that studies how to achieve maximal model performance gains while labeling as few samples as possible. It assumes samples differ in their value for updating the model and focuses on selecting the most informative instances from an unlabeled pool for annotation by an oracle (e.g., human annotator). The core objective is to reduce annotation cost while maintaining or improving model performance.

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Active learning as cost-efficient labeling
topic_metadata.description: Active learning is presented as a strategy to select the most informative observations for labeling, thereby reducing the amount of labeled data needed for training. Query strategies aim to balance labeling cost against model quality by choosing which data points to annotate. This selective labeling streamlines the learning process and improves efficiency by focusing annotation efforts where they most improve model performance.

In this paradigm, the model assists experts during annotation (e.g., by proposing segmentations that are then corrected), thereby reducing annotation difficulty and cost. This approach tailors the active learning loop to pixel/region-level labeling tasks and is further detailed elsewhere in the survey.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Active Learning for Interactive Segmentation
topic_metadata.description: Interactive segmentation allows clinicians to refine automatic medical image segmentations in real time using user inputs such as clicks, bounding boxes, and scribbles, addressing errors from domain shifts or unseen regions of interest. Active learning is proposed to guide where annotations should be placed, instead of allowing completely free annotation locations, to make the interaction more efficient. By having the model suggest the most informative regions for user input, annotation cost can be further reduced while improving model adaptation to current clinical cases.

topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-based Query Strategies
topic_metadata.description: This topic covers methods that select informative samples based on model uncertainty estimates in deep active learning. It includes gradient-based uncertainty, performance estimation techniques, uncertainty-aware model architectures, and adversarial-based uncertainty measures. These approaches typically rely on model outputs, gradients, or adversarial perturbations to quantify how unsure the model is about each unlabeled instance and prioritize them for annotation.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-based query strategies
topic_metadata.description: Multiple works characterize informativeness by model uncertainty, using single-model scores such as entropy, margin, and least confidence, or gradient-based uncertainty derived from network gradients. Some methods extend this with adversarial samples to probe decision boundaries or with multiple inferences to measure data disagreement via inequality-based metrics. Other works frame uncertainty as performance estimation, learning surrogate or directly learnable estimators (e.g., using Dice) to predict per-sample segmentation quality. These uncertainty scores drive which instances are selected for annotation in each active learning round.

topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-based querying strategies
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty-based querying strategies select samples for annotation where the current deep model is least confident in its predictions. These methods estimate predictive uncertainty using model outputs or internal representations, assuming that labeling such ambiguous instances will most improve the model. They are central in deep active learning because they directly target the model’s decision boundaries. Typical implementations rely on probability distributions over classes or Bayesian uncertainty estimates.

topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-based query strategies
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty-based approaches select unlabeled samples for which the current model is most uncertain, under the assumption that labeling these samples yields the greatest information gain. Typical uncertainty measures include prediction entropy, margin, or confidence scores. While effective, pure uncertainty sampling can introduce sampling bias because selected samples may not represent the overall data distribution.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-based sampling with margin and entropy
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty-based query strategies select samples that the current model finds most uncertain, and are especially common in shallow models such as SVMs and KNN. Margin sampling defines uncertainty via the difference between the highest and second-highest predicted class probabilities, with smaller margins indicating more uncertain samples, and selects the top-K smallest margins. Entropy-based sampling measures uncertainty using the Shannon entropy of the predictive class distribution and selects samples with the highest entropy, with both approaches forming standard baselines for batch construction.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty and diversity query strategies
topic_metadata.description: Deep active learning is currently centered on query strategies that explicitly or implicitly combine uncertainty-based and diversity-based sample selection. Uncertainty measures how unsure the model is about a sample's label, while diversity aims to cover varied regions of the input space to avoid redundancy. Hybrid selection strategies that jointly consider both criteria are increasingly favored by researchers as they better balance informativeness and coverage.

By querying labels for these uncertain examples, the model is expected to learn decision boundaries more efficiently.

topic_metadata.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Hybrid uncertainty–diversity querying
topic_metadata.description: Hybrid or combined strategies explicitly balance uncertainty and diversity to select informative yet non-redundant samples. They typically construct a joint acquisition function or a two-stage procedure: first filtering by uncertainty and then refining by diversity (or vice versa). This helps avoid pathological selections where many similar uncertain samples are chosen. The goal is to maximize expected information gain under a labeling budget.

topic_metadata.title: Hybrid uncertainty-diversity query strategies
topic_metadata.description: Hybrid query strategies combine uncertainty and diversity criteria to leverage the strengths of both while mitigating their weaknesses. They attempt to balance selecting highly uncertain samples with maintaining representativeness of the unlabeled data distribution. This design addresses issues such as sampling bias from pure uncertainty sampling and unnecessary labeling of low-information samples from pure diversity sampling.

topic_metadata.article_title: A survey of deep active learning
topic_metadata.title: Uncertainty-based and hybrid query strategies
topic_metadata.description: Uncertainty-based strategies rank unlabeled samples by model uncertainty and preferentially query the most uncertain ones, assuming these will most improve the model. However, focusing solely on uncertainty can ignore relationships among samples, such as diversity or representativeness. Hybrid strategies incorporate multiple attributes—e.g., uncertainty plus diversity or density—to better balance informativeness and coverage of the data space. This reflects a move from single-criterion to multi-criterion query design in DeepAL.

topic_metadata.title: Pseudo-labeling for AL–SSL integration
topic_metadata.description: Pseudo-labeling is identified as one perspective for integrating active learning and semi-supervised learning. In such approaches, the model assigns tentative labels to unlabeled medical images, which are then used as additional training targets alongside truly labeled data. Active learning can govern which samples receive true labels versus pseudo-labels, balancing reliability and coverage. This mechanism enables the exploitation of large unlabeled pools without fully relying on expert annotation.

topic_metadata.title: Pseudo-labeling in semi-supervised learning
topic_metadata.description: Pseudo-labeling uses a model’s own predictions on unlabeled data as surrogate labels and combines them with labeled data for supervised training. This approach can leverage large unlabeled datasets but risks introducing noisy labels when predictions are unreliable. The method is a foundational strategy in semi-supervised learning pipelines and underpins several deep active learning extensions discussed in this section.

topic_metadata.description: Pseudo-labeling assigns provisional labels to unlabeled samples using the current model, treating confident predictions as additional training data. In an active learning context, pseudo-labels can be combined with human-annotated data to improve representation learning while focusing expensive queries on truly uncertain cases. This reduces the effective labeling cost while still leveraging the large pool of unlabeled images.

topic_metadata.title: Semi-supervised learning with unlabeled data
topic_metadata.description: Semi-supervised learning aims to improve model performance by leveraging large quantities of unlabeled data alongside a smaller labeled set. In this context, it is positioned as an extension of supervised deep learning, where unlabeled medical images help regularize and guide the model beyond what purely labeled data could achieve. The approach is particularly relevant when annotation is costly and limited, as in medical imaging. It serves as a foundational concept for later integration with active learning.

topic_metadata.description: Unlabeled images undergo weak augmentation to generate predictions that are treated as pseudo-labels. Strongly augmented versions of the same images are then trained to match these pseudo-labels, enforcing consistency between weak and strong augmentations. This semi-supervised scheme exploits abundant unlabeled data while maintaining label efficiency.

topic_metadata.description: Active learning and semi-supervised learning are described as complementary strategies for reducing human annotation effort in medical image analysis. Active learning focuses on querying the most informative samples for labeling, while semi-supervised learning exploits the remaining unlabeled samples to further improve performance. Their combination is motivated by the desire to reduce tedious expert annotations from doctors. This complementarity underpins the proposed integrated training frameworks.

topic_metadata.title: Link between active and semi-supervised learning
topic_metadata.description: This topic addresses the relationship between active learning, which selectively queries labels, and semi-supervised learning, which exploits large amounts of unlabeled data alongside a few labeled examples. In streaming contexts, both paradigms interact: unlabeled stream instances can be used for semi-supervised updates while a subset is actively labeled to refine the model. Understanding this connection helps design hybrid methods that better use limited labeling resources.
topic_metadata.text_span: Middle of the paragraph: '...and the connection between active learning and semi-supervised learning.'

topic_metadata.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey
topic_metadata.title: Relationship between active and semi-supervised learning
topic_metadata.description: Active learning is framed as a special case of semi-supervised learning, where a learner not only exploits unlabeled data but also actively selects which instances to query for labels. Semi-supervised techniques on data streams, such as those surveyed by Kulkarni et al. (2016), focus on leveraging unlabeled instances for classification but do not answer the core active learning question of when to query. Combining semi-supervised methods with active learning can improve data selection strategies, model updating, and retraining under limited labeled data, yielding more efficient learning than either approach alone.
